body:
An AI assistant on your system sends something to an AI provider every time someone asks a question. Whether that is safe depends on exactly what is sent, so start there, and get the vendor's answer in writing.

## What is sent with each question?

There are three designs, and they send very different amounts:

| Design | What goes to the AI provider | Ahrom Labs' assistants |
|---|---|---|
| The model only chooses | The question, and the one before it for follow-ups | Atelier AI and Ohm AI by default; Ember AI for how-to answers (the question and the help-guide sections picked) |
| The model writes the answer | The question and the rows of the answer | Atelier AI when a person picks a voice for it; Ohm AI in its "write" answer mode; Ember AI's live-data answers, built and switched off at the client |
| The model reads your records | Documents or tables, loaded so it can "understand the business" | None |

In the first design the ledger never leaves: the model picks a look-up and a period, and your own system runs it and builds the table. [How it works](/ai-assistant/how-it-works) explains the design. The second design sends a few rows per answer: not the database, but your data, so you should be able to switch it off. The third sends the most: ask what, how often, and where it is kept.

Ember AI's live-data answers are switched on only when the client's approver is recorded by name in Settings, because in that mode the rows of each answer go to the writing model. On the public demo they are on, with a sample company.

## Can the assistant change anything?

It shouldn't be able to. Look-ups should be read-only queries, so the worst a wrong choice can do is show the wrong table. "Remind me to call them on Friday" should draft a task that a person saves. Ask it to mark an invoice paid or delete an order, and check nothing changed: test 6 of the [vendor test](/ai-assistant/vendor-test#read-only).

## Can a junior staff member ask what they can't see?

Only if the assistant ignores the screens' rules. Each look-up should run as the signed-in person, with the same limits as the screens:

- **Atelier AI:** staff see only their own tasks and cash entries; payroll, advances and bank statements are refused to them.
- **Ohm AI:** answers LS Technologies' own staff, never the partner store's logins or customers; its settings are for the admin.
- **Ember AI:** answers each person from the guides of their own departments, and each live-data look-up follows the same department limits as the screens.

Test it with a junior login.

## Whose account does it run on, and what does it cost?

The business's own. Ahrom Labs' assistants use the client's own key with the AI provider (OpenRouter), set in the system's Settings, so the client pays the provider directly and can switch it off at any time. A daily question limit caps the cost: at LS Technologies it is about a hundredth of a rupee per question. Ask a vendor whose key it is, what the limit is, and what happens when the credit runs out.

## What happens when the AI provider is down?

The screens carry on as before, and the assistant should get simpler, not wrong. In Savistar's system a keyword router takes over, so answers get less clever but the figures still come from the same look-ups.

## What does India's DPDP Act ask of the business?

If the assistant handles personal data (names and details of staff, customers or contacts), the business is the Data Fiduciary and the AI provider is its Data Processor. The duties stay with the business:

| Duty | Where it is | Starts |
|---|---|---|
| Reasonable security safeguards, including at the processor | Act section 8(5); rule 6 | May 2027 |
| A valid contract with the processor, with safeguards in it | Act section 8(2); rule 6(1)(f) | May 2027 |
| Breach notice to the Data Protection Board and each person affected, without delay, then a detailed report to the Board within 72 hours | Act section 8(6); rule 7 | May 2027 |
| Erase the data when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is served, and cause the processor to erase it | Act section 8(7) | With the rule on retention, rule 8: May 2027 |
| Transfer outside India allowed, subject to requirements the Government may set | Act section 16; rule 15 | May 2027 |

"May 2027" is rule 1(4): the rules that set out these duties come into force eighteen months after the Rules were published on 13 November 2025. Rules on the Data Protection Board itself are already in force. The Act's own sections are brought into force by separate notification, so check which are in force on the date you sign.

What it means for an assistant, in practice:

- **Know where the model runs.** A provider like OpenRouter routes to models run outside India. That is allowed under rule 15, but you should know which countries, and that the contract covers it.
- **Send only what the answer needs.** The question-only design sends no personal data unless the question itself contains some.
- **Put it in the contract.** Safeguards, breach notice to you, and erasure at the provider, as rule 6(1)(f) and section 8(7) expect.

How the Act applies to your business is a question for your lawyer. The same rules, for the system underneath, are in the [ERP compliance guide](/erp/compliance).

## What applies in the US?

The US has no single federal law for the personal data a business keeps. Instead:

- **State privacy laws.** A growing number of states have their own, California's CCPA the best known. They mostly reach larger businesses and those that buy or sell personal data, and they give people rights to know, delete and opt out.
- **The FTC.** The Federal Trade Commission can act against a business whose data practices are unfair or deceptive, including security that falls short of what it promised.
- **Your contracts.** Customers and insurers often ask for security terms of their own.

The practice is the same as in India: know where the model runs, send only what the answer needs, and put safeguards, breach notice and deletion at the provider in the contract. Which laws reach your business is a question for your lawyer.

title: How an AI assistant answers without inventing numbers
answer: The design that keeps figures right has four parts: a small AI model only chooses which question is being asked; code runs a fixed, read-only look-up with the same maths as the app's screens; any written sentence with a number that isn't in the result is dropped; and questions the data can't answer get a plain "the data doesn't have that". The model never produces a figure.
description: How the design works, for buyers: the model picks the question, code runs a fixed look-up, and sentences with numbers not in the data are dropped.

image.alt: A wooden pigeonhole rack with one card in a single slot.

body:
Most AI assistants on business data let the model produce the answer's figures, either by writing a database query ([text-to-SQL](/systems/text-to-sql)) or by reading rows and summarising them. Both work most of the time, and that is the problem: an owner can't tell the answer that is right from the one that is nearly right (an [AI hallucination](/systems/ai-hallucination)). The design below takes the figures away from the model altogether. It is how [Atelier AI, Ohm AI and Ember AI](/ai-assistant/questions) work.

## What does the AI model actually do?

It only chooses. A small AI model reads the question and picks from fixed options: what kind of question it is (a figure, how to do something, a reminder, small talk, something the data can't answer), which look-up fits, which period, and whether it follows on from the last question. It returns a choice, not text. Names in the question (a client, an item, a reel number) are matched to real records by code; when two records could match, Ohm AI, for one, asks which one is meant.

## Where do the numbers come from?

From code running a fixed look-up, not from the model. Each question type has a [fixed look-up](/systems/fixed-look-up): a read-only query written in advance, with only the values filled in. It uses the same maths as the app's own screens, so "who owes us money?" counts the same invoices, the same way, as the unpaid-invoices screen. The answer is shown as a table, with a link to that screen.

Because the look-ups only read, the assistant can't change anything. "Remind me to call them on Friday" drafts a task that is saved only when the person presses Save.

## How are invented numbers kept out of the answer?

Every number in the words is checked against the table. A sentence above the table is optional, in the voice the person picked. Before it is shown, a [grounding check](/systems/grounding-check) compares every number in it with the table. If any number isn't there, such as a total the writer added up, a percentage it worked out or a figure it rounded, the sentence is dropped and only the table is shown. You can run the same check on any assistant with the [number check](/ai-assistant/number-check).

## What happens when it can't answer?

It says so plainly. Advice ("should we raise prices?") and data the system doesn't hold get a plain "the data doesn't have that", with questions it can answer instead. Every question it couldn't answer, and every thumbs-down, is listed for the owner, so the next look-up to add comes from what people actually asked.

## How is it tested?

Each assistant has its own set of real questions, run through the real pipeline before it goes live: plain English, fragments, typos and Hinglish. Atelier AI routed 55 of 55 test questions and 57 unseen real phrasings correctly. The questions each assistant answers are in the [question library](/ai-assistant/questions).

## What does it cost to run?

Very little, because the model only makes a choice. At LS Technologies it is about a hundredth of a rupee per question, on the client's own AI account, with a daily question limit. What is sent to the AI provider is set out in [what leaves your server](/ai-assistant/data-safety).

## What doesn't it do?

It doesn't answer questions nobody built a look-up for, and it doesn't search documents. Questions over drawings, certificates and past decisions are a different design, [retrieval and knowledge graphs](/services/rag-knowledge-graphs), where each answer shows the document it came from. The full engineering note is [an assistant that only answers from your own records](/notes/assistant-that-answers-from-your-ledger).

title: AI assistant for manufacturers: where to start
answer: For a manufacturer, start with how-to questions answered from the system's own help guide, for each person's departments, and add live-data questions (stock, purchase orders, approvals) once the owner has decided what may be sent to the AI provider. That is where Ember AI stands at a boiler manufacturer: how-to answers live, live data built and switched off.
description: An AI assistant for a manufacturing ERP: start with how-to answers from your own help guide, then stock, purchase and approval questions, and how to check it.

image.alt: A round steel pressure gauge on a short pipe stub.

body:
A manufacturing system has many departments and many screens, and most questions on the shop floor and in the office are "how do I". That is the safest place for an assistant to start: the answers come from the system's own help guide, and no business data leaves.

## Where should a manufacturer's AI assistant start?

With how-to answers from the company's own help guide. The assistant picks the right section of the help guide for the question, from the departments the person works in, and answers from it with a link to the screen. Questions like:

- How do I raise a purchase request?
- How do I send a packing list for approval before dispatch?
- How do I assign test certificates to units?
- Where do I change my password?

Unrelated questions ("write me a poem") should get a fixed reply that never reaches a writing model. Each person gets a daily question limit set per department.

## When should it answer from live data?

When the owner decides who may see what. Stock on hand, items below minimum, purchase orders not received, an order's value and payments, approvals waiting. These need a decision first: in a design where the rows are worded by a writing model, the rows of each answer are sent to the AI provider. The owner should approve that by name, and each look-up should follow the same department limits as the screens. The [data safety guide](/ai-assistant/data-safety) sets out what to ask.

## How does Ember AI do it?

Ember AI is the assistant in a boiler manufacturer's system, open to staff. How-to answers are live; the live-data look-ups are built and switched off until the client records its approval. Job-card and work-in-progress questions are not built yet. On the [boiler demo](https://boiler-erp.ahromlabs.com/demo), with a sample company, live data is on: anyone can ask it two questions. Every question it handles is listed below.

## How do I check a vendor's assistant?

Ask ten how-to questions from your own process and follow the answers: do the steps work? Then run the [vendor test](/ai-assistant/vendor-test). For the system itself, see the [ERP guide for small manufacturers](/erp/small-manufacturers).

title: ASME vs IBR 2026: how the two boiler codes fit together
question: Does IBR accept ASME boilers and materials?
answer: In India a boiler is registered under the Indian Boiler Regulations, 2026, whatever code it was designed to. IBR 2026 does accept ASME in defined ways: ASME materials, ASME welding consumables and NDT certificates, ASME-designed parts where IBR has no provision, and inspection of export boilers to a foreign code with a Form I Part A certificate.

body:
## How do ASME and IBR 2026 compare?

ASME is a private standard given legal force by the US states and Canadian provinces that adopt it; IBR 2026 is
India's statutory regulation for boilers, under the Boilers Act, 2025. They overlap on the same boilers but differ in
who approves, inspects and records:

| | ASME BPVC | IBR 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A private standard, given legal force by US states and Canadian provinces that adopt it | Statutory regulations under the Boilers Act, 2025, in force across India |
| Written by | ASME committees | The Central Boilers Board |
| Covers | Boilers, pressure vessels, nuclear, transport tanks | Boilers, steam pipes and their parts (pressure vessels are outside IBR) |
| Shop approval | ASME certificate, after a joint review ([U and S stamps](/asme/u-stamp)) | Recognition as a manufacturer by class, under IBR 2026 |
| Independent inspection | [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) from an accredited agency | Inspecting Authority, Competent Person |
| Record of the item | [Manufacturer's Data Report](/asme/data-reports) (P-2, P-3, U-1) | Forms: Inspecting Authority's certificate (Form I), maker's certificate (Form IV), material certificates (Form V) |
| Welders | Section IX qualification ([WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq)) | IBR welder certificate |
| In service | NBIC and the jurisdiction ([state rules](/asme/state-boiler-laws)) | IBR registration, periodic inspection and certificate for use |

## Does IBR accept ASME boilers and materials?

Yes, in defined ways, all quoted from the Gazette:

- **Parts IBR doesn't cover** may be designed, made, inspected and certified to the ASME Code (among others), with the Inspecting Authority's permission (regulation 3(4)).
- **Exotic tubes** (titanium and the like) may be approved to ASME and other international codes (regulation 3(5)).
- **Export boilers** may be inspected by an Indian Inspecting Authority to a foreign code and certified in Form I Part A (regulation 4). See [buying from India](/asme/buying-from-india) and [IBR Form I Part A](/ibr/forms#form-i-part-a).
- **Exemption** of a boiler or component built to an international code, ASME included, on conditions (regulation 5).
- **Materials** to ASME (and IS, BS, EN, DIN, JIS) may be used; IBR's own material table lists ASME SA and SB specifications by name (regulation 30); the [materials list](/asme/items) shows which common ones it names. See [Section II](/asme/section-ii).
- **Electrodes** are classified to ASME Section II Part C (SFA) or AWS specifications (regulation 71).
- **NDT personnel** with ASNT certificates are accepted alongside ISNT (regulation 7). See [Section V](/asme/section-v).

## Is an ASME-stamped boiler legal to run in India?

Only once it is registered under IBR 2026: in India a boiler is registered under the Indian Boiler Regulations
whatever code it was designed to. An ASME stamp doesn't replace IBR registration, and the regulation 5 exemption for
boilers built to an international code applies only on its conditions. See
[boiler registration documents](/ibr/registration-documents).

## Are pressure vessels covered by IBR?

No. IBR applies to boilers and steam pipes; unfired pressure vessels are outside it (vessels for compressed gases fall
under PESO's Static and Mobile Pressure Vessels (Unfired) Rules instead). In the US, by contrast, a pressure vessel is
usually regulated by the state and built to [Section VIII](/asme/section-viii).

## Who inspects a boiler under each?

Under ASME, an [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) employed by an ASME-accredited inspection agency;
under IBR 2026, the Inspecting Authority and Competent Persons it recognizes. A boiler built in India for export to the
US can have both: the Authorized Inspector for the ASME stamp and the Indian Inspecting Authority's Form I Part A under
regulation 4.

## Does an IBR welder certificate count for ASME work?

No: ASME work needs a Section IX qualification ([WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq)), and IBR boiler work needs an IBR welder
certificate. A welder working on both needs both, and each has its own renewal rules; see
[welder continuity](/asme/welder-continuity) for the ASME side.

## What does a shop working to both codes need?

Two sets of approvals, two sets of welder qualifications and two report formats over the same welds and materials. The
records underneath are the same: [heat numbers](/asme/mtr), welders, procedures, NDE, tests. That is the case for
keeping them once and printing either set of forms. Our boiler software does this both ways: the India build, which a
boiler maker runs today, assembles the IBR statutory folder from the certificate bank (see
[the IBR statutory folder](/notes/ibr-statutory-folder-from-bom)), and the US demo prints the ASME record package. The
IBR side is covered in the [IBR 2026 guide](/ibr).

body:
## What does an ASME Authorized Inspector do?

An Authorized Inspector (AI) independently checks that a Code boiler, vessel or part was built to the Code, then
certifies the data report so the item can be stamped. They review the design, check materials and welding, review
NDE and heat treatment, witness the pressure test and sign the [data report](/asme/data-reports). ASME's handbook
says that for most certificates "an agreement with an ASME Accredited Authorized Inspection Agency (AIA) is
required", which is why there is an Inspector on nearly every stamped job.

## Who employs the Authorized Inspector?

An Authorized Inspection Agency (AIA) accredited by ASME. ASME's [accreditation page](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/Authorized-Inspection-Agency-Accreditation) says an AIA is an
organization that meets the criteria of ASME's QAI-1 standard, "Qualifications for Authorized Inspection", and that
AIAs are responsible for inspections of ASME pressure equipment during manufacture. Most are insurance companies
that write boiler and machinery cover; some are state or provincial jurisdictions acting as their own agency. ASME
publishes the list of accredited agencies with its downloadable resources.

## What commission does an Authorized Inspector hold?

The National Board Authorized Inspector Commission (AI). The National Board's [commissioned inspectors page](https://www.nationalboard.org/Index.aspx?pageID=392)
describes two commissions: the AI, for inspections required by the ASME Code during construction, and the Inservice
Inspector Commission (IS), for periodic inspections of equipment in operation. Each is earned by meeting the
education, experience, employment and examination requirements of NB-263, RCI-1, Rules for Commissioned Inspectors,
and the commission card is renewed every year.

## Can a shop hire an Authorized Inspector directly?

No. A shop signs an inspection agreement with an AIA, and the agency assigns the Inspector. ASME's handbook says the
AIA representative "is appointed by the Authorized Inspection Agency", and ASME won't schedule a shop's joint review
until the agency confirms the agreement. If a certificate holder changes agency, ASME's FAQ says it must tell ASME's
Conformity Assessment Department straight away, or risk losing its certification. See
[how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

## Which certificates don't need an inspection agency?

The Section IV H certificate for cast iron and cast aluminum boilers, and the Section XIII pressure relief device
certificates (V, HV, UV, UD, UV3, UD3, TV, TD), per the table in ASME's handbook. The UM certificate needs one
indirectly, because it is only issued alongside a U or S certificate. Every other boiler and vessel certificate needs
an AIA agreement. See [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps).

## Do inspection agencies work outside the US?

Yes. ASME's FAQ says most AIAs operate worldwide and points to its list of agencies for local offices and contacts.
That is how a shop in India or elsewhere gets an Inspector for U or S work; see
[buying from India](/asme/buying-from-india).

## What does the Inspector check on a job?

On a stamped job the Inspector, in outline:

- reviews the design calculations and drawings for Code compliance;
- checks material against its [MTR](/asme/mtr) and its marking;
- checks that every weld is made to a qualified [WPS](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq) by a qualified welder in [continuity](/asme/welder-continuity);
- reviews NDE results and heat treatment records;
- witnesses the [hydrostatic or pneumatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test);
- signs the data report and authorizes stamping.

A common check is to pick one weld and walk it back: weld number on the weld map, the welder's stamp, that welder's
qualification and continuity, the WPS, the PQR behind it, and the filler and base metal certificates.

## What are hold points?

Hold points are the steps in the shop's [quality control manual](/asme/quality-control-manual) where work stops until
the Inspector has seen it: typically material review, fit-up of critical joints, NDE review, the PWHT chart and the
hydro test. The manual and the inspection plan for the job name them, and the Inspector signs each one off.

## Is the Authorized Inspector the shop's quality control?

No. The Inspector checks that the shop's system worked; the shop runs it. If the shop's own inspection is missing,
the Inspector raises it as a nonconformity rather than doing it for them. The Inspector also sits on the review team
at the shop's ASME joint review, alongside the ASME Designee.

## Who inspects repairs to equipment in service?

A National Board commissioned inspector, for work done by a holder of the National Board's R certificate under the
National Board Inspection Code. The National Board's [R certificate page](https://www.nationalboard.org/Index.aspx?pageID=115&ID=160) requires an R holder to keep an
inspection agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency too. See
[National Board registration and the R stamp](/asme/national-board-registration).

## What should a shop's records give the Inspector?

Everything the Inspector checks should come from records the shop already keeps, linked once: each weld to its
welders, WPS and NDE report, each part to its heat number and MTR. Our US boiler demo prints that as one ASME record
package, with the weld map, WPS and PQR, QW-322 continuity, MTRs by heat number, NDE, PWHT and hydro records, and the
Inspector's name and agency on the data report layout. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: ASME B31.1 vs B31.3: power piping and process piping
question: What is the difference between ASME B31.1 and B31.3?
answer: B31.1 is the Power Piping code, for power stations, industrial and heating plants and boiler external piping. B31.3 is the Process Piping code, for refineries, chemical, pharmaceutical, hydrogen and similar plants, with fluid service categories that scale the rules to the hazard. Neither is part of the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, but both use Section IX for welding. The current editions are B31.1-2026 and B31.3-2024.

body:
## What is the difference between ASME B31.1 and B31.3?

B31.1 is for power piping and B31.3 for process piping. ASME describes B31.1 as covering "piping systems typically
found in electric power generating stations, industrial plants, geothermal heating systems, and heating and cooling
systems", and B31.3 as setting "process piping requirements typically found in petroleum, chemical, pharmaceutical,
hydrogen, paper & pulp, and power generation industries". Both are ASME standards outside the Boiler and Pressure
Vessel Code, and both are paid; this guide cites their paragraphs.

| | B31.1 Power Piping | B31.3 Process Piping |
|---|---|---|
| Current edition | 2026 | 2024 |
| Typical plants | Power stations, industrial steam, district heating and cooling | Refineries, chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, hydrogen, food |
| Special scope | Boiler external piping (BEP) | Fluid service categories: Normal, Category D, Category M, High Pressure, High Purity |
| Hazard approach | One set of rules, conservative | Rules scale with the fluid's hazard |
| Hydrostatic test | 1.5 × design pressure | 1.5 × design pressure, adjusted by the stress ratio at temperature |
| Welding qualification | Section IX | Section IX, with B31.3's own additions |
| Certification | BEP by a Section I certificate holder; CC-1 and CC-2 certificates of compliance | None |

## What are the current editions of B31.1 and B31.3?

B31.1-2026 and B31.3-2024, the latest editions ASME lists on its store as of 6 November 2026. Piping codes have their
own cycles, separate from the BPVC's two-year cycle, so check which edition your contract or jurisdiction names; Ohio's
rule, for example, adopts B31.1 at 2022 and Michigan's at 2018.

## What is boiler external piping?

The piping from a power boiler out to and including the valves Section I requires. Texas's boiler rules define it as
starting where the Section I or Section VIII boiler proper ends (at the first circumferential joint, flange face or
threaded joint) "and which extends up to and including the valve or valves required by ASME". It is designed to B31.1
but is part of the Section I boiler: built by a holder of a Section I certificate (S, A or PP) and inspected by the
[Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector). That is why ASME lists B31.1 among the required books for the S and
PP certificates. See [Section I vs Section IV](/asme/section-i-vs-iv).

## Is there an ASME form for B31.1 piping?

Yes: ASME publishes two certificates of compliance for B31.1, CC-1 for the complete piping system and CC-2 for
fabricated components, subassemblies and assemblies, free on its [data report forms page](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/asme-data-report-forms). B31.3 has no
equivalent ASME form; the owner's records and the examination and test reports carry the evidence.

## What are B31.3 fluid service categories?

- **Normal**: most services.
- **Category D**: non-flammable, non-toxic fluids at low pressure and moderate temperature; lighter rules.
- **Category M**: fluids where a single small exposure can cause serious harm; stricter rules.
- **High Pressure** and **High Purity**: chapters of their own.

The owner assigns the category, and with it the examination, testing and design rules that apply.

## What hydrostatic test does each require?

B31.1: at least 1.5 × design pressure (paragraph 137). B31.3: at least 1.5 × design pressure, multiplied by the ratio
of allowable stress at test temperature to that at design temperature (paragraph 345.4.2), the same logic as a
Division 1 vessel's stress ratio. See the [hydrostatic test guide](/asme/hydrostatic-test).

## Do B31.1 and B31.3 use Section IX?

Yes. Welding procedures and welders are qualified to [Section IX](/asme/section-ix), so a shop's
[WPSs and PQRs](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq) can serve its vessel and piping work where the variables fit both codes, and the
same continuity rule (QW-322) applies to its welders.

## Where do piping NDE and materials come from?

NDE methods from [Section V](/asme/section-v), with the piping code setting how much and the acceptance criteria;
materials are mostly ASME or ASTM specifications, see [Section II](/asme/section-ii).

## What does our software keep for piping jobs?

Our US boiler demo keeps the weld map (shell seams and nozzles), WPS and PQR, welder continuity, MTR and NDE records
for each boiler or vessel inside the job's ASME record package; the same records serve piping welds made under
Section IX. It has no piping module, no B31.3 categories and no CC-1 form. See
[job shop ERP](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp) and [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: ASME BPVC sections I to XIII explained
question: What are the sections of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code?
answer: The ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code has thirteen sections. Construction sections set the rules for a product: I for power boilers, IV for heating boilers, VIII for pressure vessels, X and XII for plastic vessels and transport tanks, III for nuclear. Reference sections serve them all: II for materials, V for NDE, IX for welding, XIII for relief devices. VI and VII are recommendations and XI covers nuclear in-service inspection.

body:
## What are the sections of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code?

Thirteen, numbered I to XIII, and easiest to read as two kinds of book. A **construction section** is the rulebook
for one kind of equipment: what it may be made of, how it is designed, welded, examined, tested and stamped. A
**reference section** holds rules several construction sections point to, so they aren't written out in each.

| Section | Title, in short | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| I | Power boilers | Construction |
| II | Materials (Parts A to D) | Reference |
| III | Nuclear facility components | Construction |
| IV | Heating boilers | Construction |
| V | Nondestructive examination | Reference |
| VI | Care and operation of heating boilers | Recommended practice |
| VII | Care of power boilers | Recommended practice |
| VIII | Pressure vessels (Divisions 1, 2 and 3) | Construction |
| IX | Welding, brazing and fusing qualifications | Reference |
| X | Fiber-reinforced plastic pressure vessels | Construction |
| XI | In-service inspection of nuclear plants | Inspection |
| XII | Construction and continued service of transport tanks | Construction |
| XIII | Overpressure protection | Reference |

The whole Code is republished every two years; the current one is the [2025 Edition](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/bpvc-standards/bpvc-2025).

## What is the difference between a construction and a reference section?

A construction section is what a product is built and stamped to; a reference section is what it points to for one
topic. Section IX, for example, "contains rules relating to the qualification of welding, brazing, and fusing
procedures as required by other BPVC sections", in ASME's words, and Section XIII "sets requirements for design,
materials, inspection, testing, and marking of pressure relief valves, rupture disks, and related devices". A shop
working to Section VIII Division 1 therefore also works to Sections II, V, IX and XIII.

## Which books does a pressure vessel shop need?

For the U certificate, ASME's [required list](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/ASME-Certification-Process/Required-Code-Books) is Section II Parts A, B, C and D, Section V,
Section VIII Division 1, Section IX and CA-1, ASME's Conformity Assessment Requirements. Section II Part C and Sections
V and IX may be left out only if welding, brazing and fusing aren't in the shop's scope. Division 2 work (U2) needs
Division 2 instead. See [Section VIII](/asme/section-viii).

## Which books does a boiler shop need?

For the S certificate: Section I, Section II Parts A to D, Section V, Section IX, B31.1 Power Piping and CA-1. For an H
heating boiler certificate (except cast iron): Section II Parts A, B and C, Section IV, Section IX and CA-1; for cast
iron H, Section IV and CA-1. B31.1 is on the S list because boiler external piping is part of the Section I boiler.
See [Section I vs Section IV](/asme/section-i-vs-iv).

## Can a shop use photocopies or older books?

No. ASME's handbook says subscription to the required sections "is required for certification to assure that Code
users have the latest applicable Code rules", and that "Reproduced/unauthorized documents from any source are not
accepted for ASME Certification". Electronic editions from a licensed reseller are accepted. Each new edition becomes
mandatory six months after publication; see [ASME Code editions](/asme/editions).

## Which sections are not construction rules?

Sections VI and VII are recommended practice for owners caring for heating and power boilers: nothing is built or
stamped to them. Section XI is for in-service inspection of nuclear plants. In-service rules for other boilers and
vessels are in the National Board Inspection Code, not the BPVC; see [National Board registration](/asme/national-board-registration).

## How are ASME paragraph numbers read?

Each construction section uses letter prefixes for its parts. In Section VIII Division 1, UG paragraphs are general
requirements for every vessel, UW is welded construction, UCS is carbon and low-alloy steel and UHA is high-alloy
steel. Section I uses PG for general requirements and PW for welding; Section IX uses QW for welding. A reference such
as UG-27 therefore reads "Section VIII Division 1, general requirements, paragraph 27": the
[shell thickness rules](/asme/shell-thickness).

## How many shops hold ASME certificates?

ASME's certification page says "Today there are more than 6,800 Certificate Holders in the ASME BPVC Certification
Program", across power boilers, heating boilers, pressure vessels, plastic vessels, transport tanks and valves. Its
Certificate Holder Search lists them; see [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps).

## What does our software keep for the Code?

Our US boiler demo files each job to a named Code section and edition (Section I with Form P-2 for boilers, Section
VIII Division 1 with Form U-1A for vessels) and prints the job's ASME record package from its own records. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

body:
## Can an Indian manufacturer build an ASME U-stamped pressure vessel?

Yes. The Code and the certificate are the same wherever the shop is: an Indian fabricator with a U certificate builds
Section VIII Division 1 vessels to the same rules, under the same quality control system review and with an
Authorized Inspector from an ASME-accredited agency, as a shop in Texas. ASME's FAQ notes there are now 74 countries
in which companies have been certified, and many Indian fabricators hold U, U2 and S certificates for export work.

## How do I check an Indian shop's ASME certificate?

On ASME's [Certificate Holder Search](https://access.asme.org/caconnect/certified-companies), which ASME's FAQ points to for exactly this and which filters by
country and certificate. Ask the supplier for a copy of the certificate too, and confirm:

- the designator covers the work (U for Division 1, U2 for Division 2, S for power boilers, PP for boiler external piping);
- the scope (shop only, or field work too) and any limits;
- the expiry date is after your job finishes, or that renewal is in hand.

See [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps).

## Who is the Authorized Inspector for a shop in India?

An inspector employed by the ASME-accredited inspection agency the shop has its agreement with; ASME's FAQ says most
agencies operate worldwide. Ask which agency it is: their [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) witnesses
the hydro test and signs your [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## Can an Indian shop register the vessel with the National Board?

Yes, if it is authorized to register. The National Board says any manufacturer meeting NB-264 may become authorized,
and NB-264 then requires registration forms to be sent within 30 days of the Inspector's certification. If your state
requires National Board registration, make authorization a condition of the order. See
[National Board registration](/asme/national-board-registration).

## Which US rules apply to an imported vessel?

The rules of the state, and sometimes the city, where it will be installed: the Code edition the jurisdiction names,
whether it regulates unfired vessels at all, National Board registration, and inspection before first use.
Pennsylvania, for example, requires the ASME stamp, the National Board number and its own keystone serial number on
every new boiler and unfired vessel. Put the jurisdiction's answers in the purchase order; see
[US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## What should I check before ordering?

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| The certificate covers the work | Designator, scope and expiry, on ASME's Certificate Holder Search and a copy from the shop |
| Who the inspection agency is | The agency named on their agreement; its Inspector signs your data report |
| National Board registration | Required by your state? Then the shop must be authorized to register (NB-264) |
| The Code edition | Name it in the order; see [editions](/asme/editions) |
| Your jurisdiction's own rules | Edition, scope, stamping and registration; see [state boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws) |
| Materials | SA specifications with mill test reports by heat number; see [MTRs](/asme/mtr) |
| Documents | The full package in English: calculations, drawings, MTRs, WPS/PQR/WPQ, welder continuity, NDE, PWHT charts, test record, data report |

## Will the documents be in English?

They must be, for the ASME side. ASME's handbook requires a certificate holder's quality control documentation to be
in English, and the data report, calculations and records the Inspector reviews follow it. Ask for the data report
package as a draft before the vessel ships, not with it.

## What does IBR add for a boiler built in India?

A step at home. Regulation 4 of IBR 2026 lets an Indian Inspecting Authority inspect a boiler meant for export,
through its stages of construction, against a foreign code such as ASME, and certify it in Form I Part A. That
certificate is for India's records: it doesn't replace the ASME stamp or the Authorized Inspector. See
[ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr) and [IBR Form I Part A](/ibr/forms#form-i-part-a).

## How should I manage the order?

- **Inspection and test plan**: agree the hold points (material review, fit-up, NDE, PWHT, hydrostatic test) and who witnesses each, yours and the Inspector's.
- **Document review before shipping**: get the data report package as a draft before the vessel ships.
- **Logistics**: plan oversized vessels' shipping early; the data report and nameplate must match what arrives.

## What do records that travel well look like?

A buyer overseas sees a shop through its documents. Shops that keep heat numbers, welders and NDE in one system send
a complete package the day the vessel is ready. Our boiler software does this for an Indian boiler maker today (the
India build, with its IBR folder), and the US demo shows the same records printed as an ASME record package; a
customer portal can show the order's progress live. See
[one order, every department](/notes/customer-portal-one-order-every-department) and
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

body:
## What is a Manufacturer's Data Report?

A Manufacturer's Data Report is the signed record of a stamped boiler, vessel or part as built: who made it and for
whom, design conditions, materials, thicknesses, joints, examinations, heat treatment and test pressure, certified
by the manufacturer and by the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector). It is what the stamp points to:
the nameplate says the item is a Code item, and the data report says what that item is. Section VIII Division 1 sets
its data report rules in UG-120 (2025 Edition).

## Which data report form do I use?

The form follows the Code section and the kind of item. ASME publishes them free as fillable PDFs on its
[data report forms page](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/asme-data-report-forms); the ones most shops use:

| Item | Form |
|---|---|
| Section VIII Div. 1 vessel | U-1, or U-1A (alternative form for single-chamber vessels) |
| Part of a Div. 1 vessel built by another shop | U-2 or U-2A (partial data report) |
| Plate heat exchanger | U-1P |
| Supplementary sheet, shell-and-tube heat exchanger | U-5 |
| Owner's design conditions | U-DR-1 (single chamber) or U-DR-2 (multi-chamber) |
| Section VIII Div. 2 vessel | A-1 (A-2 for parts) |
| Section VIII Div. 3 vessel | K-1 (K-2 for parts) |
| Section I boiler, except watertube and electric | P-2 (P-2A electric) |
| Section I watertube boilers, superheaters, waterwalls, economizers | P-3 |
| Section I parts and fabricated piping | P-4 and P-4A |
| Section IV boiler, except watertube and cast iron | H-2 (H-3 watertube, H-5 and H-5A cast iron and cast aluminum) |
| Section XIII relief valve or rupture disk | Certificates of conformance (UV-1, UD-1 and others) |
| B31.1 power piping | CC-1 and CC-2 certificates of compliance |

## What is the difference between U-1 and U-1A?

U-1A is the shorter alternative to U-1 for a single-chamber vessel. ASME's 2025 form is titled for "Single Chamber,
Completely Shop- or Field-Fabricated Vessels Only", so it now covers field-fabricated single-chamber vessels too.
Use U-1 for multi-chamber vessels such as heat exchangers (with the U-5 supplementary sheet for shell-and-tube units).

## What goes in a U-1A?

The report describes the vessel as built, not as quoted:

- manufacturer, purchaser and installation location, serial and National Board numbers;
- design pressure, [MAWP](/asme/mawp) at its coincident temperature, and the [MDMT](/asme/impact-testing);
- for each shell and head: material specification and grade, nominal thickness and corrosion allowance, inside diameter, length, [joint efficiency](/asme/joint-efficiency) and type, extent of radiography;
- nozzles and openings, with their reinforcement;
- heat treatment ([PWHT](/asme/pwht)) and impact testing;
- the [hydrostatic or pneumatic test pressure](/asme/hydrostatic-test);
- code cases used, and parts from other shops, with their U-2 reports attached;
- certification by the manufacturer and by the Authorized Inspector.

## Which edition of the forms must I use?

The 2025 forms, for anything built to the 2025 Code. The National Board's [registration page](https://www.nationalboard.org/Index.aspx?pageID=9) says the 2025
revisions to the ASME and NBIC report forms became mandatory on 1 January 2026, and that reports on outdated forms
are returned for correction. ASME's forms page stars the forms revised or new in the 2025 Edition (U-1, U-1A, U-2,
P-7, H-2 among them) and marks the metric versions such as P-2M and P-3M with a double star: "Form no longer included
in Code". See [ASME Code editions](/asme/editions).

## Can I make my own layout of the form?

Not for a report sent on paper to the National Board: it must be in the exact format and content of the form in the
Code and the NBIC, with National Board minimum font sizes, and a multi-page report must repeat its header and leave
space for the company representative and the Authorized Inspector to initial each page. ASME's own forms page warns
users to keep track of font and field size. A shop's software can still assemble the data and fill the official
form, or send it through the National Board's Electronic Data Transfer (EDT).

## Who signs the data report?

The manufacturer's representative certifies that the item meets the Code, and the Authorized Inspector certifies
that they inspected it; for a registered item the registration form bears the Inspector's signature and National
Board commission number. Without the Inspector's signature the item can't be stamped.

## How long must the shop keep the data report?

Division 1 requires the manufacturer to keep a copy for a period set in UG-120, or to register it with the National
Board, which keeps it permanently. Registration also means an owner can get a copy at any later inspection, repair or
sale. See [National Board registration](/asme/national-board-registration).

## How soon must a data report be filed with the National Board?

Within 30 days of certification. The National Board's criteria for registration (NB-264, Revision 19) require a
manufacturer authorized to register to submit registration forms no more than 30 days after the Inspector certifies
the item. Many US jurisdictions require registration before installation; see
[US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## What sits behind the one-page report?

The file the Inspector checked: calculations, drawings, [MTRs](/asme/mtr), weld map,
[WPS, PQR and welder qualifications](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq), NDE reports, heat treatment charts and the test record.
Assembling that file at the end of a job is where most shops lose days. Our US boiler demo builds it as the job runs
and prints it as one record package: a Form U-1A or P-2 layout (our own, carrying the form's fields, not ASME's form;
file the official form or use EDT), the weld map with welder stamps, WPS and PQR, QW-322 continuity, MTRs by heat
number, NDE, PWHT and the hydro test. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

## What is the Indian equivalent?

Under IBR 2026 the equivalents are the maker's certificate (Form IV Part A) and the Inspecting Authority's
certificate (Form I); see [IBR Form I Part A](/ibr/forms#form-i-part-a), [boiler registration documents](/ibr/registration-documents)
and [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

body:
## When does the ASME 2025 Edition become mandatory?

It became mandatory on 1 January 2026, six months after it was published on 1 July 2025. ASME's handbook states the
rule: "The edition becomes mandatory six months after the date of publication." The six months give shops time to
buy the new books and update procedures and their quality control manual.

## How often is the ASME Code published?

Every two years, in odd years, with all the changes made in committee since the last edition. There are no addenda
between editions any more; the two-year cycle replaced them.

| Edition | Published | Mandatory |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 1 July 2023 | 1 January 2024 |
| 2025 | 1 July 2025 | 1 January 2026 |
| 2027 | Due July 2027 | Six months after |

The National Board's inspection code (NBIC) follows the same rhythm: a new edition each July of an odd year.

## Do data report forms change with the edition?

Yes. The National Board says the 2025 revisions to the ASME and NBIC report forms became mandatory on 1 January
2026; items built to the 2025 Code must be documented on the current forms, and reports on outdated forms are sent
back. See [data reports](/asme/data-reports).

## Which edition applies to my vessel?

The edition agreed for the job, normally the one mandatory when the contract was signed, unless the jurisdiction where
it will be installed fixes another. The edition is fixed per job, not per day: write it into the purchase order and
the design basis, and make sure the quality control manual says how a job's edition is recorded.

## Do states require a specific edition?

Many do, and they lag. The National Board's 2026 Synopsis table of editions lists, for example: Ohio 2023, Illinois
2023, Michigan 2019, Pennsylvania 2010, Texas "Current" and Minnesota "Current". The rules themselves say:

- **Ohio** (OAC 4101:4-3-01, effective 1 July 2024) adopts the Code sections at the 2023 edition, "as well as
  amendments, supplements, and addenda subsequently published prior to issuance of the next edition".
- **Michigan** (R 339.5204, effective 3 May 2023) requires boilers, blowdown vessels and expansion tanks to be built to
  the 2019 edition.
- **Texas** (16 TAC §65.2) defines the ASME Code without a year, as the Code, code cases and interpretations adopted by
  ASME.
- **Pennsylvania** (34 Pa. Code §3a.1) still defines the ASME Code as the 2004 edition with its published cases and
  interpretations, older than the Synopsis entry.

Ask the jurisdiction's chief inspector before building to an edition newer than its rule names. See
[US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## Do I have to buy new books each edition?

Yes, if you hold an ASME certificate. ASME's FAQ answers "Yes, the latest edition/addenda becomes mandatory six months
after publication", and its handbook says reproduced or unauthorized copies aren't accepted. Electronic editions from
a licensed reseller are accepted. See [BPVC sections](/asme/bpvc-sections).

## Do welding qualifications expire with an edition?

No. A PQR or WPQ qualified under an earlier edition stays valid; new qualifications follow the edition in force when
they are made. The [Section IX guide](/asme/section-ix) covers the 2025 changes.

## What is a code case?

An approved alternative or addition published between editions: a new material, a new method, a relaxation in a
defined situation. ASME's [code cases page](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/code-cases) says code cases "are effective immediately upon ASME approval and do not
expire", and are published in two books, Boiler and Pressure Vessels (CC-BPV) and Nuclear (CC-NUC), with seven
supplements through each two-year cycle. Using one is optional, must be recorded on the data report, and in many
states needs the jurisdiction's acceptance: the National Board's Synopsis has a code case column for each state.

## What is an interpretation?

ASME's written answer to a question about what the Code says. It isn't a change to the Code and doesn't approve a
design; it tells you how the committee reads a paragraph. Interpretations are published by ASME and searchable
online.

## What does our software keep for editions?

Our US boiler demo records the Code edition on each job's ASME record package and data report layout, so every job
says which edition it was built to. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: Essential and nonessential variables in ASME Section IX
question: What are essential variables in ASME welding?
answer: ASME Section IX classifies each welding variable. Changing an essential variable, such as the base metal P-number, filler F-number, thickness range or post-weld heat treatment, needs a new PQR. Supplementary essential variables count only when impact testing is required. Nonessential variables, such as groove design, can change by revising the WPS.

body:
## What are essential variables in ASME welding?

Essential variables are the welding conditions that affect a weld's mechanical properties, so changing one beyond
what a PQR covers needs a new PQR. Section IX classifies every variable for every process in its variable tables
(QW-250 onwards for procedures, QW-350 onwards for welders) as essential, supplementary essential or nonessential. A
procedure test proves one set of conditions; the tables say how far you can move from it before you test again.
The Code text is ASME's and paid; this guide gives common examples, and your 2025 tables are the authority.

## What are the three kinds of procedure variable?

| Kind | If you change it beyond the PQR | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|
| Essential | Qualify a new PQR | Base metal P-number; filler F-number and A-number; thickness beyond the qualified range; adding or removing post-weld heat treatment; a decrease in preheat of more than 100 °F (56 °C); a change of process; adding or removing shielding or backing gas in some processes |
| Supplementary essential | New PQR only if the construction code requires impact testing | Group number within a P-number; an increase in heat input; single to multi-pass in some processes |
| Nonessential | Revise the WPS; no new test | Groove design, backing type, technique details, cleaning methods |

The exact list differs by process (SMAW, GTAW, GMAW, SAW, FCAW), so read the table for the process on your WPS.

## When do supplementary essential variables apply?

Only when the construction code requires toughness (impact) testing of the weld. Then a change in, for example, the
base metal Group number or an increase in heat input needs a PQR with impact tests in that condition. Impact-tested
work is where supplementary essentials catch shops out; see [MDMT and impact testing](/asme/impact-testing).

## What thickness range does a PQR qualify?

A groove-weld PQR qualifies a range of base metal thickness and of deposited weld metal thickness from the coupon's
thickness (QW-451). As a general picture, a coupon of moderate thickness qualifies from a minimum up to twice its
thickness, and a coupon 1½ in (38 mm) or thicker qualifies up to 8 in (203 mm); impact-tested work changes the lower
limit. Check QW-451 for the coupon you weld.

## Can you show a worked example?

A shop holds a PQR on ¾ in (19 mm) P-No. 1 plate, SMAW with E7018 (F-4, A-1), no PWHT. It can write a WPS for P-No. 1
from about 3/16 in up to 1½ in, as-welded. A new job needs a 2 in shell with PWHT: that is outside the thickness range
and adds PWHT, two essential variables, so the shop welds a new coupon (for example 1½ in thick, heat treated) before
issuing the WPS. Changing the groove angle on the same job needs only a WPS revision.

## What are a welder's essential variables?

QW-350 onwards: the process, position, backing (welding without backing when qualified only with it), the filler
F-number, and the diameter and deposited thickness ranges. Changing one beyond the WPQ means a new welder test. See
[welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification).

## Does PWHT count as an essential variable?

Yes. Adding or removing post-weld heat treatment, or changing its temperature and time range, is a procedure
essential variable (QW-407), so the PQR must have been heat treated the way the job will be. See [PWHT](/asme/pwht).

## Can one WPS cite two PQRs?

Yes, for example to cover two thickness ranges, provided every essential variable on the WPS is covered by at least
one of the PQRs. Keep a PQR register with each PQR's qualified ranges worked out once: most WPS errors are ranges
copied wrong. ASME's suggested PQR format (QW-483) lays the variables out in the order of the tables.

## Did the 2025 Edition change the variables?

Section IX changes in every edition, and the 2025 changes apply to new qualifications from 1 January 2026, as the
American Welding Society's summary notes. Check the "Summary of Changes" at the front of your 2025 Section IX before
relying on any list here, including this one.

## What does our software keep for it?

Our US boiler demo prints each WPS with its PQR, P-numbers, thickness range and PWHT condition in the job's ASME record
package, next to the weld map that shows which WPS each seam used, so a reviewer can see each seam's thickness against
the WPS range. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: Pressure vessel heads (UG-32): ellipsoidal vs torispherical
metaTitle: Pressure vessel heads (UG-32): 2:1, F&D and hemi
question: What is a 2:1 ellipsoidal head?
answer: A 2:1 ellipsoidal head is half an ellipse in section, its depth a quarter of its diameter, and it needs about the same thickness as the shell it closes. Torispherical (flanged and dished) heads are shallower and cheaper to form but thicker; hemispherical heads are the deepest and need about half the shell thickness. ASME UG-32 gives a formula for each, and Mandatory Appendix 1-4 covers other proportions such as 80:10.
description: ASME UG-32 heads compared: 2:1 ellipsoidal, F&D and 80:10 torispherical, hemispherical, with formulas, a worked 48 in example and how to order them.

checks.quote: ASME BPVC Section VIII Division 1 provides design, fabrication, inspection, testing & certification rules for pressure vessels operating over 15 psig, fired/unfired.

body:
## What is a 2:1 ellipsoidal head?

A formed head that is half an ellipse in section, with a depth of a quarter of its inside diameter (a 2:1 ratio of
diameter to twice the depth). Under UG-32 of Section VIII Division 1 its required thickness for internal pressure is
t = PD / (2SE − 0.2P), about the same as the cylinder it closes, which is why it is the default head for most vessels.
The Code text is ASME's and paid; formulas are written out here to check against your 2025 book.

## What are the three common formed heads?

| Head | Shape | Thickness (UG-32), internal pressure | Relative thickness | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2:1 ellipsoidal | Depth = D/4 | t = PD / (2SE − 0.2P) | About the shell's | The default for most vessels |
| Torispherical, standard "ASME F&D" (crown radius L about equal to the diameter, knuckle radius 6% of L) | Shallower: a spherical crown with a knuckle | t = 0.885PL / (SE − 0.1P) | Thicker than the shell | Low pressure, storage, where height matters |
| Hemispherical | Half a sphere | t = PL / (2SE − 0.2P) | About half the shell's | High pressure, large diameters |

D is the inside diameter, L the inside crown (or sphere) radius, and P, S and E are as in the
[shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness) guide. Each formula has validity limits.

## What is an 80:10 torispherical head?

A torispherical head with a crown radius of 80% of the diameter and a knuckle radius of 10%: deeper and thinner than
a standard F&D. Its proportions aren't those of the 0.885 formula, so it is designed with Mandatory Appendix 1-4's
general torispherical formula, t = PLM / (2SE − 0.2P), where M = ¼ (3 + √(L/r)) and r is the knuckle radius. For
L/r = 8, M = 1.457.

## Can you show a worked example?

A 48 in inside diameter vessel at 150 psi, S = 20,000 psi, seamless heads with E = 1.0, before corrosion allowance:

| Head | Working | Thickness |
|---|---|---|
| 2:1 ellipsoidal | 150 × 48 / (40,000 − 30) = 7,200 / 39,970 | **0.180 in** |
| Standard F&D (L = 48 in) | 0.885 × 150 × 48 / (20,000 − 15) = 6,372 / 19,985 | **0.319 in** |
| 80:10 (L = 38.4 in, r = 4.8 in, M = 1.457) | 150 × 38.4 × 1.457 / 39,970 | **0.210 in** |
| Hemispherical (L = 24 in) | 150 × 24 / 39,970 | **0.090 in** |

Add the corrosion allowance to each (0.125 in gives 0.305, 0.444, 0.335 and 0.215 in), then order the head with a
minimum thickness after forming at least that.

## Which head is cheapest?

Usually the 2:1 ellipsoidal overall. A hemispherical head is the thinnest but the hardest to form and the deepest; a
standard F&D head is the cheapest to form but the thickest, so it wins at low pressure, where thickness is set by
minimums anyway. Torispherical heads also save height; hemispherical heads add the most volume.

## What thickness should I order a head at?

A minimum thickness after forming equal to or above the required thickness plus corrosion allowance. Forming thins
the plate, most at the knuckle, and the head maker adds their own thinning allowance to the starting plate. The
minimum thickness after forming goes on the [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## What joint efficiency does a seamless head use?

It depends on the radiography of the weld joining it to the shell: 1.0 with that joint spot radiographed to the rule
for this case, otherwise 0.85. See [joint efficiency and radiography](/asme/joint-efficiency).

## How are flat heads designed?

Under UG-34, with a factor for how the head or cover is attached. Flat heads, blind flanges and bolted covers are far
thicker than a formed head for the same pressure, which is why formed heads are used wherever they fit.

## Do heads need checking for vacuum?

Yes: external pressure is a separate check (UG-33), often governing for thin heads on vessels that see vacuum.

## When does UG-32 apply?

To heads of Section VIII Division 1 vessels, the Division ASME describes as covering "pressure vessels operating over
15 psig, fired/unfired". Boilers under Section I have their own head rules in Part PG.

## What does our software keep for heads?

Our US boiler demo records head material and thickness on the job's data report layout and files the head plate's MTR
by heat number in the ASME record package. How offcuts from head and shell plate go back into stock with their heat
number is in [plate remnants back into stock](/notes/plate-remnants-back-into-stock).

title: ASME hydrostatic test pressure calculator (UG-99)
question: What is the ASME hydrostatic test pressure for a pressure vessel?
answer: For a Section VIII Division 1 vessel, the minimum hydrostatic test pressure is 1.3 times the MAWP, multiplied by the lowest ratio of allowable stress at test temperature to allowable stress at design temperature (UG-99(b)). A pneumatic test uses 1.1 instead (UG-100). A Section I boiler is tested to at least 1.5 times its MAWP (PG-99).
description: ASME hydrostatic test pressure with a free calculator: UG-99 (1.3 × MAWP × stress ratio), pneumatic UG-100 (1.1), Section I PG-99 (1.5), gauges and holds.

body:
## What is the ASME hydrostatic test pressure?

For a Section VIII Division 1 vessel it is at least 1.3 × MAWP × the lowest stress ratio (UG-99(b)); for a Section I
boiler, at least 1.5 × MAWP (PG-99). The calculator above works out either, and the pneumatic test, for any unit.
The Code text is ASME's and paid; this guide cites the 2025 Edition's paragraphs.

| Equipment | Test | Minimum test pressure |
|---|---|---|
| Section VIII Div. 1 vessel | Hydrostatic, UG-99(b) | 1.3 × MAWP × stress ratio |
| Section VIII Div. 1 vessel | Pneumatic, UG-100 | 1.1 × MAWP × stress ratio |
| Section I boiler | Hydrostatic, PG-99 | 1.5 × MAWP |

## What is the stress ratio in UG-99?

It is the allowable stress at the test temperature divided by the allowable stress at the design temperature, taken
for the pressure-part material where that ratio is lowest; bolting is left out. Both values come from Section II
Part D. At ordinary temperatures they are often equal and the ratio is 1, so the test is 1.3 × MAWP; for a hot
vessel, whose allowable stress falls with temperature, the ratio is above 1 and the test pressure rises.

## Can you show worked examples?

- **Room-temperature vessel**: MAWP 100 psi, ratio 1 → 1.3 × 100 = **130 psi**.
- **Hot vessel**: MAWP 100 psi at 650 °F, allowable 20,000 psi at test temperature and 16,000 psi at 650 °F → 1.3 × 100 × 1.25 = **162.5 psi**. In metric, MAWP 10 bar with the same materials → **16.25 bar**.
- **Section I boiler**: MAWP 150 psi → 1.5 × 150 = **225 psi**.

## Is the test pressure measured at the top or the bottom?

At the top of the vessel. If the gauge is at the bottom, add the static head of the water column: a vessel 10 ft
tall adds 10 × 0.433 = 4.3 psi, so a 130 psi test reads about 134.3 psi on a bottom gauge.

## At what pressure is the vessel inspected?

After reaching the test pressure, it is reduced to not less than the test pressure divided by 1.3 and held while
every joint and connection is examined (UG-99(g)), normally with the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector)
present. For the 130 psi test above, that is at least 100 psi.

## What gauge range do I need for a hydro test?

A dial about twice the test pressure, never less than 1.5 times or more than 4 times it (UG-102), calibrated before
the test. For a 130 psi test that means a range between 195 and 520 psi, ideally about 260 psi, so a 0–300 psi gauge;
a 0–600 psi gauge is too coarse. For a 225 psi boiler test, 0–600 psi is within range.

## How warm should the test water be?

Warm enough that the metal is at least 30 °F (17 °C) above the vessel's [MDMT](/asme/impact-testing), to avoid
brittle fracture, and Division 1 recommends not above 120 °F (49 °C) so the vessel can be approached safely during
the examination (UG-99(h)).

## When is a pneumatic test used instead?

Only where water can't be: vessels that can't be supported full of water, or that must not see any water. A gas
stores far more energy than water at the same pressure, so Division 1 adds conditions (examination of certain welds
first, raising pressure in steps), the test pressure is 1.1 × MAWP × the stress ratio (UG-100), and the examination
pressure is the test pressure divided by 1.1.

## Does the Authorized Inspector have to witness it?

Yes. The pressure test is one of the Inspector's hold points on every stamped vessel and boiler, and the test pressure
goes on the [data report](/asme/data-reports) they sign.

## What should the hydro test record show?

The date, test pressure and where it was measured, water temperature, hold time, the gauge used and its calibration
date, the examination pressure, the result, and who witnessed it. How MAWP is set is in
[MAWP and design pressure](/asme/mawp); how a vessel needs Section VIII at all is in
[Section VIII](/asme/section-viii), which ASME says covers "pressure vessels operating over 15 psig".

## How does this work under IBR in India?

IBR 2026 sets its own hydraulic test rules and asks for the test record among the registration documents; see
[boiler registration documents](/ibr/registration-documents) and [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## What does our software keep for the hydro test?

Our US boiler demo records each job's hydro test (pressure, temperature, hold, gauge and its calibration date,
witness) and prints it in the ASME record package next to the data report layout: 130 psi for its Division 1 vessel
and 225 psi for its boilers. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: MDMT and impact test exemptions (UCS-66)
question: When is impact testing required for an ASME pressure vessel?
answer: Carbon and low-alloy steels can turn brittle when cold, so ASME Section VIII Division 1 requires Charpy impact tests unless an exemption applies. UCS-66 gives exemption curves (A to D) by material and thickness against the vessel's MDMT; thin parts and lower stresses earn more exemption. Below −55 °F (−48 °C) most parts need testing.
description: ASME impact testing and MDMT: UCS-66 exemption curves A to D, governing thickness, the stress-ratio credit, the UG-20(f) exemption and Charpy tests.

body:
## When is impact testing required for an ASME pressure vessel?

When a carbon or low-alloy steel part's minimum design metal temperature (MDMT) is colder than the exemption
Division 1 allows for its material and thickness (UCS-66, 2025 Edition), and no other exemption applies. Steel that
is tough at room temperature can fracture like glass when cold; impact testing proves the steel, welds and
heat-affected zones are tough at the MDMT. The Code text and its curves are ASME's and paid; this guide outlines the
method, and your 2025 book is the authority.

## What is MDMT?

The coldest metal temperature at which the vessel may be at its MAWP: a cold winter start-up, an autorefrigerating
flash, a cold fluid. It goes on the nameplate and the [data report](/asme/data-reports) with its coincident pressure.
See [MAWP and MDMT](/asme/mawp).

## How does the UCS-66 exemption work?

Division 1 works it out part by part:

1. **Assign the material to a curve.** Figure UCS-66 has curves A to D. Curve A is for materials with the least toughness assurance; Curve D for the best (for example, normalized fine-grain plate). The Code lists which specification and heat treatment goes on which curve.
2. **Find the governing thickness** of each part: for a butt joint, the thicker of the two members, with rules for corner, fillet and lap joints and for flat heads.
3. **Read the curve.** It gives the coldest MDMT allowed without impact testing at that thickness. If the vessel's MDMT is warmer than that, the part is exempt.
4. **Take credit for low stress.** When the part is stressed below its full allowable (thicker than needed, or at lower pressure), Figure UCS-66.1 lowers the exemption temperature further.

## What are curves A to D?

Four material groups by toughness: A the least assured, D the best. Plate on a better curve is exempt to a colder
temperature at the same thickness, so when the MDMT is cold, buying plate to a specification and heat treatment on
the better curves (normalized SA-516, for example) can avoid impact testing altogether. The curve assignments are in
the Code; check the note for your specification and heat treatment.

## Is there a simple exemption for ordinary vessels?

Yes: UG-20(f) exempts P-No. 1 materials of limited thickness from impact testing when the vessel is hydrostatically
tested to UG-99(b) or (c), has a design temperature between −20 °F (−29 °C) and 650 °F (343 °C), and has no unusual
thermal or mechanical shock or cyclic loading. Most small carbon steel vessels in mild climates use it.

## Is impact testing always required below a certain temperature?

Generally below −55 °F (−48 °C): at such low MDMTs Division 1 requires impact testing unless the part is very lightly
stressed.

## What does impact testing involve?

Charpy V-notch specimens are cut from the material, or from a test weld for weld metal and heat-affected zones, and
broken at the test temperature. The energy absorbed must meet a minimum that depends on the material's strength and
thickness (UG-84). When impact testing applies, the welding procedure must also be qualified with impact tests,
which brings in Section IX's supplementary [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables).

## Can PWHT reduce the need for impact testing?

It can: Division 1 gives a temperature credit for post-weld heat treatment that the Code doesn't otherwise require
(UCS-68). See [PWHT](/asme/pwht).

## Who supplies the impact test results?

The mill, for the base metal: the results come on the [MTR](/asme/mtr) for the heat, tested at the temperature you
ordered. The shop supplies weld and heat-affected zone results from its PQR or production test plates. Order plate
with the impact test temperature on the purchase order, because adding it later means retesting.

## How do I specify MDMT?

Honestly: too warm is unsafe, too cold forces testing you didn't need. Set it from the coldest metal temperature at
pressure the vessel will really see, including start-up and upset cases, and write it on the purchase order with its
coincident pressure.

## When does UCS-66 apply?

To carbon and low-alloy steel parts (Part UCS) of Section VIII Division 1 vessels, the Division ASME describes as
covering "pressure vessels operating over 15 psig, fired/unfired". Other materials have their own toughness rules.

## What does our software keep for MDMT?

Our US boiler demo prints MDMT on the job's data report layout and files the plates' MTRs by heat number in the ASME
record package. It has no separate impact test records. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: Joint efficiency and radiography (UW-11, UW-12)
question: What is joint efficiency in ASME Section VIII?
answer: Joint efficiency (E) is the factor ASME Section VIII Division 1 applies to a welded joint in the thickness formulas. It depends on the joint type and how much it is radiographed: a double-welded butt joint is 1.0 with full radiography, 0.85 with spot radiography and 0.70 with none (Table UW-12). Less radiography means a thicker shell.
description: ASME UW-12 joint efficiency by joint type and radiography, joint categories A to D, when full RT is mandatory (UW-11), seamless parts, and the cost trade-off.

body:
## What is joint efficiency in ASME Section VIII?

Joint efficiency (E) is the factor Division 1 applies to a welded joint in the thickness formulas, set by the joint
type and how much of it is radiographed (Table UW-12, 2025 Edition). It goes straight into the
[shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness) and [head](/asme/heads) formulas, so a lower E means a thicker wall. The
Code text is ASME's and paid; this guide cites paragraphs.

## What are the joint efficiency values?

For the common butt joints, from Table UW-12:

| Joint type | Description | Full radiography | Spot radiography | None |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Double-welded butt joint, or equivalent full penetration | 1.00 | 0.85 | 0.70 |
| 2 | Single-welded butt joint with a backing strip left in | 0.90 | 0.80 | 0.65 |
| 3 | Single-welded butt joint without backing | – | – | 0.60 |

Lap and fillet joints (Types 4 to 6 and others) have lower values again and are limited in where they may be used.

## What is the difference between joint type and joint category?

Type is what the joint is (its form, Types 1 to 8); category is where it sits (A to D), because location decides how
much stress it carries:

- **Category A**: longitudinal welds in shells and nozzles, and the weld joining a hemispherical head to the shell. They carry the hoop stress, the higher one.
- **Category B**: circumferential welds between shell courses and between the shell and most formed heads.
- **Category C**: welds attaching flanges, tubesheets and flat heads.
- **Category D**: welds attaching nozzles and communicating chambers.

Both go on the [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## When is full radiography mandatory?

UW-11(a) makes full radiography of butt welds mandatory in several cases, among them:

- vessels in **lethal service**;
- butt welds thicker than the limit for the material (for P-No. 1 carbon steel, 1¼ in, 32 mm);
- **unfired steam boilers** with a design pressure above 50 psi (3.4 bar);
- wherever the designer has taken the full-radiography efficiency (E = 1.0 for a Type 1 joint).

Otherwise the choice is the designer's, and it is commercial: full radiography costs more in examination and saves
steel.

## How much thicker does a shell get with less radiography?

Take a 48 in inside diameter shell at 150 psi, S = 20,000 psi, corrosion allowance 0.125 in, Type 1 longitudinal
joints:

| Radiography | E | Hoop thickness | With corrosion | Plate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full | 1.00 | 3,618.75 / 19,910 = 0.182 in | 0.307 in | 5/16 in or ⅜ in |
| Spot | 0.85 | 3,618.75 / 16,910 = 0.214 in | 0.339 in | ⅜ in |
| None | 0.70 | 3,618.75 / 13,910 = 0.260 in | 0.385 in | 7/16 in |

The [shell calculator](/asme/shell-thickness) takes a separate E for the circumferential joints, which govern the
longitudinal-stress check.

## What joint efficiency does a seamless shell or head get?

A seamless part has no longitudinal joint, but its E still depends on the circumferential welds joining it: with
those spot radiographed to the rule for this case (UW-11(a)(5)(b)), a seamless part uses E = 1.0; without, 0.85
(UW-12(d)).

## Does full radiography of the long seams need anything else?

Yes: to take E = 1.0 on Category A joints, the Category B and C butt joints that intersect them must at least be spot
radiographed (UW-11(a)(5)(b)). That is why designers often specify "full RT of Category A, spot of Category B".

## Who sets the radiography method and acceptance?

The method comes from [Section V](/asme/section-v), which ASME describes as its NDE standards; acceptance comes from
Division 1: UW-51 for full radiography and UW-52 for spot. Division 1 also allows ultrasonic examination in place of
radiography in defined cases; check your 2025 book for the conditions.

## When does joint efficiency apply at all?

To Section VIII Division 1 vessels, which ASME describes as covering "pressure vessels operating over 15 psig,
fired/unfired". Section I boilers have their own weld rules in Part PW.

## What does our software keep for joint efficiency?

Our US boiler demo's weld map records each seam's category (A, B or D), joint type, WPS, welder stamps, NDE method
(RT spot or full, UT, MT) and report, and prints it in the job's ASME record package, so the E on the calculation and
the radiography actually done can be compared. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: MAWP, design pressure, operating pressure and MDMT
question: What is the difference between MAWP and design pressure?
answer: Design pressure is the pressure a vessel is designed for, set from the process with a margin. MAWP (maximum allowable working pressure) is the highest pressure the finished vessel can take at its top, at the design temperature, worked out from the thicknesses actually used, so it is at least the design pressure. Operating pressure sits below both, and the relief device is normally set at or below MAWP.
description: MAWP vs design pressure vs operating pressure in ASME Section VIII, worked from plate thickness, with static head, relief set pressure and MDMT.
