body:
## What is the difference between MAWP and design pressure?

Design pressure is what the vessel is designed for; MAWP is what the finished vessel can actually take. The owner
or designer sets the design pressure, with its coincident temperature, from the process (UG-21 in Section VIII
Division 1, 2025 Edition). MAWP is calculated afterwards from the thicknesses actually used, less corrosion
allowance, for every part, and the weakest part sets it (UG-98 and Mandatory Appendix 3). It is therefore at least
the design pressure. The Code text is ASME's and paid; this guide cites paragraphs and works examples.

| Pressure | What it is | Who sets it |
|---|---|---|
| Operating pressure | What the process normally runs at | The process |
| Relief set pressure | Where the relief device opens; normally at or below MAWP | The designer, within Code limits |
| Design pressure | What the vessel is designed for, at the top, with the coincident temperature | The owner or designer (UG-21) |
| MAWP | The most the completed vessel can take at the top, at the design temperature, from its actual thicknesses | Calculated (UG-98) |

## How do you calculate MAWP from a plate thickness?

Rearrange the thickness formula for pressure, using the corroded thickness and radius. For a cylindrical shell under
UG-27(c)(1), MAWP = SEt / (R + 0.6t). Worked example, the same shell as the [shell thickness guide](/asme/shell-thickness):
⅜ in plate, corrosion allowance 0.125 in, inside radius 24 in, S = 20,000 psi, E = 0.85.

1. Corroded thickness t = 0.375 − 0.125 = 0.250 in; corroded radius R = 24 + 0.125 = 24.125 in.
2. Hoop stress: MAWP = 20,000 × 0.85 × 0.25 / (24.125 + 0.6 × 0.25) = 4,250 / 24.275 = **175.1 psi**.
3. Longitudinal stress (UG-27(c)(2)): 2SEt / (R − 0.4t) = 8,500 / 24.025 = 353.8 psi, so the hoop case governs.
4. If the plate may arrive 0.01 in thin (the under-tolerance UG-16(c) allows for plate), t = 0.240 in and MAWP = 4,080 / 24.269 = **168.1 psi**.

The shell calculator on that page does the same, taking the lower of the two cases. The heads, nozzles and flanges
have their own MAWPs, and the vessel's MAWP is the lowest of all of them.

## Can MAWP be higher than design pressure?

Yes. Plate comes in standard thicknesses, so the shell above, designed for 150 psi, can take 168 psi as built. Many
owners still stamp MAWP equal to the design pressure to keep the relief valve and the nameplate simple; that is
allowed. A higher MAWP leaves room for a later rerate.

## Where is MAWP measured?

At the top of the vessel in its normal operating position, at the stated temperature. Parts lower down also see the
static head of the liquid and are designed for it: 20 ft of water adds 20 × 0.433 = 8.7 psi, so with an MAWP of 150 psi
at the top the bottom course is checked for 158.7 psi.

## Does MAWP use new or corroded thickness?

Corroded: the thickness left at the end of the corrosion allowance, at the design temperature, where the allowable
stress from Section II Part D is lowest. Some owners also ask for a "new and cold" pressure, which is higher; it is an
owner's term, not a Division 1 one. The [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) is set from MAWP.

## What design pressure margin should I use?

A common practice is design pressure about 10% above the maximum operating pressure, or 25 psi (1.7 bar) above it at
low pressures, so normal swings don't lift the relief valve. That margin is practice, not a Code rule: the Code only
requires that the vessel is protected and the relief device set within its limits.

## Where should the relief valve be set?

Normally at or below MAWP for a single device. Division 1's overpressure protection rules (the UG-150 series since the
2021 Edition) say when a vessel needs protection and how much pressure may rise while it relieves; the device itself
is built to [Section XIII](/asme/section-xiii), which ASME describes as setting "requirements for design, materials,
inspection, testing, and marking of pressure relief valves, rupture disks, and related devices".

## How far can pressure rise above MAWP while a valve relieves?

In Division 1, generally by 10% or 3 psi (whichever is greater) with one device, 16% or 4 psi with several, and 21%
for fire exposure. Worked example: MAWP 150 psi, one valve set at 150 psi → pressure may reach 165 psi while
relieving; under fire, 181.5 psi. Check the overpressure paragraphs of your 2025 Division 1 for the exact conditions.

## What is MDMT?

The minimum design metal temperature: the coldest the metal may be while the vessel is at its MAWP, from a winter
start-up, an autorefrigerating flash or a cold fluid. It decides whether materials need impact testing; see
[MDMT and impact testing](/asme/impact-testing). MAWP at its temperature and MDMT at its pressure both go on the
nameplate and the [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## When does a vessel have to be designed to Section VIII at all?

ASME describes Division 1 as providing rules "for pressure vessels operating over 15 psig, fired/unfired"; at 15 psi
or less a vessel is outside its scope, though the law where it is installed may still regulate it. See
[Section VIII](/asme/section-viii) and [US boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## What does our software keep for MAWP?

Our US boiler demo keeps each job's calculation sheet (UG-27(c)(1) for vessel shells, PG-27 for boiler shells) and
prints MAWP at temperature and MDMT on the job's data report layout in the ASME record package, with the hydro test
record set from it. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: Material test reports (MTR) and heat number traceability
question: What does an MTR need to show for ASME pressure vessel material?
answer: A material test report (MTR, or mill test certificate) certifies one heat of material: its specification and grade, heat number, chemical analysis, mechanical test results and heat treatment. For ASME Section VIII work the shop checks plate against its MTR on receipt (UG-93), keeps the heat number on every piece when it is cut (UG-77), and records it against every part of the vessel.

body:
## What is an MTR?

An MTR (material test report, also called a mill test report, mill test certificate or CMTR) is the producer's
certificate that one heat of material meets its specification, with the test results to prove it. A mill makes
steel in **heats** (one melt); the MTR certifies a heat, or a lot from it, against a specification such as SA-516
Grade 70.

| On the MTR | What the shop checks |
|---|---|
| Specification, grade, class and edition, e.g. SA-516 Grade 70 | Matches the drawing and a specification the Code accepts; see [Section II](/asme/section-ii) for SA vs A |
| Heat number (and slab or plate number) | Matches the number stamped or stenciled on the material |
| Size, thickness and quantity | Matches what was delivered |
| Chemical analysis (heat, and product if ordered) | Within the specification's limits |
| Tensile and yield strength, elongation | At or above the specification's minimums |
| Heat treatment (as-rolled, normalized, quenched and tempered) | What was ordered; it affects the [impact test](/asme/impact-testing) exemption |
| Charpy results, if ordered | Present, at the temperature ordered, when the part isn't exempt |
| Supplementary requirements | E.g. ultrasonic examination, simulated post-weld heat treatment, as ordered |
| Certification statement, signature, producer | Who certified it, and that the certificate is the producer's |

India and Europe usually call it a [material test certificate](/systems/material-test-certificate) and order it to
EN 10204 type 3.1; the US says MTR or CMTR. What the Code needs from it is the same.

## What does ASME Section VIII require for material certification?

[Section VIII, Division 1](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/bpvc-standards/bpvc-2025) requires plate for pressure parts to come with the producer's material test report (or a
certificate of compliance where the material specification allows one), which the shop obtains and the Authorized
Inspector examines to confirm it represents the material and meets its specification (UG-93). The paragraphs that
matter, in outline (the Code is copyrighted; read the edition your shop works to):

| Paragraph | What it covers |
|---|---|
| UG-93, inspection of materials | Plate: obtain the MTR and have the Inspector examine it. Other product forms (pipe, tube, forgings, fittings, bolting) may be accepted on the specification's marking on each piece, with supplementary reports where extra requirements were ordered. The shop also examines material for imperfections |
| UG-94, marking on materials | The Inspector checks that the material carries the marking its specification requires |
| UG-77, material identification | When plate is cut, the identification is transferred to every piece that goes into the vessel, or a coded marking system acceptable to the Inspector is used |
| UG-10 | How material not fully identified, or made to a specification not permitted, may be recertified for use |
| Section II, Part A | The material specifications themselves (SA-516 and others), and for plate, SA-20's general requirements for marking and test reports |

How the shop does all of this is written in its [quality control manual](/asme/quality-control-manual), which the
ASME joint review checks before the [U stamp](/asme/u-stamp) is issued.

## What is the difference between EN 10204 3.1 and 3.2?

An [EN 10204](https://knowledge.bsigroup.com/products/metallic-products-types-of-inspection-documents) type 3.1 certificate is issued by the manufacturer and validated by its own authorized inspection
representative, who is independent of the manufacturing department; a type 3.2 is validated jointly by that
representative and either the purchaser's authorized representative or an inspector designated by the regulations.
Both report specific test results on the material delivered.

| EN 10204 type | What it is | Who validates it |
|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Declaration of compliance, no test results | The manufacturer |
| 2.2 | Test report, results from non-specific inspection (typical production, not this lot) | The manufacturer |
| 3.1 | Inspection certificate, results of tests on the product supplied | The manufacturer's inspection representative, independent of production |
| 3.2 | Inspection certificate, as 3.1 with a second, independent witness | The manufacturer's representative and the purchaser's or a regulator's inspector |

For ASME work, an MTR equivalent to 3.1 is normal. Specify 3.2 only when the purchase order, the customer or a
regulator needs a third party to witness the tests, and allow for the cost and lead time it adds. Types 2.1 and 2.2
don't carry the heat's own test results, so they don't serve as an MTR for plate.

## Is a distributor's certificate as good as a mill MTR?

A distributor (service center) usually passes on a copy of the mill's MTR; that copy is what the shop needs, provided
it is legible, complete and traceable to the heat delivered. EN 10204 covers intermediaries too: they may pass the
producer's document on, but not change its content. Watch for:

- **A distributor's own certificate of conformance** that lists only the grade. It isn't the producer's test report
  and won't satisfy UG-93 for plate.
- **Cut-to-size plate.** If the distributor cut the plate, each piece must still carry the heat number; ask how they
  transfer it.
- **A re-typed MTR on the distributor's letterhead.** Ask for the mill's original document.
- **Mixed heats in one delivery.** One MTR per heat; check every piece's heat number against a certificate.

## What should you check when material arrives?

Before material goes into stock:

1. The heat number on each piece matches an MTR in the delivery.
2. The specification, grade, class and size match the purchase order and the drawing.
3. Chemistry and mechanical results are within the specification; supplementary tests ordered are reported.
4. Heat treatment and any Charpy tests are as ordered.
5. The material isn't damaged, laminated or pitted beyond what the specification allows.
6. The MTR is the producer's, signed or otherwise certified, and filed against the receipt.
7. Anything that fails goes to a nonconformance hold, not the rack.

## How do you keep heat numbers when plate is cut?

Before the plate is cut, transfer the heat number (and any plate number) to every piece that will go into the
vessel, by stamp, stencil or a coded system the Inspector accepts, so each piece stays traceable (UG-77). Then record
which pieces came from which heat. A made-up example: one SA-516 Grade 70 plate, heat A71234, cut for one job.

| Piece | Part | Marking | Recorded against |
|---|---|---|---|
| A71234-1 | Shell course 1 | Heat number stenciled before cutting | Job 5021, shell 1 |
| A71234-2 | Shell course 2 | Heat number stenciled before cutting | Job 5021, shell 2 |
| A71234-3 | Nozzle reinforcing pad | Low-stress stamp | Job 5021, N1 pad |
| A71234-R | Remnant, 1.2 m × 0.8 m | Heat number transferred, back to stock | Remnant stock, MTR attached |

The [data report](/asme/data-reports) then lists the material of each part, and the Inspector can trace any part
back to its MTR.

## Where does traceability break?

- Offcuts and remnants returned to stock without their heat number, then reused on the next job.
- One MTR filed for a delivery that held two heats.
- Nozzle necks and pipe cut from a length whose marking ended up on the scrap end.
- Markings ground off or painted over in fabrication before anyone recorded them.
- MTRs scanned into a folder with no link to the parts they cover.

Each of these turns up at the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector)'s check of the data report package.

## What should material traceability software do?

When comparing systems, check that it can:

- Record the heat number and attach the MTR at receipt, against the purchase order line.
- Hold material that fails the receipt check, with the reason.
- Split a plate into cut pieces and remnants that each inherit the heat number.
- Show, for any vessel part, its heat and MTR; and for any heat, every part and job it went into.
- Link welds to the WPS and welder, so the data report package comes from one record.

That is [material traceability](/systems/material-traceability): recording the heat number at receipt and carrying
it to every cut piece, remnant and weld removes the search at the end.

## What does India's IBR require?

IBR 2026 asks for the steel maker's certificate in Form V Part A and an extract of every material certificate (Form V
Part B) with the registration papers, and lists ASME SA specifications among acceptable materials. See
[ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr) and [IBR Form V Part A](/ibr/forms/form-v-part-a).

body:
## What is National Board registration for a pressure vessel?

It is the filing of a stamped item's Manufacturer's Data Report with the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel
Inspectors (NBBI), which keeps it as a permanent record; the nameplate then carries the NB mark and a National Board
number. The National Board describes registration as "the culmination of a three-step process": construction to the
ASME Code, inspection by a National Board commissioned inspector, and the documentation certifying compliance.

## Who is the National Board?

The body of the chief boiler inspectors of most US states and Canadian provinces and territories, and many large US
cities. ASME writes the construction code; the National Board commissions inspectors, keeps the registry of built
items, and writes the code for equipment once it's in service, the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC).

## Is National Board registration required?

In many jurisdictions, yes. ASME's handbook warns that registration "may be required by the legal authority of a
state or municipality of the United States or province of Canada". Pennsylvania, for example, requires an ASME boiler
or unfired pressure vessel to be stamped with "its National Board registration number" (34 Pa. Code §3a.21(b)), and
California requires new air tanks to be National Board registered. Check the jurisdiction for the place of
installation; see [US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## How does a manufacturer become authorized to register?

By meeting the National Board's criteria in NB-264 and applying online. The National Board says: "There is no charge
to become authorized to register, but there is a fee for each item registered." The manufacturer's quality control
manual then says how registration numbers are controlled, who submits the forms and how fast.

## How soon must a data report be registered?

Within 30 days of certification. NB-264 (Revision 19) says the time between the Inspector's certification and
submitting the registration forms "shall not exceed 30 days".

## How are data reports filed?

On paper (the original report, in the exact format of the Code's form) or through the National Board's Electronic
Data Transfer (EDT) system. Since 1 January 2026 items built to the 2025 Code must be on the 2025 forms; reports on
outdated forms are returned. See [data reports](/asme/data-reports).

## What does the NB mark on a nameplate mean?

That the item's data report is on file with the National Board. In the National Board's words, "The NB mark is used by
manufacturers to identify items registered with the National Board." For an owner, it means a lost data report can
always be replaced, which matters at every later inspection, repair or sale.

## What is the NBIC?

The National Board Inspection Code: the rules for pressure equipment after it is built, in four Parts: Part 1
Installation, Part 2 Inspection, Part 3 Repairs and Alterations, and Part 4 Pressure Relief Devices. The National Board
says the NBIC "is adopted into law by most US and Canadian jurisdictions", and it is published every two years; the
current edition is 2025.

## What changed in the 2025 NBIC?

Among hundreds of revisions, the National Board's summary says "Quality System" became "Quality Management System"
throughout, and new supplements were added for classifying repairs and alterations (Supplement 10) and for engineered
repairs and alterations (Supplement 11). Check the (25) markers in your copy for the details.

## What are the R, VR, NR and T/O stamps?

| Stamp | For |
|---|---|
| R | Repairs and alterations to boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items |
| VR | Repair of pressure relief valves |
| NR | Repair and replacement of nuclear components |
| T/O | In-service testing of pressure relief valves |

## How does a company get the R stamp, and what does it cost?

By having an inspection agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency, a written quality system that meets the
current NBIC and NB-415, the current NBIC itself and the construction code for its scope, then passing an on-site
review, which can be held together with an ASME joint review. The National Board's page gives the certificate fee as
$1,150 for three years, plus a one-time $150 for the loan of the steel R stamp for new holders.

## Which forms record a repair or alteration?

NBIC Form R-1, Report of Repair (NB-66), and Form R-2, Report of Alteration (NB-229), both available through EDT; R-3
reports parts fabricated by welding and R-4 is a supplementary sheet. For registered items, the R-1 or R-2 is filed
with the National Board too.

## What does our software keep for registration?

Our US boiler demo records each job's National Board number on its ASME record package and data report layout, with
the full record behind it. It doesn't file through EDT; a shop files the official form there or on paper. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers in ASME Section IX
question: What is a P-number in welding?
answer: A P-number groups base metals with similar welding behaviour, so a procedure or welder test on one covers the others in the group: P-No. 1 is carbon steel, P-No. 8 austenitic stainless. F-numbers group filler metals by usability, such as F-4 for low-hydrogen electrodes like E7018, and A-numbers group steel weld metal by chemistry.
description: ASME Section IX P-numbers, Group numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers explained, with common materials and electrodes in each and what they mean for a PQR or WPQ.

body:
## What is a P-number in welding?

A P-number is Section IX's group for base metals that weld alike, so that a procedure qualified on one material
covers the others in its group. There are thousands of material specifications; without grouping, every pairing
would need its own procedure test. Section IX lists the assignments in QW/QB-422, by specification and grade.
Section IX is ASME's paid Code; this guide gives common cases, and the 2025 tables are the authority.

## What are the common P-numbers?

| P-No. | Materials | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Carbon and carbon-manganese steels | SA-516 Gr 70, SA-106 Gr B, SA-105 |
| 3 | C–½Mo and low-chromium steels | SA-204, SA-335 P1 |
| 4 | 1–1¼Cr–½Mo steels | SA-387 Gr 11, SA-335 P11 |
| 5A | 2¼Cr–1Mo steels | SA-387 Gr 22, SA-335 P22 |
| 5B | 5Cr to 9Cr steels | SA-335 P5, P9 |
| 7 | Ferritic stainless | SA-240 Type 405, 409, 430 |
| 8 | Austenitic stainless | SA-240 Type 304, 316, 321 |
| 10H | Duplex stainless | SA-240 S31803, S32205 |
| 15E | Creep-strength enhanced ferritic steels | SA-335 P91 |
| 21–26 | Aluminum alloys | SB-209 5083 |
| 31–35 | Copper alloys | SB-171 |
| 41–49 | Nickel alloys | SB-168 Alloy 600, SB-443 Alloy 625 |
| 51–53 | Titanium | SB-265 Grade 2 |

The base metal's specification and grade come from its [MTR](/asme/mtr); see [Section II](/asme/section-ii) for SA
versus ASTM A specifications.

## What P-number is SA-516 Grade 70?

P-No. 1, Group 2. SA-516 is the carbon steel plate most pressure vessel and boiler shops buy, and Grade 70 sits in
Group 2 of P-No. 1 with other carbon steels of its strength. Check the grade's line in QW/QB-422 of the edition
you're working to before writing it on a WPS.

## What is a Group number for?

Group numbers split a ferrous P-number by toughness behaviour. They matter only when the construction code requires
impact testing: a change of Group number is then a supplementary essential variable, so a PQR on P-No. 1 Group 1
may not cover Group 2 for impact-tested work. See [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables) and
[impact testing](/asme/impact-testing).

## Do I need a new PQR to weld P-No. 1 to P-No. 8?

Yes. A joint between two different P-numbers is a dissimilar-metal joint and needs a procedure qualified for that
combination (or one the rules let it cover), usually with a nickel alloy or austenitic filler. A PQR for P-No. 1 to
P-No. 1 does not cover it.

## What is an F-number?

An F-number groups filler metals by usability, meaning how hard they are to weld with (QW-432):

| F-No. | Filler | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Heavy iron-powder steel electrodes | E7024 |
| 2 | Rutile steel electrodes | E6013 |
| 3 | Cellulosic steel electrodes | E6010, E6011 |
| 4 | Low-hydrogen steel electrodes | E7018 |
| 5 | Stainless steel electrodes | E308L-16 |
| 6 | Solid and metal-cored steel wires and rods (GTAW, GMAW, SAW) | ER70S-6 |
| 43 | Nickel alloy filler | ERNiCrMo-3 |

The filler metal specifications themselves (SFA-5.1 for carbon steel covered electrodes, SFA-5.18 for wires and rods)
are in Section II Part C, which ASME lists among the required code books for certificate holders that weld.

## Does an F-4 welder qualify for E6010?

Generally yes within the same process: F-numbers matter most for welders, and a welder qualified with an F-4
electrode is generally also qualified for F-1 to F-3, but not the other way round. Section IX's QW-433 table sets the
exact pairings, including the effect of welding with or without backing, so check it before assigning a welder.

## What is an A-number?

An A-number classifies the chemistry of deposited steel weld metal (QW-442): A-1 carbon steel, A-2 carbon–molybdenum,
up to A-8 austenitic chromium–nickel and others. A change of A-number is a procedure essential variable for most
processes, so a PQR made with a carbon steel filler doesn't cover a chromium–molybdenum one.

## Where should P-, F- and A-numbers be recorded?

On every WPS and PQR: ASME's suggested PQR format (QW-483) has fields for them, and reviewers check them first. Check
a material's P-number in the current edition, since new materials are added and occasionally regrouped. The
documents themselves are explained in [WPS vs PQR vs WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq).

## How does this connect to material traceability?

The P-number on a WPS is only as good as the record that says which plate is in which seam. A shop that keeps each
piece's heat number when plate is cut can show which specification, grade and P-number went into every weld; see
[MTRs and heat numbers](/asme/mtr). Our US boiler demo prints each WPS with its P-number range (for example P-No. 1
to P-No. 1) next to MTRs by heat number in the job's ASME record package.

title: Post-weld heat treatment requirements (UCS-56)
question: When is post-weld heat treatment required by ASME?
answer: ASME Section VIII Division 1 requires post-weld heat treatment (PWHT) by material and thickness: Table UCS-56-1 sets, for each P-number, the minimum holding temperature, the time per inch of thickness and when it can be skipped. For P-No. 1 carbon steel, PWHT is generally required above 1½ in (38 mm), held at 1,100 °F (595 °C) or more, and some services need it at any thickness.

body:
## When is post-weld heat treatment required by ASME?

For Section VIII Division 1 carbon and low-alloy steel vessels, PWHT is required by P-number and thickness under
Table UCS-56-1, and by service whatever the thickness in some cases. The table gives, for each P-number, the minimum
holding temperature, the minimum time at temperature by thickness, and the conditions under which PWHT may be
omitted; its notes carry most of the detail. The Code text is ASME's and paid; this guide outlines the 2025 rules and
your copy of UCS-56 is the authority.

## Why heat treat after welding?

Welding leaves high residual stresses and hard zones beside the weld. PWHT (stress relieving) heats the part below
its transformation temperature and holds it there, which relaxes the stresses and tempers the hard zones. It improves
toughness and resistance to some kinds of cracking, at the cost of furnace time and, sometimes, strength.

## What are the PWHT requirements for carbon steel?

For P-No. 1, the commonest case, Table UCS-56-1 sets in outline:

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Minimum holding temperature | 1,100 °F (595 °C) |
| Holding time, up to 2 in (50 mm) thick | 1 hour per inch, at least 15 minutes |
| Holding time, over 2 in (50 mm) | 2 hours plus 15 minutes for each inch over 2 in |
| Exemption by thickness | Not mandatory up to 1¼ in (32 mm) nominal thickness, and up to 1½ in (38 mm) with a minimum preheat of 200 °F (95 °C), subject to the table's notes |

Other P-numbers have their own temperatures and much narrower exemptions; chromium–molybdenum steels (P-No. 4, 5A)
nearly always need it.

## When is PWHT required whatever the thickness?

- **Lethal service**: Division 1 requires PWHT of carbon and low-alloy steel vessels in lethal service (UW-2).
- **Low temperature**: some impact-test exemptions depend on it; see [impact testing](/asme/impact-testing).
- **The owner's specification**: caustic, amine, wet H₂S and similar services often call for PWHT to resist stress-corrosion cracking, beyond the Code minimum.

## Can you show a worked example?

A 1½ in (38 mm) P-No. 1 shell that needs PWHT (no preheat credit taken): hold at no less than 1,100 °F for
1.5 hours. Above 800 °F (425 °C), UCS-56(d) limits the heating rate to 400 °F per hour divided by the thickness in
inches, so 400 / 1.5 = 267 °F/h at most, and the cooling rate to 500 °F per hour divided by the thickness, so
500 / 1.5 = 333 °F/h, each with an overall cap. A 3 in shell holds for 2 h 15 min, with heating at no more than 133 °F/h.

## How is PWHT done and recorded?

In a furnace (whole vessel or in sections) or locally around a weld band, under UW-40's rules. Temperatures are
recorded by thermocouples on the part, and the chart showing heating rate, hold temperature and time, and cooling
rate is part of the vessel's record. PWHT is declared on the [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## Does PWHT change the welding procedure?

Yes. Adding or removing PWHT, or changing its temperature and time range, is a procedure essential variable in
Section IX (QW-407), so the WPS must be supported by a PQR heat treated the same way. Section IX is the Code's section
that ASME says "contains rules relating to the qualification of welding, brazing, and fusing procedures as required
by other BPVC sections". See [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables).

## What about Section I boilers?

Section I has its own PWHT table (PW-39) with its own thickness exemptions. A boiler shop and a vessel shop working
the same steel can therefore have different PWHT triggers on the same day.

## When does UCS-56 apply?

To carbon and low-alloy steel parts of Section VIII Division 1 vessels, the Division ASME describes as covering
"pressure vessels operating over 15 psig, fired/unfired". High-alloy steels follow Part UHA.

## How does this work under IBR in India?

IBR 2026 asks for heat treatment charts of welded drums with a boiler's registration documents; see
[boiler registration documents](/ibr/registration-documents) and [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## What does our software keep for PWHT?

Our US boiler demo records each job's PWHT decision with its basis (for example "P-No. 1 at ½ in nominal thickness,
below 1½ in"), and the temperature, hold, rate and chart where it is done, and prints it in the ASME record package
next to each WPS's PWHT condition. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

The joint review checks the manual against ASME's checklist, then watches the shop work the way it says.

body:
## What should an ASME quality control manual include?

Every element of the quality control system the Code lists for the shop's scope, described as the shop actually works.
ASME's handbook puts it plainly: the applicant "must address each element of the QCS in the Code", but "need only
demonstrate those elements within the intended scope of activities that apply to their program". For Section VIII
Division 1 the elements are listed in its quality control system appendix (Mandatory Appendix 10); Section I and the
other construction sections have equivalents. In outline:

| Element | What the manual says |
|---|---|
| Authority and responsibility | Who is responsible for quality, and that they can stop work |
| Organization | An org chart showing the quality function's independence |
| Drawings, calculations and specifications | How they are prepared or received, checked, approved, revised and issued |
| Material control | Receiving, checking against the [MTR](/asme/mtr), marking and traceability through cutting |
| Examination and inspection program | What is checked, when, and the Inspector's hold points |
| Correction of nonconformities | How a nonconformity is recorded, decided and closed |
| Welding | [WPS, PQR and WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq) control, welder identification, [continuity](/asme/welder-continuity) |
| Nondestructive examination | Procedures to [Section V](/asme/section-v), personnel qualification |
| Heat treatment | Procedures and records, including [PWHT](/asme/pwht) charts |
| Calibration | Gauges and test equipment, intervals and records |
| Records retention | Which records are kept, where, for how long |
| Sample forms | Every form the manual refers to |
| Inspection of vessels and parts | How the Authorized Inspector is given access and information |

## Does the manual have to follow ASME's format?

No. The handbook says "The Manual need not follow the format of this Guide." What it must do is cover every element
for the scope, and the shop must show where: ASME's review checklist (below) maps each element to the manual's own
paragraphs.

## Does the manual have to be in English?

Yes. The handbook requires that "The written description and documentation which support understanding of the
program must be in English." A shop in India or elsewhere may run the floor in another language, but the manual and
the documents the review team reads are in English.

## What is ASME's review checklist?

The "Guide for ASME Review Teams for Review of Applicants": a checklist of the quality control system's elements for
the certificate applied for. ASME has four: one for pressure relief devices, one for RP (Section X), one for cast iron
and cast aluminum H boilers, and a General checklist for A, M, PP, S, E, H, HLW, U, UM, U2, U3, PRT and T. The
applicant fills in, against each element, the paragraph of its manual that addresses it, and gives the completed
guide to the review team.

## What is CA-1 and does the manual need it?

CA-1 is ASME's Conformity Assessment Requirements standard, which ASME now lists among the required code books for
every boiler and pressure vessel certificate. Buy it with the Code sections for your scope and check the manual
against both; where the 2025 construction section and CA-1 place a quality system requirement is worth confirming with
your Authorized Inspection Agency before the review.

## Can I buy a quality control manual template?

You can, but it has to describe your shop, and ASME won't write it for you: its FAQ says "ASME does not provide
consulting services to develop a Quality Control System". A bought template with another company's job titles and
forms fails the moment the team asks someone to show a step. Every form in the manual should be the form used on the
shop floor.

## How does the joint review test the manual?

It reads the manual, then watches the shop do what it says. The handbook describes an on-site evaluation of both the
written description and "a demonstration of implementation of the program", which may use "current work, a mock-up,
or a combination of the two". A reviewer typically picks a weld on the demonstration item and follows it to the welder,
their qualification and continuity, the WPS, the PQR, the filler metal and the NDE report; each link has to be there.
See [how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

## Who checks the manual is followed after certification?

The [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector), on every job and at the agency's periodic audits, and the
next joint review at renewal. The manual's hold points are where the Inspector signs off, so the manual and the job's
inspection plan should name the same ones.

## How should records be kept so the manual works?

So that each link is recorded once: a record per weld, heat number and welder, joined to the job, rather than files
cross-referenced by hand. That is the test most shops find hardest on paper. Our US boiler demo keeps nonconformities
(with a QC verification step before an NCR can close), incoming inspection, hold points and the welding and
material records on each job, and prints the job's ASME record package from them. See
[material traceability](/services/material-traceability).

title: ASME Section I vs IV: power vs heating boilers
question: What is the difference between ASME Section I and Section IV boilers?
answer: Section IV covers heating boilers: steam boilers up to 15 psi (1 bar), and hot water boilers up to 160 psi (11 bar) and 250 °F (121 °C). Anything above those limits is a power boiler under Section I, which has stricter design, material, examination and inspection rules. The certificates differ too: S (with A, E, M and PP) for Section I, H and HLW for Section IV.

body:
## Where is the line between a Section I and a Section IV boiler?

The line is pressure and temperature: Section IV covers steam boilers up to 15 psi (1 bar) and hot water boilers up
to 160 psi (11 bar) and 250 °F (121 °C); anything above either limit is a power boiler under Section I. Section IV
states its limits in its scope paragraph (HG-101 in the 2025 Edition).

| | Section IV (heating boilers) | Section I (power boilers) |
|---|---|---|
| Steam boilers | Up to 15 psi (1 bar) | Above 15 psi (1 bar) |
| Hot water boilers | Up to 160 psi (11 bar) and 250 °F (121 °C) | Above 160 psi (11 bar) or above 250 °F (121 °C) |
| Typical use | Space heating, domestic hot water | Process steam, power generation, high-temperature hot water |
| ASME certificates | H; HLW for lined potable water heaters | S, plus A (assembly), E (electric), M (miniature), PP (pressure piping) |
| Main data reports | H-2, H-3; H-5 and H-5A for cast iron and cast aluminum | P-2, P-3, P-4 family |

The certificates are as ASME's [certification page](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/Boiler-and-Pressure-Vessel-Certification) lists them. Section IV allows cast iron and cast
aluminum sectional boilers, which Section I does not, and its rules are simpler throughout because far less energy
is stored at low pressure.

## Which certificate does each kind of boiler need?

A power boiler is built and stamped by an S certificate holder; a heating boiler by an H holder. Section I also has
A for assembling power boilers, E for electric boilers, M for miniature boilers and PP for boiler external piping;
Section IV has HLW for lined potable water heaters. Parts makers without design responsibility can hold PRT in both
sections. Each is a separate certificate with its own joint review, though ASME's FAQ says an S holder can add A or PP
without a full new review. See [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps).

## Which data report does each use?

A Section I boiler is reported on Form P-2 (all types except watertube and electric), P-2A (electric) or P-3
(watertube boilers, superheaters, waterwalls and economizers), with P-4 for parts and P-4A for fabricated piping. A
Section IV boiler uses H-2 (all types except watertube and cast iron), H-3 (watertube) or the H-5 and H-5A master
data reports for cast iron and cast aluminum. All are free fillable PDFs on ASME's
[data report forms page](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/asme-data-report-forms); see [data reports](/asme/data-reports).

## Does a Section IV boiler need an Authorized Inspector?

Yes, except a cast iron or cast aluminum boiler. The H certificate for cast iron and cast aluminum boilers needs no
inspection agency agreement: ASME's handbook says it is issued for one year, renewed by an annual joint review led by
an ASME Designee with no Authorized Inspection Agency involved. Every other Section IV and Section I certificate needs
an agreement with an ASME-accredited agency, whose [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) inspects the
boiler and signs its data report.

## What changes for the shop between Section I and Section IV?

Section I is stricter at every step:

- **Design**: Section I has its own formulas in Part PG (PG-27 for cylindrical shells and tubes) and sets thicknesses
  for drums, headers and tubes; Section IV's rules are simpler and include minimum thicknesses.
- **Examination**: more volumetric examination of welds under Section I.
- **Testing**: a Section I boiler is hydrostatically tested to at least 1.5 times its maximum allowable working
  pressure (PG-99); Section IV sets its own, lower test.
- **Code books**: ASME's [required list](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/ASME-Certification-Process/Required-Code-Books) for an S certificate is Section I, Section II Parts A to D,
  Section V, Section IX, B31.1 Power Piping and CA-1; for H and HLW (except cast iron) it is Section II Parts A, B and
  C, Section IV, Section IX and CA-1; for cast iron H, Section IV and CA-1.

## What hydrostatic test does a Section I boiler need?

At least 1.5 times its MAWP (PG-99): a firetube boiler with an MAWP of 150 psi is tested to at least 225 psi, with
the Authorized Inspector present. The [hydrostatic test guide](/asme/hydrostatic-test) has a calculator for Section I
and Section VIII.

## Who builds the boiler external piping?

A holder of a Section I certificate that covers it: S, A or PP. Boiler external piping runs from the boiler to the
first stop valve and beyond, as Section I defines it; it is designed to [B31.1](/asme/b31-1-vs-b31-3) but is part of
the Section I boiler, inspected by the Authorized Inspector. That is why B31.1 is on the required code book list for
those certificates.

## How does this work in India?

Boilers in India are registered under the Indian Boiler Regulations, 2026, whichever ASME section they were designed
to; IBR draws its own lines for small industrial boilers. How the two fit together is in
[ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## What does our software keep for a Section I boiler?

Our US boiler demo prints the ASME record package for a firetube boiler from the job's records: a Form P-2 layout
(our own, carrying the form's fields, not a copy of ASME's form), the weld map, WPS and PQR, QW-322 welder continuity,
MTRs by heat number, NDE, PWHT and the hydro test at 1.5 × MAWP. There are no Section IV jobs in the demo. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

body:
## What is the difference between SA-516 and A516?

SA-516 is ASME's adopted version of ASTM A516, printed in Section II Part A; a Code pressure part must be certified to
the SA specification, or to an ASTM edition the Code accepts as identical. ASTM writes most material standards; ASME
adopts them into Section II, adds an "S" (SA for ferrous, SB for nonferrous) and sometimes adds requirements. Each
adopted specification in Section II notes the ASTM edition it matches and any differences.

## What are the four Parts of Section II?

| Part | Contents | Typical specifications |
|---|---|---|
| A | Ferrous material specifications (two volumes) | SA-516 plate, SA-106 pipe, SA-105 forgings, SA-240 stainless plate |
| B | Nonferrous material specifications | SB-168 nickel alloy plate, SB-209 aluminum plate |
| C | Welding rods, electrodes and filler metals | SFA-5.1 (carbon steel covered electrodes such as E7018), SFA-5.18 (carbon steel wires and rods) |
| D | Properties | Allowable stresses, tensile and yield strength at temperature, external pressure charts, physical properties |

ASME describes Part A as providing "material specifications for ferrous materials adequate for safety in the field
of pressure equipment", and Part D as providing "material properties, allowable stress values, and design data".

## What is a dual-certified MTR?

A mill test report that certifies the material to both specifications at once, reading for example "SA-516/A516
Grade 70". Mills dual-certify so the same plate can go into Code and non-Code work; for a pressure part the SA
certification is the one that matters. See [MTRs and heat numbers](/asme/mtr).

## What if the MTR shows only the ASTM number?

Then the material isn't certified to the SA specification on its face. Division 1 has routes for accepting or
recertifying material that wasn't produced to the SA specification (UG-10), and the
[Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) decides whether the documentation is acceptable. The
[MTR guide](/asme/mtr) explains the options.

## Where do allowable stresses come from?

From Part D. Section VIII Division 1 and Section I take their maximum allowable stresses from Table 1A (ferrous) and
Table 1B (nonferrous), by specification, grade and temperature; Division 2 uses its own tables (5A and 5B), with
higher values because of its smaller design margin. The [shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness) and
[hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) calculators ask you to enter these values rather than supply them,
because the tables are ASME's and change between editions.

## Which Part D volume should I buy?

Customary (psi, °F) or Metric (MPa, °C): ASME sells both, and its required code book list for the U and S
certificates names "Part D-Properties-(Customary or Metric)", so one is enough. Use the volume that matches the units
of your calculations.

## Which Parts does a shop need for an ASME certificate?

For a U or S certificate, ASME's [required list](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/ASME-Certification-Process/Required-Code-Books) is Parts A, B, C and D. Part C (filler metals) can
be left out only if welding, brazing and fusing aren't in the shop's scope. See [BPVC sections](/asme/bpvc-sections).

## How do filler metals connect to Section IX?

Part C's SFA specifications classify filler metals; Section IX then groups them by F-number and A-number for
qualification. See [P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers](/asme/p-numbers).

## Does IBR in India accept SA materials?

Yes. IBR 2026's material rules allow materials to ASME and other international codes, and its own table names ASME SA
and SB specifications; covered electrodes are classified to ASME Section II Part C (SFA) or AWS specifications. See
[ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## What does our software keep for Section II materials?

Our US boiler demo files each plate, tube and pipe's MTR by heat number and prints them in the job's ASME record
package, so every part on the data report points back to a certified specification and grade. The calculation sheets
use an illustrative SA-516 Grade 70 stress excerpt, not ASME's table. See
[material traceability](/services/material-traceability).

A procedure is qualified by welding a test coupon and testing it (the PQR), then written up as a WPS; each welder is qualified by a test of their own (the WPQ). Section IX doesn't decide where welds go or how they're examined: the construction code does.

body:
## What is ASME Section IX?

ASME Section IX is the Code section that qualifies welding, brazing and fusing: the procedures a shop uses and the
people who use them. ASME's own description is that it "contains rules relating to the qualification of welding,
brazing, and fusing procedures as required by other BPVC sections". It answers two questions with test coupons: can
this procedure make a sound weld, and can this person make it. The Code text is ASME's and paid; this guide cites
paragraphs and explains them, and your copy of the [2025 Section IX](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/find-codes-standards/bpvc-ix-bpvc-section-ix-welding-brazing-fusing-qualifications) is the authority.

## What does Section IX not cover?

It doesn't say which joints are welded, the joint design, how much NDE a weld gets or when heat treatment is
needed. Those come from the construction code: [Section VIII](/asme/section-viii), [Section I](/asme/section-i-vs-iv)
or a [B31 piping code](/asme/b31-1-vs-b31-3), which then sends you to Section IX for qualification. That is why a
WPS cites Section IX for its qualification and the vessel's data report cites Section VIII for everything else.

## What are the parts of Section IX?

Section IX has four parts:

| Part | Covers |
|---|---|
| QG | General requirements shared by all processes, including the organization's responsibility for its qualifications |
| QW | Welding: procedure qualification (QW-200), performance qualification (QW-300), welding data and variables (QW-400) and standard welding procedure specifications (QW-500) |
| QB | Brazing |
| QF | Plastic fusing (polyethylene pipe) |

## What are a WPS, a PQR and a WPQ?

They are the three documents Section IX qualification produces:

- **WPS** (welding procedure specification): the written instruction a welder follows, with a range for each variable.
- **PQR** (procedure qualification record): the record of the test coupon that proves the WPS works: what was actually used, and the test results.
- **WPQ** (welder or welding operator performance qualification): the record that a person passed their test, and what it qualifies them for.

How they link and what goes in each is in [WPS vs PQR vs WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq); which changes need a new PQR is in
[essential variables](/asme/essential-variables); what a welder's test covers is in
[welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification); and how a welder keeps a qualification alive is the
[continuity rule](/asme/welder-continuity).

## Where do I get Section IX forms?

ASME publishes suggested formats free on its [data report forms page](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/asme-data-report-forms): QW-482 for a WPS, QW-483 for a PQR,
QW-484A for a welder's WPQ, QW-484B for a welding operator's, and QW-485 for demonstrating a standard welding
procedure specification, with QB and QF equivalents for brazing and fusing. They are suggested formats: a shop may use
its own layout if it records everything Section IX requires.

## How does Section IX group materials and filler metals?

It groups base metals by **P-number** (with Group numbers where toughness matters) and filler metals by **F-number**
and, for steel weld metal, **A-number**, so one test covers a family of materials instead of one specification. See
[P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers](/asme/p-numbers).

## Can a shop use another company's PQR?

No: each organization qualifies its own procedures and welders and takes responsibility for them (Part QG). The
exception is the standard welding procedure specifications published by AWS that Section IX accepts in Article V
(QW-500): a shop may use one after demonstrating it, recorded on the QW-485 format.

## Does a shop need Section IX for an ASME certificate?

Yes, if it welds. ASME's [required code books](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/ASME-Certification-Process/Required-Code-Books) list Section IX for the U, S, H and other certificates, and note
that Section II Part C and Sections V and IX are not required "if welding, brazing and fusing are not within the
scope of their work".

## Do B31.1 and B31.3 use Section IX?

Yes. Both piping codes send welding procedure and welder qualification to Section IX, and B31.3 adds some
requirements of its own. A shop's WPSs and PQRs can serve its vessel and its piping work where the variables fit
both codes; see [B31.1 vs B31.3](/asme/b31-1-vs-b31-3).

## What changed in the 2025 Edition of Section IX?

The changes are listed in the "Summary of Changes" at the front of the book, and they apply to new qualifications from
1 January 2026: the American Welding Society's [Welding Journal summary](https://www.aws.org/magazines-and-media/welding-journal/2025/july/wj-july-25-feature-05-sperko/) says the changes "will become
mandatory for new qualifications on January 1, 2026" (the article's detail is for AWS members). Procedures and
welders qualified under an earlier edition stay qualified; a new qualification follows the edition in force when it
is made. See [ASME Code editions](/asme/editions).

## What does our software keep for Section IX?

Our US boiler demo keeps the Section IX side of each job with the job: a weld map with each seam's WPS and welder
stamps, the WPS list with each PQR, P-numbers, thickness range and PWHT basis, and each welder's QW-322 continuity
per process, all printed in the job's ASME record package. It doesn't write or qualify procedures. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

It covers the method, not the verdict: which welds are examined, how much, and what counts as a rejectable flaw come from the construction section, such as Section VIII or Section I.

body:
## What is ASME Section V?

Section V is the Code's book of nondestructive examination methods: how radiography, ultrasonic, magnetic particle,
liquid penetrant, visual and leak testing are performed, written so that every construction section can point to one
set of methods. ASME describes it as its "NDE standards and specifications". The Code text is ASME's and paid; this
guide cites its Articles, and your 2025 Section V is the authority.

## Does Section V say whether a weld passes?

No. Section V covers the method; the verdict comes from the construction section. A radiograph is taken as Section V
says (film or digital, source and geometry, image quality indicators, density), but whether an indication on it is
acceptable is judged by, for example, Section VIII Division 1's UW-51 for full radiography or UW-52 for spot
radiography. That split is why an NDE procedure cites Section V and the NDE report cites Section VIII.

## Which Article covers which method?

| Article | Method |
|---|---|
| 1 | General requirements |
| 2 | Radiographic examination (RT), film and digital |
| 4 | Ultrasonic examination (UT) of welds, including phased array and time-of-flight diffraction |
| 5 | Ultrasonic examination of materials |
| 6 | Liquid penetrant examination (PT) |
| 7 | Magnetic particle examination (MT) |
| 9 | Visual examination (VT) |
| 10 | Leak testing |

Section V has further Articles for other methods (eddy current, acoustic emission and more) and a second subsection
that adopts ASTM standards for NDE.

## Who decides how much of a vessel is examined?

The construction section and the designer. Division 1 makes full radiography mandatory in some cases (UW-11) and
otherwise lets the designer choose, and the choice sets the [joint efficiency](/asme/joint-efficiency) and so the
wall thickness. Section I sets its own examination for boilers.

## How are NDE personnel qualified?

To a written practice, as the construction section requires. In US and Canadian shops that is usually the employer's
written practice to ASNT's SNT-TC-1A, with Level I, II and III personnel; the construction section names the standards
it accepts. India's IBR 2026 accepts Level III certificates from the Indian Society for Non-destructive Testing or the
American Society for Non-destructive Testing; see [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## Does a shop need Section V for an ASME certificate?

Yes, if it welds. ASME lists Section V among the required code books for the U and S certificates, and allows it to be
left out only if welding, brazing and fusing aren't in the shop's scope. See [BPVC sections](/asme/bpvc-sections).

## Can a welder be qualified by radiography?

Yes, for most processes: Section IX allows radiography or ultrasonic examination of the test coupon in place of bend
tests, with Section V setting the method. GMAW short-circuit welders are bend-tested. See
[welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification).

## What should an NDE report show?

The method and procedure, the Section V and construction-code references, the welds or areas examined, the extent
(full, spot), the technique, the examiner and their level, the date, the results with any indications, and the
acceptance decision. NDE reports go in the vessel's file and the [data report](/asme/data-reports) records the extent
of radiography.

## What does our software keep for NDE?

Our US boiler demo records each NDE report (method, extent, welds covered, examiner and level, date, result), links
it to the seams on the weld map, and prints both in the job's ASME record package. The demo has no film or image
storage. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: ASME Section VIII: Division 1 vs 2 vs 3

answer: Section VIII sets the rules for pressure vessels in three Divisions. Division 1 designs by rule with a design factor of 3.5 on tensile strength and covers most vessels. Division 2 uses a factor of 2.4, so walls are thinner, in return for more analysis, a User's Design Specification and a certified design report. Division 3 is for very high pressures. Each needs its own certificate: U, U2 or U3.

body:
## What does ASME Section VIII cover?

Section VIII is the Code's pressure vessel section: tanks, columns, reactors, heat exchangers, receivers and other
vessels that hold internal or external pressure, in three Divisions. Fired equipment that generates steam belongs to
[Section I](/asme/section-i-vs-iv) instead. Division 1's scope paragraph (U-1 in the 2025 Edition) excludes some
equipment outright, among them vessels for 15 psi (1 bar) or less and vessels of 6 in (152 mm) inside diameter or
less, which is why many low-pressure tanks are built to other standards. The Code text is ASME's and paid; this
guide cites paragraphs and explains them, and your copy of the [2025 Edition](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/bpvc-standards/bpvc-2025) is the authority.

## What is the difference between Division 1 and Division 2?

The difference is the design margin and the engineering that pays for a smaller one. Division 1 sets allowable
stresses with a design factor of 3.5 on tensile strength and designs mostly by formula; Division 2 uses 2.4 and
designs by rule or by analysis, with stricter material and examination rules and more paperwork.

| | Division 1 | Division 2 | Division 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approach | Design by rule: formulas and charts | Design by rule or by analysis (stress analysis, finite elements) | Design by analysis, with fracture mechanics |
| Design factor on tensile strength | 3.5 | 2.4 | Based on yield, with further checks |
| Typical use | Most vessels | Large, thick or alloy vessels where steel is the bigger cost | Very high pressure, generally above 10,000 psi (690 bar) |
| Owner's input | Design conditions on the order, or ASME's U-DR-1 / U-DR-2 forms | A User's Design Specification | A User's Design Specification |
| Design certification | The manufacturer | A Manufacturer's Design Report, certified as the Division requires | As Division 2, and more |
| ASME certificate | U (UM for miniature vessels) | U2 | U3 |
| Data report | U-1 or U-1A | A-1 | K-1 |

The certificate names and forms are from ASME's [certification page](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/Boiler-and-Pressure-Vessel-Certification) and [data report forms list](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/asme-data-report-forms). The same vessel needs less steel
under Division 2, so it pays mainly on large, thick or expensive-alloy vessels; elsewhere the extra analysis and
examination cost more than the steel saved.

## When is Division 3 used?

Division 3 is for very high pressure, generally above 10,000 psi (690 bar): isostatic presses, high-pressure
reactors, some hydrogen storage. It designs by analysis with fracture mechanics, needs the U3 certificate, and is
reported on Form K-1 (K-2 for parts). It is a specialist field, and few shops hold the certificate.

## How do I choose between Division 1 and Division 2?

Start with Division 1 unless the vessel gives a reason not to. More shops hold the U certificate, more inspectors
know it, and the owner's paperwork is lighter. Consider Division 2 when:

- the wall gets thick (a rough sign: shells over about 2 in, 50 mm);
- the material is expensive (stainless, nickel alloys, clad plate), so thinner walls save real money;
- the vessel is cyclic and needs a fatigue assessment anyway.

The Division also decides who can build it: a fabricator with only a U certificate can't build or stamp a Division 2
vessel.

## Can a shop with a U certificate build Division 2 vessels?

No. Division 2 vessels need the U2 certificate, which ASME lists separately from U, with its own required code books
(Section VIII Division 2 instead of Division 1). A U holder that wants Division 2 work applies for U2 and goes through a
joint review for it. See [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps) and [how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

## Does a vessel under 15 psi need a U stamp?

Not under Section VIII: Division 1's scope excludes vessels for 15 psi (1 bar) or less, so there is nothing to stamp
them to. A buyer can still ask for Code construction in the order, and the law where the vessel is installed sets
its own scope. Check the jurisdiction's rules before assuming a small or low-pressure vessel is exempt; see
[US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## Can a vessel be built to Section VIII without the U stamp?

A shop can design to the Section VIII formulas without a certificate, but the vessel isn't a Code vessel: there is no
Authorized Inspector, no Manufacturer's Data Report and no Certification Mark, and it can't be registered with the
National Board. Whether that is acceptable is a legal question for the place of installation. The National Board's
[stamping table](https://www.nationalboard.org/SiteDocuments/Synopsis/asme_requirements.pdf) (2024 Synopsis) lists the ASME stamps each jurisdiction requires: most list
U, while some do not include it (Florida, Louisiana, Montana, New Mexico, South Dakota and West Virginia among them),
and Idaho lists none.

## What paperwork does a Division 1 vessel need?

A Division 1 vessel's file holds:

- the design calculations: [shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness), [heads](/asme/heads), nozzles and openings, flanges, supports;
- material certificates ([MTRs](/asme/mtr)) traced to each part by heat number;
- welding procedures and welder qualifications ([WPS, PQR and WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq)), with each welder's [continuity](/asme/welder-continuity);
- NDE reports, heat treatment charts and the [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) record;
- the [Manufacturer's Data Report](/asme/data-reports), U-1 or U-1A, signed by the manufacturer and the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector).

ASME also publishes User's Design Requirements forms, U-DR-1 for single-chamber and U-DR-2 for multi-chamber
vessels, for the owner to state design conditions.

## What does our software keep for a Section VIII vessel?

Our US boiler demo builds the record package for a Division 1 vessel from the job's own records: a Form U-1A layout
(our own, carrying the form's fields, not a copy of ASME's form), the weld map with welder stamps, WPS and PQR,
QW-322 continuity, MTRs by heat number, NDE, PWHT and the hydro test record. It covers Division 1 vessels and
Section I boilers, not Division 2. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

body:
## What is ASME Section XIII?

Section XIII, Rules for Overpressure Protection, is the Code's section for pressure relief devices; ASME says it "sets
requirements for design, materials, inspection, testing, and marking of pressure relief valves, rupture disks, and
related devices". It was first published in the 2021 Edition, and the current one is 2025. The Code text is ASME's and
paid; this guide cites paragraphs and your 2025 book is the authority.

## Why did the relief valve rules move to Section XIII?

So that a device maker works to one book. Until 2021 each construction section carried its own relief device rules:
Section VIII Division 1 in its UG-125 series, Sections I and IV in theirs. The 2021 Edition gathered the device rules
into Section XIII, and the construction sections kept the requirement to protect the equipment, pointing to Section
XIII for the device. Older drawings and data sheets still say "UG-125"; on new Division 1 work the vessel side is in
the UG-150 series and the device side in Section XIII.

## Which certificates does Section XIII use?

| Designator | Device |
|---|---|
| V | Boiler pressure relief valves |
| HV | Heating boiler safety valves |
| UV | Pressure vessel pressure relief valves |
| UD | Pressure vessel pressure relief devices (rupture disks and similar nonreclosing devices) |
| UV3, UD3 | High-pressure vessel (Division 3) valves and devices |
| TV, TD | Transport tank valves and devices |

The list is as ASME's [certification page](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/Boiler-and-Pressure-Vessel-Certification) gives it. See [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps) for the full set.

## How does a relief valve maker get certified?

Through a review led by the National Board, not an inspection agency. ASME's handbook says that for these
certificates ASME "will notify the ASME Designated Organization, The National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel
Inspectors, to appoint an ASME Designee to conduct the review", and no Authorized Inspection Agency agreement is
needed. The device's relieving capacity must also be certified by test at an ASME-accepted laboratory: the tests must
be scheduled within 90 days of the review and completed within six months, or the review is repeated.

## What stays with the vessel or boiler designer?

The construction section still decides:

- that the vessel or boiler needs protection, and from what (a blocked outlet, a fire, a failed control);
- the set pressure, normally not above the [MAWP](/asme/mawp);
- how far pressure may rise while the device relieves: in Division 1, generally 10% or 3 psi above MAWP for one device, 16% or 4 psi with several, and 21% for fire.

The designer sizes the device for the worst relieving case and specifies it; the device maker certifies its capacity
and marks it.

## Can a vessel be protected without a relief valve?

In defined cases. Division 1 allows overpressure protection by system design, where the vessel can't be
overpressured by the system it sits in, under conditions the Code sets and the owner documents. It is the owner's
responsibility and needs the jurisdiction's acceptance in many states; check your 2025 Division 1 and the
jurisdiction before relying on it.

## Who repairs relief valves in service?

Not a Section XIII certificate holder as such: repair and resetting of valves in service is done under the National
Board's VR program to Part 4 of the National Board Inspection Code, which the National Board says is adopted into law
by most US and Canadian jurisdictions. In-service testing has its own T/O program. See
[National Board registration and the R stamp](/asme/national-board-registration).

## What does our software keep for relief devices?

Our US boiler demo records each boiler's safety valves (size, set pressure, capacity) on its data report layout in
the ASME record package. It doesn't size or certify valves. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: Shell thickness and MAWP (UG-27), with a calculator
question: How do you calculate pressure vessel shell thickness to ASME?
answer: For a cylindrical shell under internal pressure, ASME Section VIII Division 1 (UG-27) gives the required thickness as t = PR / (SE − 0.6P), where P is design pressure, R the inside radius, S the allowable stress and E the longitudinal joints' efficiency. Check the longitudinal-stress formula PR / (2SE + 0.4P) with the circumferential joints' efficiency too, take the larger, and add the corrosion allowance.

body:
## How do you calculate pressure vessel shell thickness to ASME?

Use UG-27 of Section VIII Division 1 with the inside radius in the corroded condition, then add the corrosion
allowance. The formulas for internal pressure (2025 Edition):

| Shell | Required thickness | Valid while |
|---|---|---|
| Cylinder, circumferential (hoop) stress, governs the longitudinal joints | t = PR / (SE − 0.6P) | P ≤ 0.385SE and t ≤ R/2 |
| Cylinder, longitudinal stress, governs the circumferential joints | t = PR / (2SE + 0.4P) | P ≤ 1.25SE and t ≤ R/2 |
| Sphere | t = PR / (2SE − 0.2P) | P ≤ 0.665SE and t ≤ 0.356R |

- **P**: design pressure, plus any static head at that point.
- **R**: inside radius, increased by the corrosion allowance.
- **S**: maximum allowable stress at the design temperature, from [Section II Part D](/asme/section-ii).
- **E**: [joint efficiency](/asme/joint-efficiency) of the joint the formula governs.

The Code text is ASME's and paid; formulas are written out here so they can be checked against your 2025 book.

## Which joint efficiency goes in which formula?

The hoop-stress formula uses the efficiency of the **longitudinal** (Category A) joints, because hoop stress pulls
them apart; the longitudinal-stress formula uses the efficiency of the **circumferential** (Category B) joints. They
differ when the seams are radiographed differently, for example full radiography of the long seams and spot of the
girth seams. The calculator above takes both; leave the second blank when they are the same.

## Why use the corroded radius?

Because the shell has to hold the pressure at the end of its life, when the corrosion allowance has gone: the
inside wall has moved out and the wall is thinner. Using the corroded radius in the formula, then adding the
allowance to the result, gives the thickness to order.

## Can you show a worked example?

A carbon steel shell, 48 in inside diameter, design pressure 150 psi, allowable stress 20,000 psi, spot-radiographed
Type 1 joints (E = 0.85 for both), corrosion allowance 0.125 in:

1. Corroded radius: 24 + 0.125 = 24.125 in.
2. Hoop: t = 150 × 24.125 / (20,000 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 150) = 3,618.75 / 16,910 = **0.214 in**.
3. Longitudinal: t = 3,618.75 / (2 × 20,000 × 0.85 + 0.4 × 150) = 3,618.75 / 34,060 = 0.106 in. Hoop governs.
4. Add corrosion: 0.214 + 0.125 = **0.339 in** minimum.
5. Choose plate: ⅜ in (0.375) covers it, after allowing for mill under-tolerance and any forming thin-out.

With the long seams fully radiographed (E = 1.0) and the girth seams spot (0.85), hoop becomes 3,618.75 / 19,910 =
0.182 in and the longitudinal check is still 0.106 in, so the minimum falls to **0.307 in**. In metric: 1,220 mm
inside diameter, 1.03 MPa, 138 MPa, E = 0.85, 3 mm corrosion → corroded radius 613 mm, t = 1.03 × 613 / (138 × 0.85 −
0.6 × 1.03) = **5.4 mm**, plus 3 mm = 8.4 mm, so a 10 mm plate. Use MPa with mm or psi with inches; never mix them.

## How do you get the MAWP of a chosen thickness?

Rearrange each formula for pressure and take the lower: P = SEt / (R + 0.6t) for hoop stress and
P = 2SEt / (R − 0.4t) for longitudinal stress, with t and R corroded. The ⅜ in plate above allows 175.1 psi; see
[MAWP and design pressure](/asme/mawp) for the full working.

## Where does the allowable stress come from?

From Section II Part D, which ASME describes as providing "material properties, allowable stress values, and design
data for pressure equipment": Table 1A for ferrous materials, by specification, grade and temperature. The calculator
asks you to enter it rather than supplying it, because the values are ASME's and change between editions; read them
from your copy of the 2025 tables.

## What if the shell is thick or the pressure high?

Beyond the limits in the table (t > R/2, or P above 0.385SE for the hoop formula), the thin-shell formulas no longer
apply: use the thick-shell formulas in Mandatory Appendix 1-2. The calculator warns when you are outside the range.
Mandatory Appendix 1-1 gives formulas in terms of the outside radius, used for pipe ordered by outside diameter.

## What does the formula not cover?

- **Heads**: their own formulas; see [heads](/asme/heads).
- **Openings**: every nozzle needs reinforcement checked (UG-37 onwards).
- **External pressure and vacuum**: a separate check (UG-28) with Section II Part D charts, often thicker than internal pressure needs.
- **Other loads**: wind, seismic, supports, lifting and piping loads (UG-22).
- **Minimum thickness**: Division 1 sets a floor for shells and heads regardless of pressure (UG-16).

## When does a vessel need Section VIII at all?

ASME describes Division 1 as covering "pressure vessels operating over 15 psig, fired/unfired"; see
[Section VIII Division 1 vs 2](/asme/section-viii).

## What does our software keep for shell design?

Our US boiler demo keeps each job's calculation sheet with the UG-27(c)(1) shell formula (PG-27 for boiler shells)
and its inputs, then the plate actually issued with its heat number, so the [MTR](/asme/mtr) and the calculation
point at the same plate. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

body:
## What do the ASME stamp letters mean?

The letters are the **designator** stamped under the ASME Certification Mark (the cloverleaf), and they say which
Code section and what kind of work the item was built to: U for a Section VIII Division 1 vessel, S for a Section I
power boiler, H for a heating boiler, and so on. ASME's handbook says the mark "can only be used by a company that
holds a valid Certificate of Authorization", so the letters also tell you the maker held that certificate. People
still say "U stamp" for the mark with the U designator, and this guide does too.

## What happened to the old Code symbol stamps?

ASME replaced its 28 separate Code symbol stamps with one Certification Mark used together with a designator. Its
[FAQ](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/resources-and-events/frequently-asked-questions) says the old stamps for Sections I, IV, VIII, X and XII were discontinued on 31 January 2013 and must be
returned to ASME, and that the designator must appear directly below the mark, though it may be printed rather than
stamped. An older nameplate with a U inside the cloverleaf means the same as the new mark with U below it.

## Which ASME certificates and designators are there?

ASME's [certification page](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/Boiler-and-Pressure-Vessel-Certification) lists these for the boiler and pressure vessel Code; how long each lasts and whether
it needs an agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency are from ASME's handbook (Exhibit A):

| Section | Designator | For | Valid | Inspection agency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | S | Power boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | A | Assembly of power boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | E | Electric boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | M | Miniature boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | PP | Pressure piping (boiler external piping) | 3 years | Yes |
| IV | H | Heating boilers (not cast iron or aluminum) | 3 years | Yes |
| IV | H | Cast iron and cast aluminum heating boilers | 1 year | No |
| IV | HLW | Lined potable water heaters | 3 years | Yes |
| VIII-1 | U | Pressure vessels | 3 years | Yes |
| VIII-1 | UM | Miniature pressure vessels (needs a U or S too) | 1 year | Through the U or S |
| VIII-2 | U2 | Pressure vessels, alternative rules | 3 years | Yes |
| VIII-3 | U3 | High-pressure vessels | 3 years | Yes |
| X | RP | Fiber-reinforced plastic vessels | 3 years | Yes |
| XII | T | Transport tanks | 3 years | Yes |
| I, IV, VIII-1, VIII-2, XII | PRT | Parts, without design responsibility | 3 years | Yes |
| XIII | V, HV, UV, UD, UV3, UD3, TV, TD | Relief valves and other pressure relief devices | 3 years | No |

Every certificate also needs the Code books ASME lists for it; since the CA-1 standard (ASME's Conformity Assessment
Requirements) appears on every list, a shop buys that too. See [how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

## What is the difference between the U and U2 stamp?

U is for vessels built to Section VIII Division 1 and U2 for Division 2, the alternative rules with a smaller design
margin and more analysis. They are separate certificates with separate joint reviews, and a U holder can't stamp a
Division 2 vessel. See [Section VIII Division 1 vs 2](/asme/section-viii).

## What is a PRT certificate?

PRT is for a maker of parts who builds to someone else's design: in the handbook's words, for "Manufacturers of parts
who do not perform or assume any design responsibility for the parts they manufacture." The certificate holder who
buys the part takes design responsibility, and the part comes with a partial data report.

## What are the UM, V and UV stamps?

UM is for miniature pressure vessels and can only be held alongside a valid U or S certificate; it is issued for one
year. The Section XIII letters are for pressure relief devices: V for boiler relief valves, HV for heating boiler
safety valves, UV for pressure vessel relief valves, UD for nonreclosing devices such as rupture disks, UV3 and UD3
for high-pressure vessels, TV and TD for transport tanks. Their reviews are run through the National Board and their
capacities certified by test; see [Section XIII](/asme/section-xiii).

## What is the R stamp?

The R stamp is not ASME's: it is the National Board's certificate for repairs and alterations to boilers, pressure
vessels and other pressure-retaining items already in service, done under the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC).
The National Board's [R certificate page](https://www.nationalboard.org/Index.aspx?pageID=115&ID=160) says a holder must keep an inspection agreement with an Authorized
Inspection Agency, a written quality system to the NBIC and the current NBIC, and that the certificate costs $1,150
for three years. Its sister programs are:

- **VR**: repair of pressure relief valves;
- **NR**: repair and replacement of nuclear components;
- **T/O**: in-service testing of pressure relief valves.

The National Board's [accreditation page](https://www.nationalboard.org/Index.aspx?pageID=115) notes that authorized repair organizations are issued an NBBI stamp applied
to the nameplate.

## What does NB on a nameplate mean?

NB means the item's data report is registered with the National Board, which keeps it permanently; the nameplate
carries the NB mark and a National Board number. The National Board's [registration page](https://www.nationalboard.org/Index.aspx?pageID=9) says the NB mark is
used by manufacturers to identify items registered with it. Many US jurisdictions require registration; see
[National Board registration](/asme/national-board-registration).

## Which stamps does my state require?

Each state sets its own list. The National Board's [stamping table](https://www.nationalboard.org/SiteDocuments/Synopsis/asme_requirements.pdf) (2024 Synopsis) gives, per jurisdiction, the
National Board and ASME stamps it requires. Most states list all ASME stamps or a long list that includes U and S;
Florida, Louisiana and Montana list boiler stamps without U; Wyoming lists only U, U2, U3 and UV; Idaho lists none.
NB registration is listed for Arizona, North Dakota, Washington and West Virginia, among others. Confirm with the
state's chief inspector; see [US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## How do I check that a company really holds a stamp?

Use ASME's [Certificate Holder Search](https://access.asme.org/caconnect/certified-companies), which ASME's FAQ points to for exactly this: it lists certified companies
with their certificates, filterable by country and certificate. Ask the supplier for a copy of the certificate too,
and check the designator, scope (shop or field) and expiry date cover your order. For repair firms, the National
Board's Manufacturer and Repair Directory lists R, VR and NR holders.

## What does a stamp tell a buyer?

A stamp says the item was built under an ASME-accepted quality system, inspected by an
[Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector), and documented on a [data report](/asme/data-reports). It doesn't
say the design suits your process: that is set by the design conditions you specify in the order.

## Is the ASME Code required by law in the US?

Not federally: the Code gets legal force when a state, a city or a Canadian province adopts it in its own boiler and
pressure vessel rules. Pennsylvania's rule is typical in form: "The Department adopts and incorporates by reference
the following codes", with the ASME Code on the list. The adopting rule then says which equipment is covered, which
edition applies, who inspects it in service, and what must be stamped, registered or permitted before it runs.

## Which ASME edition does each state require?
