| Texas | Current | Current |
| Washington | Current | Current |
| Wisconsin | 2010 | 2011 |
| Wyoming | 1968 | – |

The National Board adds its own caveat: "Synopsis data is subject to change", and users should consult the
jurisdiction's chief inspector. Most of these rules govern what may be installed and inspected; a new item built to a
later edition is often accepted, but confirm it in writing before you build. Code cases have their own column in the
Synopsis, with some states accepting them only "on a conditional basis".

## What do the state rules themselves say?

Five read in full on 6 November 2026:

- **Ohio**: OAC 4101:4-3-01 (effective 1 July 2024) adopts Sections I to XI and the code case book at the 2023
  edition, plus "amendments, supplements, and addenda subsequently published prior to issuance of the next edition".
- **Michigan**: R 339.5204 (effective 3 May 2023) requires "A boiler, blow down vessel, and expansion tank" to be built
  to the 2019 edition and B31.1 2018. Its scope names those items, not pressure vessels in general.
- **Texas**: 16 TAC §65.2 defines ASME as the Code, code cases and interpretations "adopted by the council of the
  society", with no year: effectively the current edition. The Texas rules are the Board of Boiler Rules', for boilers.
- **California**: 8 CCR §453 defines the ASME Code with no edition, and §454(a) requires new air tanks to be
  "constructed, inspected and stamped in compliance with the ASME Code" and, except UM vessels, registered with the
  National Board.
- **Pennsylvania**: 34 Pa. Code §3a.1 still defines the ASME Code as the 2004 edition with its cases and
  interpretations, older than the Synopsis entry, and §3a.21(b) requires the ASME stamp and the National Board
  registration number on every ASME boiler and unfired pressure vessel, plus a Pennsylvania keystone serial number.

## Which states don't require the U stamp?

Those that don't regulate unfired pressure vessels. The National Board's stamping table (2024 Synopsis) lists the ASME
stamps each jurisdiction requires: Florida, Louisiana, Montana, New Mexico, South Dakota and West Virginia list
boiler stamps without U; Idaho lists none; Wyoming lists only U, U2, U3 and UV. A buyer in those states may still
want the U stamp for insurance, resale or a plant standard.

## Which states require National Board registration?

Many, in different ways. The stamping table lists the NB mark as a requirement for Arizona, North Dakota, Washington
and West Virginia among others; Pennsylvania requires the National Board number on the stamping; California requires
registration of new air tanks. ASME's handbook says registration "may be required by the legal authority of a state
or municipality". See [National Board registration](/asme/national-board-registration).

## Do cities have their own boiler rules?

Some large ones do. The Synopsis lists separate entries for cities and counties including Chicago, Detroit, Los
Angeles, Miami and Miami-Dade, Milwaukee, New Orleans, New York City, Omaha, Seattle, Spokane, St. Louis and
Washington, D.C., several with their own editions; New York City's entry is the 1986 edition. Check the city as well
as the state.

## Who leads a shop's ASME joint review in each state?

ASME's handbook says the jurisdiction appoints the team leader in Alaska, Delaware, Hawaii, Louisiana, Minnesota,
Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington; ASME appoints for Idaho, Wyoming, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands and all
Canadian provinces; and the National Board appoints for the remaining states. See [how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

## How does Canada regulate pressure equipment?

Province by province, with designs registered and given a Canadian Registration Number (CRN) under CSA B51. Alberta's
ABSA handles national applications for "Boilers, Pressure Vessels or Fittings to be Registered in Multiple Provincial
or Territorial Jurisdictions in Canada", and Ontario's TSSA guidelines for fittings (January 2026, citing CSA B51:24)
require that "The Canadian Registration Number (CRN) shall be identified whenever physically possible." The National
Board's tabulation shows most provinces requiring the ASME construction sections by law, with Québec the exception for
most sections. Register the design in each province where the equipment will go before it is built.

## How do I check a jurisdiction before ordering?

1. Find the jurisdiction's chief inspector on the National Board's [Synopsis page](https://www.nationalboard.org/ViewAllSynopses.aspx), which has an entry per state, province and city.
2. Confirm: is this equipment in scope, which edition, is NB registration required, are code cases accepted, what inspection or permit before first use.
3. Put the answers in the purchase order, so the [data report](/asme/data-reports) and nameplate come out right the first time.

The National Board's members are those chief inspectors, which is why its Synopsis is the starting point. For buying
from a shop outside the US, see [buying from India](/asme/buying-from-india).

## What does our software keep for jurisdiction rules?

Our US boiler demo records the Code edition and National Board number on each job's ASME record package. The demo
company is in Ohio, whose rule adopts the 2023 edition plus later supplements, while the demo files its jobs to 2025:
a real shop would confirm the edition with its jurisdiction. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: How to get the ASME U stamp: steps, cost and timeline

ASME's fee is $4,500 per certificate; the certificate lasts three years.

body:
## What are the steps to get a U stamp?

A shop gets the U stamp by preparing its quality system, applying to ASME, and passing an on-site joint review; ASME
then issues a Certificate of Authorization for Section VIII, Division 1 pressure vessels and the Certification Mark
with the U designator. ASME's [certification process](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/asme-certification-process) and [informational handbook](https://www.asme.org/getmedia/cb8f63c5-3aa2-45ee-a2d1-b999d37733f7/bpv-gui-03-informational-handbook_1.pdf) set out the route. In the order a shop
usually does it:

1. **Decide the scope.** U for Division 1 vessels, shop only or field work too, and any limits. The scope drives everything else; see [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps).
2. **Buy the Code books.** ASME lists the books required per certificate (below). Copies and unauthorized reproductions aren't accepted.
3. **Sign an inspection agreement** with an ASME-accredited Authorized Inspection Agency. The agency's [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) joins the review and then inspects every stamped job.
4. **Write the quality control manual** and train the people who will follow it. In English, covering every element the Code requires for the scope. See [the quality control manual](/asme/quality-control-manual).
5. **Apply** through ASME's CA Connect, return the signed ASME Accreditation/Certification Agreement, and pay the certificate fee, stamp fee and any deposit.
6. **ASME checks the file.** It asks your agency to confirm the inspection agreement and checks the application is complete; only then does it schedule the joint review.
7. **Prepare the demonstration.** Real Code work, a mock-up, or both, taken through your system from drawing to data report.
8. **The joint review.** A team leader (the ASME Designee) and a representative of your inspection agency audit the manual and watch the demonstration, then report to ASME with a recommendation.
9. **Certificate and stamp issued** once ASME accepts the report. Valid for three years.

## Which Code books does a U certificate need?

ASME's [required list](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/asme-certification-process/required-code-books) for the U certificate is Section II Parts A, B, C and D (materials), Section V
(nondestructive examination), Section VIII Division 1, Section IX (welding, brazing and fusing qualifications) and
CA-1, ASME's conformity assessment requirements. Section II Part C, Section V and Section IX can be left out only if
welding, brazing and fusing aren't in the shop's scope. Electronic editions bought from a licensed reseller are
accepted; a new edition becomes mandatory six months after it is published. See [BPVC sections](/asme/bpvc-sections)
and [Code editions](/asme/editions).

## Why do you need an Authorized Inspection Agency first?

ASME won't schedule the joint review until an accredited Authorized Inspection Agency confirms it has an inspection
agreement with the shop. The handbook's table of certificates marks the U certificate as requiring an agency
agreement. The agency is an organization accredited by ASME; its Authorized Inspector sits on the review
team, then inspects and signs off each stamped vessel, so the agreement covers the review and every job after it.
ASME publishes the [list of accredited agencies](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/Boiler-and-Pressure-Vessel-Certification), and its FAQ notes most work worldwide.

When comparing agencies, ask for the review fee, the hourly or per-visit rate for job inspections, travel charges,
and how often the Inspector will be in the shop at your volume.

## What goes in the quality control manual?

The manual is the shop's written description of how it meets each Code requirement in its scope: organization and
authority, drawings and design calculations, material receipt and control, welding, NDE, heat treatment,
calibration, examination and inspection, nonconformities, records and the Inspector's access. ASME's review teams
use a "General" checklist for the U certificate, and the shop must complete it, cross-referencing each element to
the paragraph of its manual that addresses it. The manual doesn't have to follow the checklist's order, but every
element must be findable. See [the quality control manual](/asme/quality-control-manual).

## What is the demonstration item?

The demonstration item is the work the shop puts through its quality system during the joint review to show the
manual is really used. ASME's FAQ says the demonstration must cover the administrative functions and the
manufacturing, fabrication and testing of the product, and that every element of the system must be demonstrated;
fabrication can be shown on current work, a mock-up built to current Code rules, or both. ASME gives no required
size or number of items.

Most shops choose a small vessel they can take all the way through: design calculations, material receipt with
[MTRs](/asme/mtr), [WPS and PQR](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq), welder qualifications, NDE, a
[hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) and a completed [data report](/asme/data-reports). Any Code work in the shop
during the review can be examined too.

## Who leads the joint review?

The ASME Designee who leads the review is appointed by ASME, by the jurisdiction, or by the National Board,
depending on where the shop is. The handbook says the jurisdiction appoints in Alaska, Delaware, Hawaii, Louisiana,
Minnesota, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington; ASME appoints in Idaho, Wyoming, Puerto Rico, the Virgin
Islands, all Canadian provinces, and wherever the jurisdiction is itself the inspection agency; the National Board
appoints in the other US states. Who appoints changes what
the shop pays for the review (below). See [US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## How much does the ASME U stamp cost?

ASME's own fee is $4,500 per certificate plus $400 per Certification Mark stamp (plus tax and shipping), from its
[Price Guide](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/asme-certification-process/price-guide) on 5 November 2026. Where ASME appoints the Designee, ASME also takes an $11,000 advance review deposit
that is applied to the cost of the review; the guide names reviews in Idaho, Wyoming, Puerto Rico and the Virgin
Islands, and any review where the state or province is itself the inspection agency. The shop pays the Designee's
travel and ASME's administrative fees from it, and the final invoice settles the difference either way. Where the
National Board or a state appoints, it tells the shop its own review charges. ASME wants all fees and the deposit
before it schedules the review. Prices are in US dollars and change; check the current guide.

| Item | Paid to | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| U certificate | ASME | $4,500 |
| Certification Mark (stamp), each | ASME | $400 plus tax and shipping |
| Advance review deposit, where ASME appoints the Designee | ASME | $11,000, applied to the review cost |
| Expedited joint review, if wanted | ASME | $2,750 |
| Manual or document review, if needed | ASME | $1,500 each |
| Joint review, where the National Board or a state appoints | National Board or the state | Set by them |
| Inspection agency: review attendance, then every job | The agency | Set by the agency |
| Code books | ASME or a licensed reseller | Per ASME's catalog |
| Manual writing, training, demonstration item, any consultant | Your own cost | |

For example, a shop in Ohio (National Board appoints) pays ASME $4,900 for one certificate and one stamp, and the
National Board and its inspection agency separately. A shop in Idaho (ASME appoints) pays ASME $15,900 before the
review is scheduled, $4,500 plus $400 plus the $11,000 deposit, and the final invoice refunds what the review and
travel don't use or bills any balance. Withdrawing after paying costs a $1,100 administrative fee, and cancelling
dates already accepted costs $2,200 or more.

## How long does it take to get a U stamp?

Plan on several months after the application, plus the time the shop needs to be ready. [ASME's FAQ](https://www.asme.org/certification-accreditation/resources-and-events/frequently-asked-questions) says reviews are
generally scheduled about four months after it receives the completed application and fees; ASME emails proposed
dates, which must be accepted in CA Connect within seven business days, and sends review details four to six weeks
before. The certificate is issued after ASME approves the team leader's report.

The rest of the pace is set by the shop: writing a manual that matches how it really works, signing the agency
agreement, and getting a demonstration item through every step. Apply when the manual is done and the demonstration
job is planned, and book the review only when a full job can be shown end to end.

## How do you renew a U stamp?

The certificate lasts three years, and renewal is another joint review. ASME sends a reminder ten months before
expiry, and the renewal application, fees and any deposit must reach ASME at least six months before the expiry
date, or the certificate may lapse. A shop with work in progress at expiry can ask for one six-month extension to
finish the listed work: the request must reach ASME 30 days before expiry, with a $2,200 fee per certificate and a
report from the inspection agency.

## What should a shop's system keep for the review?

Whatever runs the shop, check that it can show the review team, for the demonstration job and every job after:

- The drawing and calculation revision used, and who approved it.
- Each material receipt with its MTR, heat number and the parts it went into; see [MTRs](/asme/mtr).
- The WPS used on each weld, the welder's stamp and their qualification and [continuity](/asme/welder-continuity).
- NDE, heat treatment and test records, linked to the job.
- Nonconformities and how each was resolved, with the Inspector's acceptance.
- Hold points the Inspector signed, and the data report.

## Can a shop in India get the U stamp?

Yes. The route is the same for a shop in India, and many Indian fabricators hold U and S certificates for export
work. IBR 2026 lets an Indian Inspecting Authority inspect an export boiler to a foreign code; see
[buying ASME equipment from India](/asme/buying-from-india) and [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

title: Welder continuity (QW-322): six-month rule and checker
question: How long is an ASME welder qualification valid?
answer: An ASME Section IX welder qualification has no fixed expiry date. Under QW-322 it lapses when the welder hasn't welded with that process for six months or more, and it can be revoked sooner if there's a specific reason to doubt their work. Each weld with the process restarts the six months for that process, so a shop needs a record of every welder's last weld per process.
description: ASME welder continuity under QW-322: the six-month rule per process, renewing with one coupon, revocation, the record an Inspector checks, and a free checker.

body:
## How long is an ASME welder qualification valid?

An ASME welder qualification has no expiry date: it stays valid as long as the welder keeps welding with the process,
and lapses after six months or more without it (QW-322.1(a) in the 2025 Section IX). The same rule applies to welding
operators. Section IX is ASME's paid Code; this guide cites its paragraphs, and your copy of the 2025 Edition is the
authority.

## What are the two ways a qualification ends?

Section IX's QW-322 ends a welder's or welding operator's qualification in two ways:

1. **Six months without the process** (QW-322.1(a)). If the welder hasn't welded with a process for six months or more, their qualifications for that process expire.
2. **A specific reason to question their ability** (QW-322.1(b)). If there is a reason to doubt their ability to make welds that meet the specification, the qualifications supporting the welding in question are revoked; the others stay.

## Is continuity per process or per WPS?

Per process. The clock runs separately for SMAW, GTAW, GMAW, SAW and so on, not per WPS, position, thickness or
material. A welder qualified for SMAW and GTAW who only welds SMAW for seven months keeps SMAW and loses GTAW, and any
weld with a process, to any WPS, keeps all of that welder's qualifications in that process alive.

## How do I work out a welder's lapse date?

Add six months to the date of their last weld with the process; on that date the qualification has lapsed. Some
examples:

| Welder | Process | Last weld | Lapses on | Status on 6 Nov 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| W-12 | SMAW | 2 May 2026 | 2 Nov 2026 | Lapsed: requalify |
| W-12 | GTAW | 15 Jan 2026 | 15 Jul 2026 | Lapsed: requalify |
| W-31 | GMAW | 28 Sep 2026 | 28 Mar 2027 | Current |
| W-07 | SAW | 31 Aug 2026 | 28 Feb 2027 | Current |

Where the month six months on is shorter, the lapse date is its last day: 31 August plus six months is 28 February
(29 in a leap year), not 3 March. The checker above and the Excel log both work this way.

## How does the free checker work?

Paste one line per welder and process (stamp, process, last weld date) and the checker lists who lapses when,
soonest first. A row reads "Lapsed: requalify" from the lapse date on, and anyone within 30 days is flagged with how
many days are left to weld. It runs in your browser and sends nothing anywhere. To keep the log itself, download the
free [welder continuity log for Excel](/asme/welder-continuity-log.xlsx): one row per welder and process, with the
lapse date (EDATE, six months after the last weld), days left and status worked out, and lapsed or nearly lapsed
rows coloured.

## What counts as welding with the process?

Any recorded weld with that process: production welds, repair welds or another test, on any WPS. The record must show
the welder, the process and the date, and should point to the job or weld number so it is evidence of real welding.
Most shops log continuity from production weld maps or a monthly sign-off sheet.

## How do you renew a lapsed qualification?

With one test coupon in the process (QW-322.2), of any thickness, position and diameter, tested by bend tests or by
volumetric examination. Passing it restores the welder's earlier qualifications for that process with their original
ranges, so a welder who held 6G pipe doesn't need to retest 6G. A revoked qualification is different: the welder
requalifies for the work that was in question.

## What record does an Authorized Inspector expect?

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| Welder ID (their stamp) | Links to their WPQ and to welds on the weld map |
| Process | Continuity is per process |
| Date welded | Sets the next lapse date |
| Job or weld number | Evidence that it was real welding |
| Signed off by | Who confirmed it |

Keep it next to the WPQs (ASME's suggested formats are QW-484A for welders and QW-484B for welding operators). The
[Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) checks continuity for every welder whose stamp appears on a job.

## What happens if a lapse is found after welding?

Those welds were made by an unqualified welder. It is a nonconformity: the shop records it, and the welds are
removed and rewelded, or dispositioned as the construction code and the Inspector allow, after the welder
requalifies. Checking the lapse date before assigning a welder to a seam is much cheaper.

## Does B31.3 piping use the same rule?

Yes: the B31 piping codes qualify welders to Section IX, so QW-322 applies, and an owner's specification may add
stricter rules. See [B31.1 vs B31.3](/asme/b31-1-vs-b31-3).

## What does our software keep for continuity?

Our US boiler demo keeps each welder's qualified processes with their last weld date per process and prints a QW-322
continuity table (welder, WPQ, process, last weld, lapse date, current or lapsed) in each job's ASME record package,
beside the weld map that shows whose stamp is on each seam. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: Welder qualification positions 1G to 6G explained
question: What does a 6G welding test qualify for?
answer: An ASME Section IX welder test qualifies a person for a process, a range of positions, thicknesses and pipe diameters, and a filler F-number. Positions go from 1G (flat) to 6G (pipe fixed at 45°). A 6G pipe test qualifies groove welds in all positions on plate and pipe; plate tests qualify less on pipe. The test is judged by bend tests or by radiography.
description: ASME welder qualification: what 1G to 6G tests qualify, plate vs pipe, diameter limits, bend vs radiography, welding operators, and whether a WPQ transfers.

checks.quote: Section IX of the BPVC contains rules relating to the qualification of welding, brazing, and fusing procedures as required by other BPVC sections.

body:
## What does a 6G welding test qualify for?

A 6G test, on pipe fixed at 45°, qualifies the welder for groove welds in all positions on both plate and pipe, and
for fillet welds in all positions, within the diameter and thickness ranges the test coupon earns. Section IX's
position table (QW-461.9) sets what each test position covers. It is the test pipe shops use, because one coupon
covers every position. Section IX is ASME's paid Code; this guide cites its paragraphs, and your copy of the
[2025 Edition](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/find-codes-standards/bpvc-ix-bpvc-section-ix-welding-brazing-fusing-qualifications) is the authority.

## What do 1G to 6G mean?

They are the test positions for groove welds; the F positions (1F to 5F) are the fillet weld equivalents.

| Position | Plate | Pipe |
|---|---|---|
| 1G | Flat | Pipe horizontal, rolled while welding |
| 2G | Horizontal (vertical plate, horizontal weld) | Pipe vertical, weld runs horizontally around it |
| 3G | Vertical | (plate only) |
| 4G | Overhead | (plate only) |
| 5G | – | Pipe horizontal and fixed: the welder goes flat, vertical and overhead round it |
| 6G | – | Pipe fixed at 45°: every position in one weld |

## Does 2G plus 5G equal 6G?

Yes. Passing both a 2G and a 5G pipe test qualifies the same positions as a single 6G test, which is how some shops
qualify welders who find 6G hard to pass in one go.

## Do plate tests qualify a welder for pipe?

Only in part. A plate test qualifies plate in the positions tested, but on pipe it qualifies only large diameters
(over 24 in, 610 mm, outside diameter) in those positions, with smaller pipe limited as QW-461.9 sets out. That is why
pipe shops test on pipe.

## What pipe diameter does my test qualify?

The coupon's outside diameter sets the smallest pipe a welder may weld (QW-452.3): a coupon under 1 in (25 mm)
qualifies its own size and up; 1 in to under 2⅞ in (73 mm) qualifies 1 in and up; 2⅞ in and over qualifies 2⅞ in and
up. Thickness limits come from the deposited weld metal thickness on the coupon (QW-452.1).

## How is a welder's test judged?

Either by bend tests or by volumetric examination (QW-302):

- **Bend tests**: coupons cut from the test weld and bent around a mandrel; cracks or open defects beyond the limit fail.
- **Radiography or ultrasonic examination** (QW-304): allowed instead of bends for most processes and materials, and much faster, but not for gas metal arc welding in short-circuit transfer (GMAW-S), which can hide lack of fusion; those welders are bend-tested.

## What is the difference between a welder and a welding operator?

A welder holds and guides the electrode or torch; a welding operator sets up and runs machine or automatic welding
equipment. They have separate qualifications with their own essential variables (QW-350 for welders, QW-360 for
operators), and ASME's suggested forms are separate: QW-484A for a welder's WPQ and QW-484B for a welding operator's.

## What changes force a welder to retest?

A change in one of the welder's essential variables beyond the WPQ: the process, a position not covered, backing
(welding without backing when qualified only with it), the filler F-number outside what QW-433 allows, or diameter
and thickness outside the earned range. See [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables) and
[P-numbers and F-numbers](/asme/p-numbers).

## Does an ASME welder qualification expire?

Not on a calendar date. It lapses when the welder hasn't welded with that process for six months (QW-322.1(a)), and
can be revoked sooner if there is a specific reason to question their work. See
[welder continuity](/asme/welder-continuity), which has a free checker.

## Is a WPQ valid at another employer?

Not automatically. Section IX makes each organization responsible for the qualifications it uses (Part QG), so a new
employer either qualifies the welder again or accepts the earlier qualification only as Section IX allows. Ask for the
welder's WPQ and continuity record, and check them with your Authorized Inspector.

## Does a boiler welder in India need anything else?

Yes: in India a welder on boilers under the Indian Boiler Regulations also needs an IBR welder certificate. See
[ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## What does our software keep for welders?

Our US boiler demo keeps each welder's stamp, WPQ and qualified processes with the date of their last weld per
process, shows their stamp against each seam on the weld map, and prints QW-322 continuity (lapse date, current or lapsed) in each job's ASME record package. See
[ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: WPS vs PQR vs WPQ: what each proves and how they link
question: What is the difference between a WPS and a PQR?
answer: A PQR records a test weld: the actual materials, settings and test results that prove a procedure makes sound welds. A WPS is the instruction a welder follows, written with ranges the PQR supports. A WPQ records that one welder passed their own test. In ASME Section IX the PQR comes first, the WPS cites it, and each welder needs a WPQ.
description: WPS, PQR and WPQ in ASME Section IX: what each proves, the tests behind a PQR, the free QW-482 to QW-485 forms, AWS standard WPSs, and tracing a weld back.

body:
## What is the difference between a WPS and a PQR?

A PQR is the record of a test weld that proves a procedure works; a WPS is the instruction written from it. The PQR
records what was actually used on one coupon (materials, filler, settings, preheat, heat treatment) and the test
results; the WPS gives the welder a range for each variable, within what the PQR supports. A PQR is never edited to
fit a job: if a job needs something the PQR doesn't support, a new coupon is welded.

| | PQR | WPS | WPQ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full name | Procedure Qualification Record | Welding Procedure Specification | Welder (or Welding Operator) Performance Qualification |
| Proves | The procedure makes welds with the required strength and ductility | Nothing by itself; it's the instruction | This person can make a sound weld |
| Records | What was used on one test coupon, and the test results | Ranges for every variable, within what the PQR(s) support | The welder's test, results and what they're qualified for |
| Written | Once per test | From one or more PQRs | Once per welder per test |
| ASME's suggested form | QW-483 | QW-482 | QW-484A (welder), QW-484B (operator) |

## What is a WPQ?

A WPQ is the record that one welder (or welding operator) passed a performance test, and of the process, positions,
thicknesses, diameters and filler it qualifies them for. It belongs to the person, not the procedure: a welder
qualified on one WPS may weld to other WPSs within their qualified ranges. What a test covers is in
[welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification).

## In what order does a shop build them?

1. **Draft a WPS** for the job (often called a pWPS until it's qualified).
2. **Weld a test coupon** to it and record every variable actually used.
3. **Test the coupon.** For a groove-weld procedure, Section IX requires tension tests for strength and guided bend tests for ductility (QW-451 sets how many; side bends replace face and root bends on thicker coupons). Toughness tests are added when the construction code requires impact testing.
4. **Write the PQR** from the coupon record and the test results, and certify it.
5. **Issue the WPS**, citing the PQR, with each variable's range set by what the PQR qualifies.
6. **Qualify each welder** and record it on a WPQ.

## What tests does a PQR need?

For a groove weld, tension tests and guided bend tests cut from the coupon, in the numbers Section IX's QW-451 tables
give for the coupon's thickness; for fillet welds, fillet weld tests. Charpy impact tests are added when the
construction code requires toughness, which also brings in Section IX's supplementary essential variables. The
results go on the PQR with the laboratory's report.

## Which changes need a new PQR?

Every variable in Section IX is classified. Change an **essential** variable beyond what the PQR covers (base metal
P-number, filler F-number, thickness range, post-weld heat treatment and others) and you need a new PQR; change a
**nonessential** one and you only revise the WPS. See [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables).

## Can one WPS cite more than one PQR?

Yes, as long as every essential variable on the WPS is covered by at least one of the PQRs: for example, two PQRs
that between them cover a wider thickness range. A PQR register with each PQR's qualified ranges worked out once
prevents most WPS errors, which are usually ranges copied wrong.

## Who signs the WPS and PQR?

The manufacturer or contractor that did the qualification certifies the PQR, and issues the WPS. The organization is
responsible for its own qualifications, so a shop can't use another company's PQR. The
[Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) reviews them before the procedure is used on Code work.

## Can I use an AWS prequalified WPS on ASME work?

Not an AWS D1.1 prequalified procedure: ASME work needs Section IX qualification. Section IX does accept AWS's
standard welding procedure specifications (SWPSs) listed in its Article V (QW-500), after the shop demonstrates one
with a test weld, recorded on ASME's QW-485 format.

## Where do I get the forms?

ASME publishes the suggested formats free on its [data report forms page](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/asme-data-report-forms): QW-482 (WPS), QW-483 (PQR),
QW-484A (welder WPQ), QW-484B (welding operator) and QW-485 (SWPS demonstration). A shop may use its own layout if it
records everything Section IX requires.

## How does a weld trace back through all three?

On a job's file, any weld should trace like this: weld number on the weld map → the welder's stamp → that welder's
WPQ and [continuity](/asme/welder-continuity) → the WPS used → the PQR behind it → the filler metal's certificate and
the base metal's [MTR](/asme/mtr) by heat number. An Authorized Inspector will pick a weld and walk it, and when the
links live in different binders this is where audits stall.

## What does our software keep for it?

Our US boiler demo keeps those links per job and prints them in the ASME record package: the weld map lists each
seam's joint category and type, WPS, welder stamps and NDE report; the welding page lists each WPS with its PQR,
P-numbers, thickness range and PWHT basis; welder continuity under QW-322 sits next to it. It records procedures the
shop has qualified; it doesn't write or qualify them. See [ERP for boiler and pressure vessel shops](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing).

title: Custom vs off-the-shelf ERP for a small manufacturer
question: Should a small manufacturer build a custom ERP or buy one off the shelf?
answer: Buy off the shelf if your work fits a standard package, you can live with its scheduling and reports, and nobody in the business has time to own a software project. Build custom, in phases, when your workflow is what sets you apart, packages force workarounds that bring the spreadsheets back, and you can get in writing your data, the code and licence terms, and a fixed scope per phase. Many shops are best served in between.
description: Custom vs off-the-shelf ERP for small manufacturers: when each wins, the real costs over five years, one-builder risk, and questions to ask before you sign.
body:
## Should a small manufacturer build a custom ERP or buy one?

Buy when your work fits a package; build, in phases, when your workflow is the advantage. The trade-offs side by side:

| Off-the-shelf wins when | Custom wins when |
|---|---|
| Your jobs move the way the package expects | The way you quote, schedule or trace is why customers pick you |
| You need to start in weeks, not months | Every package you've tried needs side spreadsheets to work |
| Nobody can spend time defining requirements | An owner or manager can spend a few hours a week shaping it |
| Per-user pricing stays small at your size | You'd pay for many modules and users to use a fraction |
| You want a large vendor's roadmap and user community | You want changes in days, decided by you |

Ahrom Labs builds custom systems, so read the rest knowing that. We've tried to make the case for buying as fairly as the case for building.

## What do shop owners who have done both say?

They split along predictable lines, in threads on Practical Machinist:

- **For building:** custom software is cheaper to change than custom machinery; shops that built their own say they adjust it constantly and that order entry got much faster.
- **Against building:** large custom builds can cost far more and take far longer than planned; cheap builders sometimes don't finish; one shop that had a contractor build its system was glad of it but wouldn't advise writing your own.
- **Against buying big:** packages carry modules you never use, and the scheduling is often the weak part.
- **Middle paths:** low-code tools (Airtable, FileMaker), open-source ERPs (ERPNext, Odoo), or a configurable package with in-house customization.

## What does each cost over five years?

A package's cost grows with users every year; a phased custom build costs most up front and then a care plan. Compare the same lines on both sides, not a license price against a build quote:

| Cost | Off-the-shelf | Custom |
|---|---|---|
| Up front | Implementation, setup, data migration, training | The build, data migration, training |
| Every year | Subscription or maintenance per user, usually rising with headcount | Hosting, support and changes (a care plan) |
| Changes | Configuration if it allows it; otherwise workarounds | Paid changes, but anything is possible |
| Your time | Fitting your process to the package | Defining and testing what gets built |
| Leaving | Exporting data, usually in the vendor's format | Depends on the contract: get this in writing |

A worked example for a made-up 15-person shop. The package: 15 users × $150 a month for five years is $135,000,
plus $25,000 to implement: $160,000 (illustrative; get real quotes). Built in phases by Ahrom Labs at our published US
prices: a $1,500 two-week prototype of one workflow, a first build of $7,500 to $15,000, and a $350 a month care plan
(hosting, support and small changes), so $37,500 over five years at the top of the build range, plus whatever later
phases you choose. Then add the costs neither quote shows: on the package side, a person keeping a side spreadsheet
5 hours a week at $35 an hour ($9,100 a year); on the custom side, what moving would cost if the builder stopped.

The hidden cost on the off-the-shelf side is the workaround: the spreadsheet that runs beside the ERP because it can't model one thing, and the person who keeps it. On the custom side it is dependence on one builder.

## How do you reduce the risk of a custom build?

With six protections, all of which belong in the contract:

1. **Phases with a fixed scope and price each.** A prototype of one workflow on your own data first, then the build; never one large open-ended project.
2. **Your data, exportable any time,** in plain files, without asking.
3. **Code and licence terms in writing:** who owns the code, what licence you hold, and what happens to both if you stop paying for support.
4. **Documentation and a handover path,** so another developer could take over.
5. **Acceptance tests you write:** two or three of your real jobs, run end to end before go-live, like the [ten tests in our job shop ERP guide](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp).
6. **Keep the accounting system you trust.** A shop system that posts to QuickBooks is a smaller, safer project than one that replaces it ([QuickBooks beside a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)).

## What should you ask a builder before signing?

Five questions, and the answers should be specific:

- Show me a system you built that's been running for over a year, and let me talk to its owner.
- What happens on day one if you disappear? Where is the code and who can deploy it?
- How do changes get priced, and how fast do small ones happen?
- What's in the first phase, what isn't, and what's the price?
- How will my data come out if I leave?

The same comparison for Indian manufacturers, with TallyPrime and ERPNext in place of QuickBooks, is in [Tally vs ERPNext vs custom ERP](/notes/tally-vs-erpnext-vs-custom-erp). For the scheduling piece that packages most often get wrong, see [production scheduling software](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software).

title: Inventory control for distributors: counts, lots, FIFO, barcodes
metaTitle: Distributor inventory control: counts, lots, FIFO, barcodes
question: What inventory control does a small US distributor need?
answer: Four things: cycle counts that check a few bins every day instead of one shutdown count a year; lot or serial numbers on what you receive and ship, so a recall finds the customers in minutes; a valuation method, usually FIFO, applied the same way every year; and barcodes scanned at receiving, picking and counting, so stock changes when goods move, not when someone types.

body:
## How does cycle counting replace the annual count?

By counting a small set of locations every day, so every item is counted several times a year and errors are found
while someone still remembers why. An annual physical count shuts the warehouse for a day or two and is wrong again
within a week.

| Class | Share of items (typical) | Count | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | The few items that are most of the dollar value | Monthly or more | Errors here cost the most |
| B | The middle | Quarterly | |
| C | The many cheap items | Once or twice a year | Errors cost little |

How many counts is that? A made-up distributor with 1,200 items: 120 A items counted monthly (1,440 counts a year),
360 B items quarterly (1,440) and 720 C items twice a year (1,440). That's 4,320 counts over 250 working days, about
17 bins a day: half an hour for one person, instead of a closed warehouse.

Rules that keep counts honest:

- **Blind counts.** The counter sees the bin, not the expected quantity.
- **Count, then compare, then recount.** A difference over a set tolerance gets a second count by someone else
  before anything is adjusted.
- **Freeze only the bin, not the warehouse.** Movements into or out of the bin wait until the count is posted.
- **Every adjustment has a reason** (damaged, miscount, mis-pick, receiving error), so the cause can be fixed.

## How do lot and serial numbers help in a recall?

They turn "who got that batch?" into a lookup. A lot number ties a quantity to a batch from a supplier or a production run; a serial number ties one unit to its
own history. Record them at receiving and again at shipping, and a recall, a warranty claim or a customer's quality
question becomes a lookup: which customers got lot 24-117, and what else came from that supplier's batch.

What it takes: the lot or serial captured at receiving (scanned from the supplier's label where there is one),
stock held by lot in each location, picking that records which lot went into each order, and returns that come back
to the same lot. Material reserved for one order should be reserved by lot too; see
[QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory) for where an accounting system stops.

## Which valuation method should a distributor use?

Usually FIFO, chosen with your accountant and applied the same way every year. The IRS describes FIFO (first-in first-out) as assuming the items you bought or produced first are the first sold
or used. When prices are rising, FIFO gives a lower cost of goods sold and a higher closing inventory than LIFO.
Publication 538 also covers average cost, LIFO (which has its own rules and an election) and changing methods,
which needs IRS consent. Pick a method with your accountant and apply it the same way every year.

FIFO as a valuation method is not the same as picking the oldest stock first. A system should do both: value stock
by the method you chose, and suggest the oldest lot (or the soonest to expire) when picking.

## Do you need GS1 barcodes?

Only for products you sell to retailers: barcodes on your own bins and locations need no registration, and any internal code works. Barcodes on products you
sell to retailers are different: retailers expect GS1 numbers, which identify your company as the brand owner. GS1
US licenses either a single GTIN for a product or a GS1 Company Prefix that numbers many products, cases and
pallets; its site gives the current prices.

Scan at the moments stock moves: receiving against the purchase order, putaway to a bin, picking against the order,
packing, and counting. A scan that doesn't match (wrong item, wrong lot, over the ordered quantity) should stop the
person there, not show up in next month's count.

## Can QuickBooks do this, or do you need a stock system?

QuickBooks Online can't: it has no bins, lots or serial numbers. QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise can with
[Advanced Inventory](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/desktop/enterprise/advanced-inventory/), on its Platinum and Diamond
plans: three levels of location (such as row, shelf and bin) and serial or lot numbers with expiry dates. Beyond that,
cycle-count plans, blind counts and scanning at every movement usually mean a stock system beside QuickBooks; see
[QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory).

## What should you look for in a system?

Five things, each of which you can test in a demo:

- Locations and bins, with stock by lot or serial in each.
- Cycle count plans by ABC class, blind counts and adjustment reasons.
- Lot capture at receiving and picking, and a trace report both ways (supplier to customer, customer to supplier).
- Valuation by your chosen method, posted to the books (see [QuickBooks for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)).
- Scanning on phones or handhelds at every movement.

For how the systems that do this compare, see [choosing an ERP](/manufacturing/small-business-erp-options), and for
building one to fit, [custom vs off-the-shelf ERP](/manufacturing/custom-vs-off-the-shelf-erp).

Our free checklist has 28, 19 of them must-haves, as a spreadsheet you can send to every vendor and score side by side.

body:
## Why should a checklist list tests instead of features?

Because every vendor says yes to "inventory management". The question that separates them is whether the system does what
your business needs, shown on your own data. So each line in the checklist has two parts: the requirement, in plain
words, and the test the vendor must run in the demo. A vendor that can't show it in the demo doesn't have it yet.

[Download the checklist for Excel (CSV)](/manufacturing/erp-requirements-checklist-us.csv). It opens in Excel or
Google Sheets; add a column per vendor and score Yes, Partly or No. Free to use under CC BY 4.0.

## What do the 28 requirements cover?

Ten areas, from quoting to leaving the vendor:

| Area | Requirements | Must-haves | What they test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quoting and sales | 3 | 2 | Estimate revisions to order without retyping; order status for sales |
| Purchasing | 3 | 2 | Approved purchase requests; three-way match before paying a bill |
| Inventory | 5 | 3 | Stock by location and state; reservations; lots; cycle counts; valuation |
| Production | 4 | 3 | Routings on real capacity; time from the floor; scrap; job cost while open |
| Shipping | 2 | 1 | Ship only what's ready; partial shipments; documents and tracking |
| Accounting and QuickBooks | 2 | 2 | Posting once, with failures shown; which side owns each record |
| Sales tax | 3 | 2 | Rates from the ship-to address; certificates by state; sales by state |
| Access and audit | 2 | 2 | Roles that hide money; a change log that can't be turned off |
| Reporting | 1 | 0 | One owner's screen, each figure opening to its records |
| Data and ownership | 3 | 2 | Full export now; ownership and exit terms in writing; checked migration |

Each area has its own guide: [job shop ERP](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp) for the shop floor,
[inventory control for distributors](/manufacturing/distributor-inventory-control) for stock,
[connecting QuickBooks to a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-integration) for the accounting link, and
[how an ERP should handle sales tax](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp) for sales tax.

## How do you use the checklist with vendors?

Send it before the demo and score during it:

1. Delete the lines that don't apply to you, and mark which "Should" lines are must-haves for your business.
2. Send it to each vendor before the demo, and ask them to run the tests on a copy of your items and one real order.
3. Score during the demo, not after: Yes only if you saw it work.
4. Put the scores side by side, with price and the contract terms; see
   [choosing an ERP](/manufacturing/small-business-erp-options) and
   [custom vs off-the-shelf ERP](/manufacturing/custom-vs-off-the-shelf-erp).

## How do you score vendors with it?

Must-haves are pass or fail; the "should" lines break ties. A made-up example with 19 must-haves and 9 shoulds:

| Vendor | Must-haves passed | Shoulds passed | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| A | 17 of 19 | 7 of 9 | Out: a missed must-have is a no, whatever the rest |
| B | 19 of 19 | 4 of 9 | In, weaker on reporting |
| C | 19 of 19 | 8 of 9 | In; compare with B on price and exit terms |

## Where do the QuickBooks and sales tax requirements come from?

From the rules your system has to live with. Intuit's
[App Partner Program](https://developer.intuit.com/app/developer/qbo/docs/get-started/partner-faq) makes writing to
QuickBooks Online free and reading from it metered, so a system that polls QuickBooks record by record can hit Intuit's
limits; ask how the vendor's link reads changes. QuickBooks Online tracks inventory only on Plus and Advanced. On sales
tax, the [Streamlined Sales Tax Governing Board](https://www.streamlinedsalestax.org/for-businesses/exemptions) has
buyers hand exemption certificates to the seller, who keeps them, so the certificate belongs on the customer record;
and Texas asks sellers to keep [marketplace sales records](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/sales/remote-sellers.php)
for at least four years, so the export test matters for tax as well as for leaving.

## Which five tests rule out most systems?

These five, because most systems fail at least one:

- Reserve the last units of an item for one order, then try to issue them to another.
- Add a rush job and show which jobs go late.
- Make a QuickBooks post fail and show where the failure appears.
- Ship to a state where the customer has no exemption certificate.
- Export all open orders and the item list, now, without the vendor's help.

Indian manufacturers and traders: the [ERP requirements builder](/erp/check) covers GST, e-invoicing, Tally and the
other Indian rules.

title: ERP for job shops and small manufacturers: what to look for
metaTitle: Job shop ERP: what a small manufacturer should look for
question: What should a job shop look for in ERP software?
answer: A job shop ERP should carry each job from quote to invoice on one record: the quoted routing becomes the job, material is reserved for it, operations are scheduled on real machine capacity, the floor records time and scrap per operation, and actual cost is compared with the quote while the job is open. For a shop of 10 to 50 people, start with quoting, jobs, scheduling and job cost; keep QuickBooks for accounting; and test every vendor on two of your own jobs, not their sample data.
description: Job shop ERP for small manufacturers: the quote-to-invoice flow, what to buy first, ten tests to run in a vendor demo, and what shop owners warn about.

sources.title: ERP: JobBOSS2 vs ProShop vs something actually good (forum discussion)

body:
## What should a job shop look for in ERP software?

One record that carries each job from quote to invoice. A job shop makes to order, so the unit of work is the job, not the product. An ERP for one follows a job through every department on the same record:

1. **Quote**: material, operations, setup and run times, outside processing, price.
2. **Order**: the customer's PO turns the quote into a job with nothing typed again.
3. **Job and routing**: the quoted operations become the job's [routing](/systems/routing) and its traveler.
4. **Material**: stock is reserved for the job, or bought for it, with heat or lot numbers where they matter.
5. **Schedule**: operations placed on machines with real capacity ([how scheduling works](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software)).
6. **Shop floor**: operators record start, finish, quantity and scrap for each operation ([WIP tracking](/manufacturing/wip-tracking)).
7. **Quality**: inspection results and certificates attached to the job.
8. **Ship and invoice**: packing list, invoice from what shipped, posted to the accounting system.
9. **Job cost**: actual against quoted, per operation ([a worked example](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing)).

If two of these steps live in different files, that's where errors and lost hours collect.

## What should a 10 to 50 person shop buy first?

Quoting, jobs, one shared schedule, floor time and job cost; the rest can follow:

| First | Next | Usually later |
|---|---|---|
| Quoting from operations and times | Material reservation per job | Maintenance scheduling |
| Jobs and travelers from the quote | Purchasing from job shortages | Advanced planning (optimizers) |
| One shared schedule | Quality records and certificates | Customer portal |
| Shop-floor time per operation | Heat, lot or serial traceability | EDI with large customers |
| Job cost vs quote | Inventory by location | Multi-plant |

Accounting stays where it is. Most small manufacturers already run QuickBooks, and replacing it buys nothing; the ERP should post invoices and inventory value to it ([what QuickBooks covers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)).

## What do shop owners warn about before buying an ERP?

Four things. Owners discussing ERP on forums such as Practical Machinist raise the same few points, and they are worth taking seriously:

- **Someone has to run it.** One experienced poster puts it plainly: a full ERP needs an administrator, which is real overhead for a 3 to 10 person shop.
- **Paying for what you don't use.** Large packages carry modules a small shop never touches, and the setup effort that comes with them.
- **Weak scheduling.** Several owners say the scheduling module was the weak part: not good enough to plan the floor day to day.
- **The workflow bends to the software.** If the system can't model how your jobs move, people keep the old spreadsheets, and now there are two sources of truth.

## How do you test an ERP vendor in a demo?

Run ten tests live, on your own data. Each takes about an hour. A vendor that can't show one live is telling you something.

1. Turn one of your recent quotes into a job without retyping the operations.
2. Show the job's traveler with each operation, machine and quoted time.
3. Reserve stock for the job, then show that a second job can't plan on the same material.
4. Schedule five jobs on your machines and shifts, then add a rush order and show what moves.
5. Record an operation's time and scrap from a phone or a shop-floor screen.
6. Show estimated vs actual cost for a job before it ships.
7. Find which jobs used a given heat or lot number, and the reverse.
8. Ship part of a job and invoice only what shipped.
9. Post that invoice to QuickBooks once, retry the post, and show there's still one invoice.
10. Export every record (jobs, routings, stock, costs) to files you can open without the vendor.

The last one matters more than it looks: it's what makes leaving possible.

Score as you go. A made-up example with 2 points a test (2 shown live, 1 partly, 0 not): vendor A scores 15 of 20 but
fails test 3 (reservation) and test 9 (a duplicate QuickBooks invoice); vendor B scores 13 of 20 and passes both.
Pick B, or make A fix those two in the contract: a failed must-have outweighs a higher total. If a vendor leads with AI, add the tests in [AI in ERP: what it can safely do today](/ai-assistant/ai-in-erp).

## Packaged, configurable or built for you: which fits a job shop?

Packaged fits when your jobs move the way the package expects; built for you fits when your workflow is the reason customers choose you. Three routes, each right for some shops (compared in more depth in [custom vs off-the-shelf ERP](/manufacturing/custom-vs-off-the-shelf-erp)):

- **Packaged job shop ERP.** Fastest to start if your work fits its model. You adapt to the software, pay per user, and live with its scheduling and reports.
- **Configurable platform.** A general ERP or low-code base set up for you. More flexible, but someone keeps the configuration working.
- **Built for your workflow.** Fits exactly and can change as you do. It costs more up front and depends on the builder staying around, so get in writing that you can export all your data at any time, what happens to the code and the licence if you stop paying for support, and a fixed scope per phase.

Ahrom Labs builds the third kind: operations systems for manufacturers and distributors, in phases, beside the accounting software you already use. Two things we've built show what "fits the workflow" means in practice: a cutting record where every plate cut puts its usable remnant back into stock, with weights that always add up ([remnants back into stock](/notes/plate-remnants-back-into-stock)), and a customer portal that shows each order's stage from the records departments already keep ([one order, every department](/notes/customer-portal-one-order-every-department)). Both run at a manufacturer in India. Our US [boiler demo](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing) shows the same system on a sample company: job cards with time logs and rework cards, capacity per work center, a read-only schedule of work orders, and each job's actual cost against its plan. It doesn't reschedule jobs by itself; dates move through a change note. Our US offer starts with a fixed-price prototype of one workflow, shown below.

## What should you bring to every ERP demo?

Two of your own jobs, whatever you choose, plus the [QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory) questions if stock is your pain, and the ten tests above.

title: Free job shop production schedule template (Excel)
question: Is there a free production scheduling template in Excel for a job shop?
answer: Yes. This free Excel template plans a job shop by machine: list each job's operations in routing order with their hours and a planned day, and it flags any operation planned after the job's due date or before its previous operation, and shows the hours booked on each machine each day in red when they exceed that machine's shift. It suits up to a few dozen open jobs and one planner; past that, use scheduling software.
description: A free Excel production schedule template for job shops: routings by machine, planned days, due-date checks and daily machine load against shift hours.

body:
## Is there a free production schedule template for a job shop?

Yes, this one: [**Job shop schedule template (Excel)**](/manufacturing/job-shop-schedule-template.xlsx), free under CC BY 4.0. It opens in Excel or Google Sheets and needs no macros.

It is filled in with the six made-up jobs from the [schedule demo](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software), so you can see it working before you replace them with your own.

## What's in the template?

Three sheets: machines, jobs and the daily load.

| Sheet | What you enter | What it works out |
|---|---|---|
| **Machines** | Each machine or work center and its hours per day (8 for one shift, 16 for two) | Nothing; the other sheets read it |
| **Jobs** | One row per operation, in routing order: job, due date, operation number, machine, hours, planned day | A check on every row: OK, "After due date", or "Before previous operation" |
| **Load** | The first day of the plan | Hours booked per machine for each of the next 20 working days, red where a machine is over its hours |

The machine column is a drop-down from the Machines sheet, so a typo can't create a machine that doesn't exist.

## How do you fill it in?

Machines first, then each job's operations, then a planned day for each:

1. List your machines and their shift hours.
2. Enter each open job's operations from its [routing](/systems/routing), with the quoted hours. If your quotes are built from operations and times, copy them; that's also what [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) compares against.
3. Give each operation a planned day, earliest due date first, and each operation no earlier than the one before it.
4. Look at the Load sheet. Red means that machine has more hours booked than it has that day: move an operation, split it across days, or add a shift.
5. Fix every "After due date" either by moving work or by telling the customer now, not on the due date.

The sample shows the point of step 4. Three days come up red, and the welding cell on Wednesday is the real problem: 13 hours booked on an 8-hour day, which is why frame job J-103 runs late in the demo. The other two (the laser on Monday, the press brake on Tuesday, 9 hours each) are operations that run over into the next day, which the template counts on the day they start.

## How much can your machines take in a week?

Machines × shifts × hours × days. Three machines on two 8-hour shifts, five days a week, give 3 × 2 × 8 × 5 = 240 hours
a week, and 80 hours for each machine. The Load sheet does the same sum per machine per day: the sample's welding
cell on Wednesday, 13 hours booked on an 8-hour day, is 162.5% of its capacity, so it shows red.

## When does a spreadsheet schedule stop being enough?

When more than one person plans, or when you need the later operations to move by themselves. Owners on
[Practical Machinist](https://www.practicalmachinist.com/forum/threads/machine-scheduling.393367/) describe starting
with a whiteboard, moving to an Excel grid of machines by day, and finding it works while one person owns it.
A spreadsheet schedule is honest about what it is:

- **One planner.** Two people editing copies of it will drift apart; owners on forums say this is where spreadsheets break.
- **Nothing moves by itself.** When an operation slips, you move the later ones by hand. Scheduling software moves the whole chain ([finite capacity](/systems#finite-capacity-scheduling)).
- **It doesn't know what's finished.** Progress has to be typed in; without it the plan drifts from the floor. That's what [WIP tracking](/manufacturing/wip-tracking) fixes.
- **Hours land on one day.** An operation's hours all count on its planned day, so long operations show as an overload; split them into one row per day if that matters.

When those limits cost you late jobs every week, read [what production scheduling software does](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software) and try the demo with your own jobs.

title: Production scheduling software for job shops: machines, shifts and due dates
metaTitle: Production scheduling software for job shops
question: What does production scheduling software do in a job shop?
answer: Production scheduling software places each job's operations on the machines that can run them, in routing order, within the hours each machine is staffed, and shows which jobs will miss their due date before it happens. In a job shop it replaces the spreadsheet or whiteboard with one shared schedule, built from each job's routing, real shift hours and due dates, that updates when a rush order arrives or a machine goes down.
description: How production scheduling software works in a job shop: finite capacity, routings, shifts, due dates, dispatch rules vs optimizers, with worked numbers.

sources.title: Machine scheduling software, not quite ERP (forum discussion)

body:
## What does production scheduling software do in a job shop?

It places each job's operations on the machines that can run them, in routing order, within the hours each machine is staffed, and shows which jobs will be late before they are. It needs four inputs, and most bad schedules are missing one of them:

| Input | What it is | Where it usually lives today |
|---|---|---|
| **Routing** for each job | The operations in order, the machine or work center for each, setup and run time | In the estimator's head, or on the quote |
| **Capacity** | Which machines exist, their shifts, planned downtime | On the wall, or nowhere |
| **Due dates** | When each job must ship | In the order, or the customer's email |
| **Material** | Whether the material for each job is in stock or due in | In QuickBooks or the stores, often out of date |

A [routing](/systems/routing) is the piece shops most often lack. If quotes are built from operations and times, the routing already exists; see [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing), where the same times become the estimate.

## What is the difference between finite and infinite capacity scheduling?

Finite scheduling only books a machine for the hours it has; infinite scheduling assumes every machine is free when needed. **Infinite capacity** scheduling works backward from the due date and assumes every machine is free when needed. It answers "when must this start?" and is how classic MRP plans. It is why a schedule can show the laser booked for 30 hours on a Tuesday.

**[Finite capacity](/systems#finite-capacity-scheduling)** scheduling only books a machine for the hours it has. When the laser is full, the next job waits, and its later operations move with it. That answers the question customers actually ask: "when will it ship?"

The demo above is finite. With one shift, the five sample jobs all ship on time. Add a rush order due tomorrow and it goes first, and frame job J-103 slips a day, because both the rush job and J-103 need the welding cell and the weld cell is the bottleneck. Switch to two shifts and everything ships on time again. That is the trade a scheduler weighs every day, made visible.

The numbers behind it, from the demo's own data: the weld cell has 18 hours of work (J-101's 5, J-104's 3 and J-103's
10), and the rush job adds 4 more. The rush job also takes the laser first, so every job behind it starts 2 hours later.
On one 8-hour shift, J-103's weld then ends at hour 33 of the plan, one hour into day 5, when it was due by the end of
day 4 (hour 32). On two shifts the same hour 33 falls on day 3. Notice that the weld cell is booked 22 of its 32 hours
over those four days, 69%, and a job is still late: lateness comes from the order operations queue in, not only from
how full a machine is.

## How does scheduling software decide which job goes first?

By a fixed rule, an optimizer, or a planner using the software to check capacity. From simplest to most complex:

1. **Dispatch rules.** Take jobs in a fixed order (earliest due date first is the common one, as in the demo) and give each operation the first slot its machine and the previous operation allow. Predictable: a planner can check any result by hand.
2. **Optimizers (APS).** Advanced planning and scheduling tools search many orders to cut lateness or changeovers. Better on paper, but harder to explain, and a plan nobody understands tends to be overridden on the floor.
3. **People with a tool.** The planner drags jobs around a board; the software checks capacity and shows the knock-on effect. Most small shops land here.

For a shop of 10 to 50 people, a dispatch rule plus a planner who can override it usually beats an optimizer. The bigger win is having one schedule everyone trusts.

## Where does AI help with scheduling, and where shouldn't it decide?

AI is useful around the schedule: reading a new order's drawing or email into a draft routing, warning that a job is drifting late, or explaining in plain words why J-103 moved. It shouldn't decide machine assignments by itself. A schedule must respect hard limits, such as machine hours, routing order and material on hand, and a rule or solver can guarantee those; a language model can't. Our rule: AI drafts and explains, rules and people decide, the same split we use where a suggestion ends up on a quality document ([same confidence, different autonomy](/notes/same-confidence-different-autonomy)). More on what AI can safely do across an ERP: [AI in ERP](/ai-assistant/ai-in-erp).

## Why does a spreadsheet or whiteboard schedule stop working?

Because it works only while one person owns it and keeps it current. Shop owners on [Practical Machinist](https://www.practicalmachinist.com/forum/threads/machine-scheduling.393367/) describe the same path: a sheet with one column per machine and a row per day, or a whiteboard, which works while one person owns it. It breaks when:

- two or three people edit it, and the copies drift apart;
- a job's later operations don't move when its first one slips;
- nobody can say when a new order could ship without redoing the whole sheet;
- the floor's actual progress never makes it back, so the plan slowly turns into fiction.

The last point is the real limit. A schedule needs to know what has actually finished, which means operators recording each operation as they complete it, the same data [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) needs; see [WIP tracking with barcoded travelers](/manufacturing/wip-tracking).

If you're not ready for software, the free [job shop schedule template](/manufacturing/production-schedule-template) does the capacity check in Excel.

## Does our boiler demo schedule the shop?

Partly. The US [boiler demo](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing) sets each work center's shifts, hours
per shift and working days, shows the hours booked against them, and shows open work orders as bars with a delayed
flag and a material check. It doesn't reschedule jobs by itself: dates move through a change note that someone
approves. The finite schedule on this page is a separate demo.

## What should you ask a scheduling software vendor?

Six questions, and ask for each answer live on your own jobs:

- Does it schedule to finite capacity, per machine and shift, or only backward from due dates?
- Can it take the routing straight from the quote?
- What happens to a job's later operations when an earlier one runs late?
- Can a planner override a slot without breaking the rest?
- How does finished work get back from the floor, and how quickly?
- Does it check material before scheduling a job?

Bring two or three of your own jobs to the demo and ask them to schedule them live. For choosing the rest of the system, see [ERP for job shops](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp); for where scheduling sits next to QuickBooks, see [does QuickBooks work for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing).

body:
## What happened when QuickBooks Desktop 2023 support ended?

Intuit discontinued Desktop 2023 (Pro Plus, Premier Plus including the Manufacturing & Wholesale edition, Mac Plus
and Enterprise 23.0) after May 31, 2026, so a company still on it has lost these services, per Intuit's
[discontinuation policy](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/feature-preferences/quickbooks-desktop-service-discontinuation-policy/L17cXxlie_US_en_US):

| Lost | What that means for a shop |
|---|---|
| Live technical support | No help when a file breaks |
| Critical security updates | The company file and the PC are exposed |
| Payroll tax calculation and forms (Basic, Enhanced, Assisted) | Paychecks may be wrong; Assisted no longer files for you |
| Online bank feeds and online banking | Bank transactions typed or imported by hand |
| Payment processing and eInvoice pay links | Card and check payments handled outside QuickBooks |
| Emailing forms and reports | Invoices and statements sent another way |

The books themselves are still there and still open. The risk grows with each month.

## Can you keep using an old Desktop version offline?

It opens, but without security updates or any connected service, and only on a machine where it is already
registered. Owners on r/QuickBooks still run versions as old as 2013 that way, and the trouble starts when the PC dies:
reinstalling an unsupported copy depends on finding its old registration files. Keep the old file read-only for
history, not as the live books.

## When does QuickBooks Desktop 2024 lose support?

Intuit hasn't said. Its discontinuation policy page still covers only the 2023 versions (updated August 5, 2026), and
third-party sites give different 2027 dates. Plus and Enterprise subscribers already got version 2024 at no extra
cost; watch Intuit's policy page, not a blog, for the 2024 date.

## What are a manufacturer's options?

Five, with Intuit's list prices from November 2026:

| Option | What changes | Price | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stay on Desktop Plus 2024 or Enterprise 24.0 | Little | Included in an active subscription | You want time to decide |
| QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise | Same interface, up to 40 users, industry editions | From $2,210 a year (Gold) | Desktop users who need more capacity |
| QuickBooks Online Advanced | Cloud; migration help | $340 a month, 50% off the first year when you move from Desktop | Firms ready to move to the cloud |
| Intuit Enterprise Suite | Intuit's multi-entity ERP; where its manufacturing orders are | By quote | Larger, multi-company firms |
| Keep QuickBooks for the books, add a shop system | Accounting stays in QuickBooks; jobs, stock and the floor move to a system built for them | The shop system's cost | Shops whose problem is the work, not the ledger |

Before choosing, read [QuickBooks Online vs Desktop for manufacturers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-vs-desktop):
QuickBooks Online doesn't do everything Desktop Enterprise does for inventory and assemblies.

## How much does moving to QuickBooks Online Advanced cost?

$340 a month at list price, with half off the first year for a business coming from Desktop, and Intuit says an
implementation consultant is included at no cost for simple migrations. For a made-up 14-person shop that's $4,080 a
year at list, $2,040 in the first year: a saving of $2,040. Advanced covers 25 users.

## Should you move all your Desktop history to QuickBooks Online?

Usually not. Move the lists (customers, vendors, items), open invoices and bills, and opening balances, and keep the
old file read-only for history. The top reply on a recent [r/QuickBooks thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/QuickBooks/comments/1xbs9kl/finally_understand_why_everyone_hates_quickbooks/)
about a painful migration said the same: start fresh with the current year rather than carry years of transactions.

## How do you plan the move?

Like any migration, whichever system you pick:

1. Decide what moves: lists, open invoices and bills, balances, and how much history.
2. Freeze item and account changes for the move.
3. Run both for one month-end, and compare the trial balance and stock value. A $1,250 stock difference found then is
   one recount; found next March, it's a year-end adjustment.
4. Keep the old file read-only, on a backed-up PC, for the records you must keep.

If the move is also the moment to stop running jobs in spreadsheets, see
[when a business has outgrown QuickBooks](/manufacturing/quickbooks-vs-erp) and
[connecting QuickBooks to a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-integration).
