body:
## Which QuickBooks edition works for manufacturing?

Only Intuit Enterprise Suite and QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise have bills of materials and builds; QuickBooks Online
Plus and Advanced track inventory but not manufacturing. Checked against Intuit's own pages on 5 November 2026: the [manufacturing orders help](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/sales-orders/learn-manufacturing-orders-assemblies/L7ffspckB_US_en_US), the [QuickBooks Online inventory help](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/inventory-management/set-track-inventory-quickbooks-online/L22FZLBGN_US_en_US) and the [Desktop Enterprise manufacturing page](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/desktop/enterprise/industry-solutions/manufacturing/).
Intuit changes plans often; check yours before relying on this.

| | QuickBooks Online Plus / Advanced | Intuit Enterprise Suite | QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise (Manufacturing & Wholesale) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory quantities and value | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Bill of materials and assemblies | No | Yes, single level only | Yes, including subassemblies |
| Manufacturing (build) orders | No | Yes: planned, in progress, completed | Yes: automated builds |
| Component shortages | No | Yes, a shortage column and report | Not described on Intuit's product page |
| Labor in product cost | Through projects, not per unit | As a service line on the bill of materials | Yes |
| Multiple warehouses, bins, lots, serials | Not described in Intuit's inventory setup article | Not described in Intuit's manufacturing help | Advanced Inventory, Platinum and Diamond only |
| Routings, machines, operations | No | Not described in Intuit's help | Not described on Intuit's product page |
| Machine scheduling, shop-floor time by operation | No | Not described | Not described (production forecasts and labor planning are) |

"Not described" means the Intuit page we checked doesn't mention it; ask Intuit or a ProAdvisor if it matters to you.

## What does a manufacturer need that QuickBooks may not have?

A manufacturer needs three things, and QuickBooks covers at most the first: what a part is made of, how it is made,
and when it is made. Most confusion comes from mixing them up:

1. **What a part is made of**: the [bill of materials](/systems#bill-of-materials). QuickBooks' assembly items cover this, in the editions that have them.
2. **How it is made**: the [routing](/systems/routing), the operations in order (cut, bend, weld, inspect), on which machine, with setup and run times. No QuickBooks edition models this.
3. **When it is made**: the schedule, which puts each operation on a machine with real capacity. See [production scheduling software](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software).

A shop that buys and assembles kits mostly needs the first. A job shop that machines, cuts or welds to order needs all three, which is why job shops outgrow QuickBooks sooner than assemblers do.

## Can QuickBooks Online Plus or Advanced handle manufacturing?

Not on their own: Plus and Advanced track inventory and job profit, but have no bills of materials or builds.
Inventory is included in Plus and Advanced: quantity on hand, reorder points, purchase orders, and either FIFO or moving average cost, chosen once (see [QuickBooks Online inventory for manufacturers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory)). What's missing for a manufacturer:

- **No bills of materials or builds.** Intuit's manufacturing help says these features are in Intuit Enterprise Suite; if you downgrade from it, bills of materials become view-only.
- **Bundles are not assemblies.** A bundle groups items so they go on an invoice together; no finished part sits in stock and no labor goes into its cost.
- **Job costing is by project.** Plus and Advanced group a customer's income, expenses and timesheets into a project. That gives job profit, but not setup and run hours per operation (see [job costing in QuickBooks](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing)).

A common workaround is to keep raw material as non-inventory items and adjust finished goods by hand. It keeps the books roughly right but hides what each job really used.

## What manufacturing features does Intuit Enterprise Suite have?

Intuit Enterprise Suite has single-level bills of materials, manufacturing orders and builds that compute actual
cost. It is Intuit's cloud plan above QuickBooks Online Advanced, and its manufacturing feature works like this:

- An **inventory assembly item** carries a bill of materials: components, raw materials and services such as labor for one unit. A manufacturing order can't start without one.
- A **manufacturing order** starts as Planned and reserves its components; a shortage column counts what other open orders need from the same stock.
- Completing the order creates a **build assembly** that moves components into finished stock and computes the actual cost. Estimated cost comes from each component's default purchase cost.

The limits that matter to a job shop: bills of materials are single level (no subassemblies), edits to a bill apply only to new orders, and Intuit's help doesn't describe routings, work centers or scheduling. It suits a shop that assembles from bought parts more than one that machines from bar stock.

## What does QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise do for manufacturers?

Desktop Enterprise (Manufacturing & Wholesale) has the deepest manufacturing features of the three: bills of materials with subassemblies, automated builds and purchase orders for the components a final assembly needs, and costs from raw material to finished goods including labor and landed cost. Its [**Advanced Inventory**](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/desktop/enterprise/advanced-inventory/) (multiple locations down to bin, lot and serial numbers, barcode scanning, cycle counts) is in the Platinum and Diamond subscriptions only; landed cost and sales order fulfillment are too.

It is desktop software sold by subscription, annual or monthly (Diamond is monthly only). Intuit's pages describe production forecasts and labor planning, but not routing by machine or shop-floor time by operation.

## How much do these editions cost?

On [Intuit's US pricing page](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/pricing/) on 5 November 2026, QuickBooks Online Plus listed at $140 a month and Advanced at $340 a
month, each with an introductory discount for the first three months. Intuit Enterprise Suite has no price on that
page. For Desktop Enterprise, the price depends on the tier (Gold, Platinum or Diamond), and Advanced Inventory
needs Platinum or Diamond; check Intuit's Desktop Enterprise pricing page. A shop system beside QuickBooks is a separate cost on top of whichever edition you keep.

## How do you know you've outgrown QuickBooks?

You've outgrown it when the shop's real plan lives outside QuickBooks and nobody trusts the numbers in it. From what
shop owners describe on forums such as Practical Machinist, and what we see in our own work:

- Quotes live in a spreadsheet and the job is set up again from scratch when the order arrives.
- The schedule is a whiteboard or a sheet with one column per machine, and only one person trusts it.
- You find out a job lost money weeks after it shipped, when the bills arrive.
- Stock in QuickBooks and stock on the shelf disagree, because material used on the floor is entered later, or never.
- Two people keep "the real list" of open jobs, and they differ.

None of these is a QuickBooks bug. QuickBooks is an accounting system; these are operations problems.

## Can you keep QuickBooks and add a shop system?

Yes, and for most small manufacturers it is the cheapest sound setup: QuickBooks for the books and a shop system for the work, with one owner for each record:

| Record | Owned by | Goes to the other system as |
|---|---|---|
| Customers and vendors | Either, but only one | A copy, kept in step |
| Quotes, jobs, routings, schedule | Shop system | Nothing (stays in operations) |
| Shop-floor hours, scrap, material used | Shop system | Job cost, and the inventory value at month-end |
| Customer invoices | Shop system (from the shipped job) | An invoice, posted once |
| Vendor bills and payments | Either, but only one: usually the shop system, which holds the PO and the receipt | A bill, then its payment |
| Chart of accounts, tax, payroll | QuickBooks | Nothing |

"Owned by" means people change that record in one place only. Everything that breaks between two systems starts with a record two people can edit in both.

## How do you connect a shop system to QuickBooks without duplicates?

Post each record once, under the shop system's own number, and read it back. Our QuickBooks Online connector runs in our four US demos against a QuickBooks sandbox company ([what it sends](/manufacturing/quickbooks-integration)). It follows the rules our [TallyPrime connection](/notes/connecting-tallyprime-four-ways) already runs on:

- **Post once, by our own number.** Each invoice carries the shop system's document number; before posting, the connector checks whether that number already exists, so a retry can't create a second copy.
- **Read back, don't assume.** After posting, read the record from the accounting system and store its ID and totals ([reconcile against the source of truth](/patterns/reconcile-against-source-of-truth)).
- **Fail loudly.** A rejected entry (a missing account, a closed period) waits for a person with the reason shown, instead of retrying forever or being dropped ([failures flagged, not lost](/patterns/failures-flagged-not-lost)).
- **Nobody re-keys.** On Intuit's community, many "duplicate" problems come from someone entering by hand what an integration had already posted, which also takes the stock out twice.

## What should you check in a shop system that sits beside QuickBooks?

Before choosing one, check that it:

- Holds multi-level bills of materials and routings (operations, machines, setup and run times).
- Schedules operations on machines with real capacity, not just due dates.
- Records shop-floor time and material used against each job, and shows job cost before the job ships.
- Tracks stock by location, and lots or heat numbers if your customers ask for them.
- Posts invoices (and, if it owns them, bills) to your QuickBooks edition once each, with the record's own number,
  and shows anything QuickBooks rejected.
- Lets one system own each record, as in the table above.

## Is QuickBooks an ERP?

No. An ERP covers operations (orders, production, stock, purchasing) as well as accounting, on one database. QuickBooks is accounting software with some inventory; Intuit Enterprise Suite and Desktop Enterprise add manufacturing pieces but not shop-floor control. That's fine: many good shop systems are built to sit beside QuickBooks rather than replace it. See [ERP for job shops](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp) for what the shop side needs.

body:
## Which system should own each record, QuickBooks or the shop system?

The shop system should own jobs, items and stock, and QuickBooks should own the ledger, the bank and the tax codes;
decide every record's owner before writing any code. Most failed integrations fail here: both systems let people
edit the same thing, and the sync can't tell which change wins.

| Record | Usual owner | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| Customers and vendors | Shop system (sales and purchasing create them) | Shop → QuickBooks |
| Items | Shop system (it knows stock, routings, lots) | Shop → QuickBooks |
| Invoices | Shop system (shipped against the order) | Shop → QuickBooks |
| Vendor bills | Either; usually entered where the purchase order lives | Shop → QuickBooks |
| Vendor payments | Wherever they are recorded against the bill | Shop → QuickBooks, or the reverse |
| Customer payments, deposits | Wherever they are recorded: QuickBooks if they come in through its bank feed, the shop system if staff mark invoices paid there | One direction only, never both |
| Chart of accounts, tax codes | QuickBooks (your accountant's) | Read by the shop system |

The owner is where people edit; the other side shows it read-only. A customer's address changed in QuickBooks is
then either sent back or overwritten, by a rule, not by chance.

## What can a shop system sync with QuickBooks Online?

Customers, vendors, items, invoices, payments, bills and bill payments, through an app that the company connects
once with OAuth 2.0. For changes made in the shop system, it writes to QuickBooks when the event happens (an invoice
is approved, a bill is posted) and records QuickBooks' ID for the record, so a retry updates instead of duplicating.

## How does the shop system find out about changes made in QuickBooks?

Through webhooks, with change data capture as the safety net, both described in Intuit's developer docs:

- **[Webhooks](https://developer.intuit.com/app/developer/qbo/docs/develop/webhooks/configure-webhooks)** notify your
  system when entities change, only for companies connected and authorized through OAuth 2.0. Each notification
  should be checked against the verifier token Intuit gives, so a forged call is rejected. Intuit says the first
  notification can take up to five minutes to arrive.
- **[Change data capture (CDC)](https://developer.intuit.com/app/developer/qbo/docs/learn/explore-the-quickbooks-online-api/change-data-capture)**
  returns everything that changed since a time, up to 30 days back and up to 1,000 objects a response. Run it on a
  schedule for any webhook that was missed. It doesn't cover every entity: time activities and tax codes and rates
  are among those left out, so timesheets entered in QuickBooks need a query of their own.

## Does the QuickBooks API cost anything?

Writing to QuickBooks is free; reading from it is metered. Under Intuit's
[App Partner Program](https://developer.intuit.com/app/developer/qbo/docs/get-started/partner-faq), which launched in
the US on July 28, 2025, every app starts in the free Builder tier. "Core" calls, which create or update invoices,
bills, customers and vendors, are unmetered. "CorePlus" calls, which read data (accounts, company information,
reports), are counted, and the Builder tier allows 500,000 of them a month; calls above that are blocked, not
billed. Paid tiers raise the allowance and charge for calls above it, and an app listed on Intuit's App Marketplace
must subscribe to the paid Silver tier to stay listed.

A worked example, with made-up volumes: a shop sends 1,200 invoices, 900 payments, 600 bills and 500 bill payments
a month. That's 3,200 writes, all free. If it also reads each record back after posting (3,200 reads), runs change
data capture every 15 minutes (2,880 a month) and a nightly totals check of four queries (120), it uses 6,200 metered
reads: 1.2% of the free allowance. Polling all 3,200 records every five minutes instead would be 3,200 × 8,640 =
27.6 million reads a month, and the app would be blocked within the first day or two. Poll by change data capture,
never record by record.

## Who calculates sales tax, the shop system or QuickBooks?

With QuickBooks Online's automated sales tax, QuickBooks does: it works out the tax on each invoice from the ship-to
address and whether each line is taxable, and posts it to its own liability account for each tax agency. So the shop
system sends the lines, their taxable flags and the ship-to address, not a tax amount. Decide this as deliberately as
record ownership.

What we saw testing our connector against a QuickBooks Online sandbox company (November 2026): the company was set up
to collect tax only in Arizona and California, so QuickBooks charged $0 tax to customers in other states. One invoice
came to $21,959 in our system and $21,200 in QuickBooks: the same lines, without $759 of tax. Nothing errored; the
totals simply differed. The lessons:

- **Set up every state where you collect** in QuickBooks' sales tax settings, not only in the shop system. QuickBooks
  can't charge tax for a state it doesn't know you collect in.
- **Store both totals** (yours and QuickBooks') on each invoice and flag any difference, so a gap is seen the day
  it happens, not at the return.
- **Don't post tax twice.** If QuickBooks calculates the tax, leave the shop system's own sales tax payable account
  out of the account mapping.

For what the shop system itself must track, see [sales tax in an ERP](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp).

## What goes wrong in a QuickBooks sync, and how do you catch it?

Three things, and each has a check:

- **A post fails** (a closed period, a missing tax code, an item renamed in QuickBooks). It must be logged and shown
  to a person, never dropped silently. The pattern: [failures flagged, not lost](/patterns/failures-flagged-not-lost).
- **Totals drift.** Compare open invoices and item counts on both sides every night; a difference is a ticket.
- **Someone edits on the wrong side.** Make the non-owner side read-only where you can, and alert where you can't.

## Does a private connection need Intuit's app review?

Only the first level of it. To get production credentials, an app's App Assessment Questionnaire must be approved;
after that, an app used privately is live. Listing on Intuit's App Marketplace adds a three-part review (technical, a
third-party security review, and marketing), Intuit reviews listed apps at least once a year, and the listing now
needs a paid partner tier.

## What does the Ahrom Labs connector send to QuickBooks?

Invoices, payments, vendor bills and bill payments, from our US demos connected to a QuickBooks sandbox company
(November 2026); it isn't yet running on a client's live books. In the boiler and electronics distribution demos:

- **Connecting:** the owner connects QuickBooks once in Settings, reviews the suggested account matches and saves
  them. Visitors can see the connection but not change it.
- **Sales:** issued invoices and recorded customer payments go to QuickBooks with their customer. Each line goes as
  taxable or not, and QuickBooks works out the tax.
- **Purchases:** approved vendor bills go with their vendor; vendor payments go when they name the bill they pay.
- **Payments with no invoice named:** where the cash book records who paid but not which invoice, the payment
  arrives in QuickBooks unapplied, for the accountant to match there.
- **Status on every row:** "In QuickBooks", "QuickBooks failed · Retry" or "Not in QuickBooks · Send". Every call
  carries a request ID, so a retry can't create a second copy.

What it doesn't do yet: it only sends; changes made in QuickBooks don't come back (no webhooks or change data capture
yet), credit and debit notes aren't sent, and a document edited after it was sent isn't sent again. We'd build the
read-back side with change data capture when a client's books need it.

Try it in the [boiler](https://boiler-erp-us.ahromlabs.com/demo) or
[electronics distribution](https://electronics-erp-us.ahromlabs.com/demo) demo. See also
[QuickBooks vs ERP](/manufacturing/quickbooks-vs-erp) and
[QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory).

title: Job costing in QuickBooks for manufacturers: estimated vs actual

question: Can QuickBooks do job costing for a manufacturer?

That works for a contractor. A machine shop also needs setup and run hours, machine time, scrap and rework per job, compared with what was quoted while the job is still open. QuickBooks doesn't split cost that way, so shops either keep a job-cost sheet beside it or track it in a shop system.

body:
## Can QuickBooks do job costing for a manufacturer?

Partly: QuickBooks Online Plus ($140 a month list, November 2026), Advanced ($340) and Intuit Enterprise Suite do job costing through **projects**, which group one customer job's invoices, estimates, bills, expenses and timesheets, with an income, cost and profit view. Intuit's own example in its [projects help](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/manage-projects/set-create-projects-quickbooks-online/L9GAdLMyT_US_en_US) is an auto repair job that tracks every part and labor hour. That covers a contractor. What it doesn't split is the cost a machine shop runs on, below.

## How does labor get into a QuickBooks project?

Two ways, per Intuit's [labor costing help](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/regular-payroll/track-hourly-labor-costs-profitability-project/L9ZxBA4sn_US_en_US):

- **Payroll expenses**: real wages, taxes and workers' comp, posted after each payroll run.
- **Estimated hourly costs**: hours on project timesheets times a fixed rate per employee, which can include overhead. Visible straight away, but only for time tracked after the rate was set.

Intuit Enterprise Suite, and Advanced with the construction add-on, also offer basic or detailed project costing; once you pick detailed you can't switch back.

## Why doesn't the project profitability report match my labor estimate?

Because that report uses payroll expenses only: estimated hourly costs don't feed it. If you track time at an estimated rate and run payroll elsewhere, the report shows the job without its labor.

## What does a machine shop need that QuickBooks projects don't split?

The reasons a job made or lost money, while it's still open:

| Cost a shop tracks | In a QuickBooks project |
|---|---|
| Material issued to the job | Only if bought for that job, or adjusted by hand |
| Setup hours vs run hours | One timesheet total per person |
| Machine time (the shop rate) separate from labor | No: an hourly rate per employee, not per machine |
| Scrapped parts and rework | Not separated from normal production |
| Outside processing (plating, heat treat) | Yes, as bills assigned to the project |
| Quoted hours per operation, to compare | No |

Machine time matters most. In a machine shop the machine and its overhead often cost more per hour than the operator, and one operator may run two machines. A rate per employee can't show that.

## What does one job look like, estimated against actual?

Every figure here is made up. A shop quotes 200 steel brackets at $18.50 each. Labor costs $32 an hour; the shop rate (machine plus overhead) is $65 per machine hour, so an hour of setup or run time costs $97.

| | Estimated | Actual |
|---|---:|---:|
| Material | $840.00 (200 × $4.20) | $910.00 (200 × $4.55) |
| Setup | $194.00 (2 h) | $339.50 (3.5 h) |
| Run time | $1,940.00 (6 min each) | $2,425.00 (7.5 min each) |
| Outside processing | $300.00 | $300.00 |
| Scrapped parts (8 made again) | $0.00 | $133.40 |
| Rework | $0.00 | $145.50 (1.5 h) |
| **Total cost** | **$3,274.00** | **$4,253.40** |
| Revenue | $3,700.00 | $3,700.00 |
| **Margin** | **$426.00 (11.5%)** | **−$553.40 (−15.0%)** |

The job was quoted at 22 hours and took 31: **1.41 hours used per hour quoted**. The largest part of the $979.40 miss is run time ($485.00, from a cycle 25% slower than quoted), not the scrap that people notice on the floor. The calculator above has the same job; change any figure.

## What would the same job look like in QuickBooks?

Profitable. The QuickBooks project sees income of $3,700.00 against material bills of $946.40 (the 200 brackets plus the 8 made again, at $4.55), outside processing of $300.00 and estimated labor of 31 hours × $32 = $992.00. Cost $2,238.40, profit **+$1,461.60 (39.5%)**. The shop view above shows **−$553.40**. The whole gap is the $2,015.00 of machine time (31 hours × $65) that a per-employee rate has nowhere to hold.

One owner on [Practical Machinist](https://www.practicalmachinist.com/forum/threads/how-many-shops-track-actual-hours-vs-the-bid-price.446887/) describes the habit that fixes quoting: log estimated and actual time side by side on every job, and when a few months of similar jobs show the same miss, raise the quoted time by that much. The hours factor is that number.

## How do you job cost with QuickBooks and a spreadsheet?

With projects for the money and a sheet for the hours:

1. Turn on projects and create one per job.
2. Assign material bills and outside processing to the project as they arrive.
3. Have operators record time per job daily, before they clock out; split setup from run if you can ([how shops get operators to scan](/manufacturing/wip-tracking)).
4. Keep the quoted hours and material per job in a sheet beside it. The free [job cost workbook](/manufacturing/job-cost-worked-example.xlsx) has the columns and formulas, with this example filled in.
5. Close each job by comparing the two, and feed the hours factor back into the next quote.

It works for a handful of jobs a week. It strains when material is issued from stock rather than bought per job, when one operator runs two machines, or when you want the answer before the job ships.

## When should job costing move into a shop system?

When the comparison arrives too late to matter. A shop system records material issued, setup and run time and scrap against each operation as they happen, compares them with the quoted routing while the job is open, and posts only the invoice and the inventory value to QuickBooks (see [keeping QuickBooks beside a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)). Material reserved per job keeps the material line honest; see [QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory). And costing depends on where the hours were planned: [production scheduling](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software).

Our US [boiler demo](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing) shows one version: each job's actual cost is the purchase orders issued for it plus the minutes logged on its job cards at each employee's cost rate, and work orders carry a planned cost from route steps' planned minutes at the work center's machine-hour rate. It doesn't yet allocate overhead or cost outside processing (outside work is listed, not priced); we'd build those for a shop that needs them.

title: QuickBooks Online inventory: what it tracks and where manufacturers outgrow it
metaTitle: QuickBooks Online inventory: limits for manufacturers
question: Is QuickBooks Online inventory management enough for a manufacturer?
answer: QuickBooks Online Plus and Advanced track how many of each item you have, what it's worth (FIFO or moving average cost, chosen once), what's on order and when to reorder. That covers a reseller. A manufacturer usually also needs raw material, work in progress and finished parts kept apart, material set aside for each job, and stock by location or lot, which QuickBooks Online doesn't do. That is the point to add a stock layer beside it.

body:
## Which QuickBooks Online plans track inventory?

Plus ($140 a month list, November 2026) and Advanced ($340); Simple Start ($38) and Essentials ($85) need Intuit's
inventory add-on or an upgrade, per Intuit's [inventory setup help](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/inventory-management/set-track-inventory-quickbooks-online/L22FZLBGN_US_en_US).
On those plans QuickBooks Online does this:

| Feature | QuickBooks Online |
|---|---|
| Quantity on hand | Goes down with each invoice or sales receipt, up with each receipt from a vendor |
| Reordering | Reorder points and low-stock alerts; purchase orders and what's still on order |
| Valuation | FIFO or moving average cost (MAC), chosen once |
| Item types | Inventory, non-inventory (tracked as cost, not quantity), service, and bundles that group items on a sales form |
| Reports | Stock on hand, best sellers, cost of goods sold |

For a business that buys finished products and sells them, that is a complete inventory system.

## Does QuickBooks Online now have manufacturing inventory?

Not in the sense of building products. Intuit's [pricing page](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/pricing/) now lists
"Manufacturing inventory" as an industry fit, described as knowing "what's on hand and what it's worth, with FIFO
costing and reorder points": the same quantity and valuation features above. Bills of materials, builds and
manufacturing orders are Intuit Enterprise Suite features, not QuickBooks Online ones (see
[does QuickBooks work for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)).

## FIFO or average cost: which should you choose, and can you change it later?

Choose once, with your accountant: Intuit's [valuation help](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/learn-support/en-us/help-article/inventory-management/fifo-used-inventory-cost-accounting/L1x3hkunE_US_en_US)
says the method can't be changed later, and an item created before you choose defaults to FIFO. With made-up
figures: buy 100 bars at $4.20, then 100 at $4.55, and sell 120.

| | FIFO | Moving average |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cost of goods sold | $511.00 (100 × $4.20 + 20 × $4.55) | $525.00 (120 × $4.375) |
| Stock left (80 bars) | $364.00 | $350.00 |

When prices rise, FIFO shows lower cost and higher stock value; the difference reverses as old stock runs out.

## Can QuickBooks Online track stock by warehouse, bin, lot or serial number?

No. Intuit documents lot and serial numbers, expiry dates and bin locations for QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise with
[Advanced Inventory](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/desktop/enterprise/advanced-inventory/) (three levels of location,
such as row, shelf and bin), not for Online. QuickBooks Online's "locations" are for splitting the accounts, not the
stock. On Intuit's community the usual workarounds are a separate item per location, or serials in item names,
which one Intuit community answer calls tedious.

## Can QuickBooks Online set stock aside for a job or an order?

No: quantity on hand tells you what's on the shelf, not what is already promised. Without a
[stock reservation](/systems/stock-reservation), two jobs can plan on the same bar stock and the second finds out on
the floor. With made-up figures: 500 ft of bar on hand, job A needs 300 ft, job B needs 300 ft. QuickBooks shows 500
available to both, and job B is 100 ft short the day it reaches the saw. (Intuit Enterprise Suite does reserve
components once a manufacturing order is planned.)

## Where does work in progress go in QuickBooks Online?

Nowhere as a stage of its own. Material issued to a job isn't stock on the shelf any more, but it isn't a finished
part yet either; QuickBooks Online has no [work in progress](/systems/work-in-progress), so material sits in stock
until someone adjusts it. Counts also arrive late: stock changes when someone enters a transaction, so material taken
on the floor and entered at week's end leaves the number wrong all week.

## What changes when you add a stock layer beside QuickBooks?

You keep QuickBooks for the books and keep stock movements in an operations system, which sends QuickBooks the
accounting result:

| In the stock layer | In QuickBooks |
|---|---|
| Every receipt, issue to a job, return, transfer and count, scanned as it happens | Purchase bills and the inventory asset value |
| Raw, in-progress and finished quantities per item and location | Cost of goods sold when invoiced |
| Material reserved against each job, oldest stock first | Nothing: reservations aren't accounting |
| Lots, heat numbers or serials, and which job used them | Nothing |

The [QR inventory and order reservations](/services/inventory-and-reservations) system we built for an electronic
components trader works this way: whole reels reserved per customer order line, two stores, scanning in and out, with
a manager's override needed to ship reserved stock elsewhere ([how the reels and boxes work](/notes/reels-boxes-and-two-stores)).
The US build of that system is open as a live demo with sample logins. It tracks stock by store, not by bin, and a
batch is a free-text label rather than a lot field.

## When should a manufacturer stay on QuickBooks Online inventory?

When you resell more than you make, have one location, and can count everything in an afternoon. Add a stock layer
when material is issued to jobs, when two jobs compete for the same stock, when you need lot or heat traceability, or
when the shelf and the books disagree every month. For costing those jobs, see
[job costing in QuickBooks](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing); for counting and lots in a warehouse,
[inventory control for distributors](/manufacturing/distributor-inventory-control).

body:
## Is QuickBooks Online or Desktop better for a manufacturer?

For assemblies, bins and lots, Desktop Enterprise still does more; Online wins when people need the books from
anywhere and nobody wants to look after a server. From Intuit's own pages, read on 5–6 November 2026:

| | QuickBooks Online Plus / Advanced | QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise |
|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | Browser, from anywhere | Installed on your PCs or hosted |
| Pitched for | Advanced: companies "needing industry workflows" and working from anywhere | Complex inventory, "like manufacturers and wholesalers" |
| Inventory | Quantity, FIFO or average cost, reorder points | Plus location tracking down to the bin or pallet, lots and serials with Advanced Inventory (Platinum and Diamond) |
| Assemblies and BOMs | Not in Online; Intuit lists BOM management for Advanced as coming soon | Assemblies and builds, with subassemblies |
| Manufacturing orders | In Intuit Enterprise Suite, not Online | Desktop's own assembly builds |

Details are in [QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory) and
[does QuickBooks work for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing).

## How much do QuickBooks Online and Desktop Enterprise cost?

QuickBooks Online lists at $38 (Simple Start), $85 (Essentials), $140 (Plus) and $340 (Advanced) a month on
Intuit's [pricing page](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/pricing/), with 50% off the first three months, and a free plan
with no inventory. Desktop Enterprise is sold by yearly subscription "starting at" $2,210 (Gold), $2,717 (Platinum)
or $5,363 (Diamond) on Intuit's [Enterprise pricing page](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/desktop/enterprise/pricing/)
(5 November 2026), with custom pricing by number of users, and hosting and payroll extra.

A worked example for a made-up 12-person shop at list prices: Online Advanced covers 25 users at $340 × 12 = $4,080
a year, and a business migrating from Desktop gets 50% off the first year, so three years cost $2,040 + $4,080 +
$4,080 = $10,200. Desktop Enterprise Platinum starts at $2,717 a year, from $8,151 over three years for the smallest
user band, before more users, hosting and payroll. Get a quote for your user count before comparing.

## How many users does each allow?

QuickBooks Online allows 1 user on Simple Start, 3 on Essentials, 5 on Plus and 25 on Advanced. Desktop Enterprise
allows up to 30 users on Gold and Platinum and up to 40 on Diamond.

## Can QuickBooks Online build assemblies from a bill of materials?

Not today. Intuit's [Desktop and Online page](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/desktop/) lists "BOM management" for
Online Advanced as coming soon, and its manufacturing orders, with single-level bills of materials only, live in
Intuit Enterprise Suite. If you build assemblies from components in Desktop today, Online Plus or Advanced won't
replace that yet.

## Which version tracks inventory by location, bin or lot?

Desktop Enterprise with Advanced Inventory, which Intuit includes in the Platinum and Diamond plans only: three
levels of location (such as row, shelf and bin), serial or lot numbers and expiry dates. QuickBooks Online doesn't
track stock by location.

## When is QuickBooks Online the better choice?

- People need the books from more than one place, and nobody wants to look after a server.
- You resell finished goods and don't build assemblies.
- You're coming off an unsupported Desktop version anyway (see
  [Desktop end of support](/manufacturing/quickbooks-desktop-end-of-support)).

## When is Desktop Enterprise still the better choice?

- You build assemblies from components today and need it to keep working.
- You track stock by location or bin in QuickBooks itself.
- You have large lists (up to a million names and items) or many users at once.

## Do you need QuickBooks to do inventory at all?

Many shops don't: they keep QuickBooks Online for the books and run stock, jobs and the floor in a system built for
that, which sends QuickBooks the accounting result. Then the Online vs Desktop choice is only about accounting. See
[connecting QuickBooks to a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-integration) and our
[inventory and reservations](/services/inventory-and-reservations) system.

title: QuickBooks vs ERP: signs you've outgrown QuickBooks
question: When has a manufacturer or distributor outgrown QuickBooks?
answer: When the work happens outside it: quotes and job travelers in spreadsheets, stock counted by hand because QuickBooks' numbers lag, jobs costed weeks after they ship, and two people typing the same order. QuickBooks is still fine for the books. The usual fix is to keep it for accounting and add an operations system or ERP for jobs, stock and the floor, rather than replace everything.
description: Signs a manufacturer or distributor has outgrown QuickBooks, what to keep in it, when an ERP should replace it, and what double entry really costs.

body:
## How do you know you've outgrown QuickBooks?

When the work happens outside it. Seven signs, and what each costs:

| Sign | What it costs |
|---|---|
| Quotes, routings and travelers live in spreadsheets | The same job typed three times; versions disagree |
| Stock in QuickBooks is wrong between counts | Shortages found on the floor, not at order time |
| Two jobs plan on the same material | Nothing in QuickBooks sets stock aside for a job |
| Job cost arrives after the job ships | Underpriced work keeps being quoted the same way |
| Nobody outside accounts can see an order's status | Sales calls accounts; accounts walks to the floor |
| Lots, heats or serials are tracked on paper | A customer's trace question takes a day |
| Several companies or locations share stock | Workarounds in item names, or one file per company |

One sign means a workaround; three or more mean the business runs outside its system.

## What does QuickBooks still do well for a manufacturer?

The books: invoices, bills, bank reconciliation, payroll, sales tax and the reports your accountant reads. Keeping those in
QuickBooks keeps your accountant's process intact. What QuickBooks wasn't built for is the shop: Intuit's own help
puts manufacturing orders in Intuit Enterprise Suite rather than QuickBooks Online, without multi-level bills of
materials, and lists BOM management for QuickBooks Online Advanced as coming soon. See
[does QuickBooks work for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing) for each edition.

## Does Intuit sell anything for manufacturers beyond QuickBooks Online?

Two products. QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise is pitched at companies with complex inventory, "like manufacturers and
wholesalers": assemblies and builds, and with Advanced Inventory, stock by row, shelf and bin, lots and serials.
Intuit Enterprise Suite is Intuit's cloud ERP for multi-entity companies, and where its manufacturing orders live,
with single-level bills of materials only. Prices and limits are in
[QuickBooks Online vs Desktop](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-vs-desktop).

## What does running the business outside QuickBooks cost?

More than it looks, because it's spread across people. A made-up example: 40 orders a week, each typed three times
(the quote sheet, the QuickBooks estimate, the traveler) at 4 minutes a time, is 8 hours a week, 416 hours a year.
At $28 an hour with taxes and benefits, that's $11,648 a year before anyone fixes a typo. One order shipped short
because the stock count was wrong adds freight ($180 for a second shipment) and a day's rework, and the customer
remembers it longer than the cost.

## Should you add a system beside QuickBooks or replace it with an ERP?

Add one beside it when your accounting already works; replace it when the books themselves depend on operations
detail:

| | Add an operations system beside QuickBooks | Replace QuickBooks with an ERP |
|---|---|---|
| Accounting | Stays in QuickBooks | Moves to the ERP's ledger |
| What's new | Quotes, jobs, stock, purchasing, the floor | Everything, including the close |
| Effort | Smaller; your accountant's month-end is unchanged | A full migration |
| Fits | Job shops and distributors whose accounting already works | Multi-company groups, or books that depend on operations detail |

For the vendors on each side, see [choosing an ERP](/manufacturing/small-business-erp-options); for the case for a
system built to fit, [custom vs off-the-shelf ERP](/manufacturing/custom-vs-off-the-shelf-erp). If a vendor leads
with AI, see [what AI can safely do in an ERP](/ai-assistant/ai-in-erp).

## What breaks first when you connect an ERP to QuickBooks?

Usually the rules about which system owns which record, and what happens when a post fails. Both sides let people
edit customers and items, totals drift, and a failed post disappears unless someone is shown it. Decide ownership
before any code: see [connecting QuickBooks to a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-integration).

title: Choosing an ERP: NetSuite, Acumatica, Odoo, Fishbowl, Katana
metaTitle: Small business ERP for US manufacturers: 5 options compared
question: Which ERP should a small US manufacturer or distributor choose?
answer: It depends on what runs your business. Fishbowl and Katana add inventory and production beside QuickBooks or Xero; Odoo is a modular suite with its own accounting; Acumatica and NetSuite are cloud ERPs that replace the accounting system too. A custom system fits when your process is the advantage. Test each on one of your own orders before you buy.

body:
## Which systems sit beside QuickBooks, and which replace it?

Fishbowl and Katana sit beside QuickBooks or Xero; Acumatica, NetSuite and Odoo (with its accounting app) replace it. So
the first question isn't which brand; it's whether your accounting stays where it is.

| | Beside your accounting | Replaces your accounting |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Inventory and production, posting to QuickBooks or Xero | One system for operations and the books |
| Examples | Fishbowl, Katana | Acumatica, NetSuite, Odoo (with its accounting app) |
| Your accountant | Keeps QuickBooks | Moves to the new ledger |
| Effort to start | Lower | Higher: a migration and new close process |

## What does each vendor say it does?

Inventory and production in every case, with different depth and accounting. From each vendor's own pages, read on 3 November 2026. Vendors change plans and features often: confirm in a demo.

| System | In its own words (summarised) | Accounting |
|---|---|---|
| **Fishbowl** | Inventory tracking, warehouse operations and manufacturing; integrates with QuickBooks Online | Beside QuickBooks or Xero |
| **Katana** | Lot, serial and expiry tracking from supplier to customer, across inventory and production; barcode-enabled warehouse tasks | Beside QuickBooks and others |
| **Odoo** | Serial numbers, lots, reservation strategies and cycle counting; FIFO, average, LIFO or standard valuation | Its own, as a separate app |
| **Acumatica** | Distribution and financial application: lot or serial tracking, matrix items, kits, replenishment and forecasting | Its own |
| **NetSuite** | Oracle's cloud ERP. Its site refused automated reading when we checked, so we don't summarise its features here: ask for them in writing | Its own |

Pricing isn't compared here: most of these quote per user and per module, and several don't publish prices.

## What does Intuit itself offer before you leave QuickBooks?

Three steps up, all from Intuit's own pages: QuickBooks Online Advanced ($340 a month list, November 2026), with BOM
management listed as coming soon; QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise, from $2,210 a year, with assemblies and, on its
Platinum and Diamond plans, Advanced Inventory (bins, lots, serials); and Intuit Enterprise Suite, Intuit's
multi-entity ERP, where its manufacturing orders live. Details in
[QuickBooks Online vs Desktop](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-vs-desktop).

## How much does a small business ERP cost?

Most of these quote per user and per module, and several don't publish prices, so compare five-year cost on the same
lines rather than list prices. An illustrative example (made-up prices; replace them with your quotes):

| Five years | ERP that replaces QuickBooks | Inventory app beside QuickBooks |
|---|---:|---:|
| Subscription | 15 users × $120 a month = $108,000 | 6 users × $90 a month = $32,400 |
| Implementation and data migration | $30,000 | $8,000 |
| QuickBooks Online Advanced you keep paying | $0 | $340 × 60 = $20,400 |
| **Total** | **$138,000** | **$60,800** |

The cheaper column isn't automatically the answer: add the hours your team spends on workarounds either way, and the
cost of leaving (see the export test in [the ERP requirements checklist](/manufacturing/erp-requirements-checklist)).

## When does a custom system fit better?

When the way you work is the reason customers buy from you. Off-the-shelf systems are built for the common process;
a system built for you is worth it for an unusual quote, a reservation rule, a trace your customers demand, or several
companies sharing stock. See [custom vs off-the-shelf ERP](/manufacturing/custom-vs-off-the-shelf-erp) for the
trade-offs, and [what a job shop ERP must do](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp) for a shop's checklist.

## How do you choose an ERP in two weeks?

With three of your real orders and a demo of each, on your items:

1. Write down three of your real orders end to end: quote, purchase, receipt, production or pick, ship, invoice.
2. Ask each vendor to run them in a demo, on your items, not theirs.
3. Check the inventory basics from [inventory control for distributors](/manufacturing/distributor-inventory-control):
   cycle counts, lots, valuation, scanning.
4. Ask what the [QuickBooks](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing) link posts, and what happens when it fails.
5. Get data export and the contract's ownership terms in writing before you sign.

title: WIP tracking with barcoded job travelers
metaTitle: WIP tracking in a job shop with barcoded travelers
question: How do you track work in progress on a shop floor?
answer: Give every job a traveler with a barcode, list its operations in order, and have operators scan the job at each operation's start and finish, with the good and scrapped quantities. That one habit shows where every job is, what's queued in front of each machine, the actual hours for job costing, and the value of work in progress for the books. Fixed scan stations work better than tablets on most shop floors.
description: How to track work in progress in a job shop: travelers, scan points, a work order and its WIP value, scan stations vs tablets, and getting operators to scan.

sources.title: Paperless (or less paper) job tracking and routing, job shop specific (forum discussion)
Computers and tablets on the shop floor (forum discussion)

body:
## How do you track work in progress on a shop floor?

By scanning each job at the start and finish of every operation, with good and scrapped quantities, from a barcoded traveler. [Work in progress](/systems/work-in-progress) is every job that has started and not shipped. Tracking it means recording a small set of events, always against a job and an operation:

| Event | Who records it | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|
| Material issued to the job | Stores | Stock leaves the shelf and becomes WIP cost |
| Operation started | Operator | Where the job is; queue time before it |
| Operation finished, with good and scrapped quantity | Operator | Actual run time and scrap per operation |
| Inspection passed or held | Quality | Whether it can move on |
| Job finished and packed | Shipping | WIP becomes finished goods, ready to invoice |

Each scan moves the job from one state to the next ([state transitions](/systems#state-transition)), so the system can refuse impossible moves, such as finishing an operation that never started or shipping a job still waiting for inspection.

## What does a job traveler with scan data look like?

Like the work order below, with times and quantities filled in by scans. The [job traveler](/systems#job-traveler) is the work order as it travels with the parts. A made-up example for 200 steel brackets:

| Op | Operation | Machine | Setup (h) | Run (min each) | Started | Finished | Good | Scrap |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| 10 | Laser cut blanks | Laser | 0.5 | 1.0 | Tue 07:10 | Tue 11:05 | 208 | 0 |
| 20 | Bend, two flanges | Press brake | 1.0 | 1.5 | Tue 12:30 | Wed 09:40 | 200 | 8 |
| 30 | Weld gusset | Weld cell | 0.5 | 3.0 | Wed 10:15 | | | |
| 40 | Inspect, first and last piece | Quality | | | | | | |
| 50 | Powder coat | Outside vendor | | | | | | |

The header carries the job number (and its barcode), customer, part number and revision, quantity, due date, material with heat or lot number, and the drawing. Times and quantities come from scans, not handwriting. The quoted setup and run times on each line are what [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) compares the actual times against.

## What is the job's work in progress worth?

What has gone into it so far: material issued plus the hours worked at the shop rate. The made-up traveler above, as
of Wednesday 09:40, at $97 an hour (labor plus machine) and $4.55 a blank:

| | Hours | Value |
|---|---:|---:|
| Material issued: 208 blanks | | $946.40 |
| Op 10, laser: 0.5 h setup + 208 × 1.0 min | 3.97 | $384.77 |
| Op 20, press brake: 1.0 h setup + 208 × 1.5 min | 6.20 | $601.40 |
| **Work in progress** | **10.17** | **$1,932.57** |

Eight of those blanks were scrapped at the brake: $36.40 of material plus their share of the hours is a loss to record
now, not at month-end. In the books, WIP is an asset until the job ships and becomes cost of goods sold.

## Scan stations, tablets or phones: which work on a shop floor?

Fixed stations at work centers, with phones for stores and shipping. Owners discussing this on [Practical Machinist](https://www.practicalmachinist.com/forum/threads/computers-tablets-on-the-shop-floor.322887/) land in roughly the same place:

- **Fixed stations** (a screen and scanner at each work center, or one per area) survive coolant and dust, don't get dropped or walk off, and stay on a wired network.
- **Tablets** are convenient and have a camera that reads barcodes, but touchscreens get dirty, they're dropped or misplaced, and slow Wi-Fi in a metal building makes every scan a wait.
- **Phones** work for stores and shipping, where people move around anyway.

A common setup: a barcode on the paper traveler, a cheap scanner at each station, phones for stores.

## How do you get operators to scan?

Make it one scan, tie it to pay, and say what it's for. Software is the easy part; what makes it stick, from shops that have done it:

- **One scan, not a form.** Scan the job, scan your badge, type a quantity. Anything longer gets skipped.
- **Tie it to pay.** When the same scans fill timesheets, people scan, because it pays them.
- **Say what it's for.** Scanning can feel like surveillance; it lands better framed as "so nobody has to walk the floor to find a job".
- **Watch for gaming**, such as closing an operation early. Compare scans with the schedule and look at outliers, not everyone.
- **Do it daily.** Time recorded at the end of the day, before clocking out, is close enough; time recorded at the end of the week is fiction.

## When does WIP tracking pay off?

At around seven to ten people, by one Practical Machinist owner's estimate in the threads cited below. Below that, the owner can see every job from the office door, and manual counts in QuickBooks may be enough. Above it, nobody can, and WIP tracking is what makes a [schedule](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software) trustworthy: the plan knows what has actually finished. The accounting side matters too: WIP is an asset on the balance sheet, which QuickBooks Online doesn't hold as a stage of its own ([QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory)).

title: Sales tax for contractors: lump-sum vs separated contracts
question: Do contractors charge sales tax, or pay it on their materials?
answer: Usually a contractor who builds or repairs real property pays sales tax on its materials and doesn't charge it to the customer, because the contractor is the consumer of what it installs. Texas and California follow that rule for lump-sum contracts. But a contract that states the materials separately can make the contractor the retailer of them, collecting tax from the customer instead, so how the contract is written changes who pays.
description: Sales tax for contractors: consumer of materials or retailer, lump-sum vs separated contracts in Texas and California, equipment, use tax and certificates.

sources.title: 34 Texas Administrative Code 3.291, Contractors
sources.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts rule)

sources.title: Regulation 1521, Construction Contractors
sources.publisher: California Department of Tax and Fee Administration

checks.quote: A contract in which the agreed contract price is one lump-sum amount and in which the charges for incorporated materials are not separate from any charges for skill and labor
A contract in which the agreed contract price is divided into a separately stated agreed contract price for incorporated materials and a separately stated amount for all skill and labor

A contractor who performs lump-sum contracts owes tax on all materials, consumable items, equipment, taxable services, and other taxable items that are used by the contractor or incorporated into a customer's property.
The contractor shall not collect from a customer any amount represented to be tax on a lump-sum charge or on any portion of the charge
a contractor who performs a separated contract is a retailer of all materials that are physically incorporated into the realty that is being improved.
The tax rate must be applied to the agreed contract price of materials, or to the price of the materials to the contractor, whichever is greater.
A contractor must pay sales tax at the time of purchase, lease, or rental on the sales price of equipment used to perform a contract.
A contractor who purchases items that are specifically intended for use in a lump-sum contract may not issue resale certificates in lieu of tax for such items.
performs nonresidential real property repair, restoration, and remodeling services and resells taxable items as part of those taxable services
Construction contractors are consumers of materials which they furnish and install in the performance of construction contracts.
Construction contractors are retailers of fixtures which they furnish and install in the performance of construction contracts and tax applies to their sales of the fixtures.
A lump sum contract does not become a time and material contract when the amounts attributable to materials, fixtures, labor, or tax are separately stated in the invoice.
If the seller does not have a permit or fails to charge sales and use tax, the purchaser must pay the use tax directly to our office unless an exemption applies.

body:
## Do contractors charge sales tax?

Usually not on a construction contract: a contractor who improves real property is generally the consumer of the
materials it installs, so it pays sales tax when it buys them and doesn't add tax to its bill. California's rule says
so directly: "Construction contractors are consumers of materials which they furnish and install in the performance
of construction contracts." The exceptions come from how the contract is written and what is installed, and they
differ by state.

## What is the difference between a lump-sum and a separated contract?

A lump-sum contract has one price for materials and labor together; a separated contract states the price of the
incorporated materials apart from the price of all skill and labor. Texas defines both (34 TAC 3.291), and the
difference decides who owes the tax:

| | Lump-sum contract | Separated contract |
|---|---|---|
| Contractor is | The consumer of the materials | The retailer of the materials |
| Tax on materials | Paid by the contractor to its supplier | Collected by the contractor from the customer |
| Contractor buys materials | Tax paid; no resale certificate for items bought for the job | May give suppliers a resale certificate |
| Tax on the bill | None; tax can't be shown on any part of the charge | On the materials price (or the contractor's cost, if higher) |
| Sales tax permit | Not needed for this alone | Needed, and the contractor files returns |

A guaranteed-maximum contract that doesn't break out materials and all labor counts as lump-sum in Texas.

## How does it work on a Texas job, in numbers?

Take a made-up $200,000 commercial job with $60,000 of materials, at an assumed 8% combined rate:

- **Lump-sum:** the contractor pays $4,800 tax to its suppliers on the $60,000 of materials and bills $200,000 with no
  tax line. The tax is a cost of the job, so it belongs in the bid.
- **Separated:** the contract states materials at $70,000 (cost plus markup) and labor at $130,000. The contractor buys
  the materials on a resale certificate and charges the customer $5,600 tax on the $70,000, which it reports and pays
  to the state. Tax applies to the agreed materials price or the contractor's cost, whichever is greater.

The rate is made up for the example; use the rate for the job's location.

## Does a contractor pay tax on tools and equipment?

Yes. In Texas a contractor pays sales tax when it buys, leases or rents equipment used on a contract, under either
kind of contract, and owes use tax on equipment from an out-of-state seller that didn't charge Texas tax. Separately
stating an equipment charge to the customer doesn't make it a rental to the customer.

## What about consumables like forms, tape and fuel?

In Texas they're taxed when the contractor buys them, because they're used up on the job rather than built in: things
like non-reusable concrete forms, drop cloths, barricade tape, natural gas and electricity. On a separated contract a
contractor can pass consumables through on a resale certificate only if title goes to the customer when it takes
them and they're marked as the customer's.

## Is repair and remodeling work taxed differently?

In Texas, yes: nonresidential repair, restoration and remodeling is a taxable service under its own rule (34 TAC
3.357), while new construction and residential repair fall under the contractor rule. New construction includes the
initial finish-out of a new building and new square footage added to an existing one; moving interior walls within
existing space is remodeling. Check which rule a job falls under before you price it.

## How does California treat contractors?

As consumers of the materials they install, and as retailers of fixtures they install. Regulation 1521 covers lump
sum, time and material and cost-plus contracts. Stating materials, labor or tax separately on an invoice doesn't turn a
lump-sum contract into a time and material contract; under a time and material contract, a contractor who bills the
customer "sales tax" on marked-up materials is assumed to be the retailer of them. Fixtures (built-in items that keep
their identity, listed in the regulation) are taxed as sales by the contractor.

## When does a contractor owe use tax?

When it uses materials or equipment on which no tax was paid: bought from an out-of-state supplier that didn't charge
the tax, or bought tax-free on a resale certificate and then built in under a lump-sum contract. The contractor reports
use tax itself for the period the items were used. See [use tax](/sales-tax/use-tax) for how it's reported, and
[resale certificates](/sales-tax/resale-certificates) for when you can buy tax-free.

## Can a contractor buy tax-free for an exempt customer?

Sometimes, with the customer's certificate. In Texas a contractor improving realty for an organization exempt under
Tax Code 151.309 or 151.310 may claim the exemption on purchases for that job, with properly completed exemption
certificates, and a contract can instead have the exempt customer buy the materials itself. If the comptroller later
finds the organization isn't exempt, the contractor owes the tax, penalties and interest, so keep the certificate and
the proof of exemption with the job.

## What should a contractor's system record for sales tax?

- Each contract's type (lump-sum or separated, or the state's equivalent), set before billing.
- Materials bought per job, with the tax paid or the resale certificate used.
- Use tax due on materials that went untaxed into lump-sum work, by period.
- Tax charged on separated contracts and supply sales, by the job's location.
- Exemption certificates per job for exempt customers.

See [sales tax in your ERP](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp) for the general case. The
[construction demo](/industries/construction-company)'s US build bills pay applications with no sales tax, treating
the contractor as paying tax on its materials, and charges sales tax on supply invoices from its materials desk. It
doesn't switch a contract between lump-sum and separated treatment or work out use tax; those are parts we'd build.
This guide explains the rules from the texts cited; your state's revenue department and your tax adviser decide how
they apply to a job.

title: Economic nexus thresholds by state, with a checker

body:
## Which sales count toward the threshold?

States measure different things, and the difference is large for a manufacturer or distributor, because so much of
what you sell goes to resellers or to buyers with an exemption certificate. The Streamlined Sales Tax Governing
Board explains the three bases with one example: a company sells $400,000 into a state in a year, made up of
$220,000 to wholesalers buying for resale, $75,000 to buyers claiming another exemption (such as use in
manufacturing), $10,000 of exempt products and $95,000 of taxable sales.

| The state counts | What's included | The example's figure |
|---|---|---|
| Gross sales | Everything, including resale and exempt sales | $400,000 |
| Retail sales | Everything except sales for resale | $180,000 |
| Taxable sales | Only sales that are (or should be) taxed | $95,000 |

The same company is over a $100,000 threshold in a state that counts gross or retail sales, and under it in a state
that counts taxable sales. Each state's rule in the table below names the basis it uses.

## Which period does each state use?

Most states look at the previous or the current calendar year: you are over as soon as either one passes. Others
use the last 12 months (Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont, Mississippi) or the previous four sales tax
quarters (New York). Check monthly against a rolling 12 months and you catch all of them.

## Are transaction thresholds going away?

Yes. Many states first copied South Dakota's "$100,000 or 200 transactions" and have since dropped the transaction
count: North Dakota in 2019, Wisconsin in 2021, South Dakota in 2023, Indiana, North Carolina and Wyoming in 2024,
Alaska and Utah in 2025 and Illinois from January 1, 2026, all as listed in the Board's chart. Kentucky followed on
**August 1, 2026**: its 2026 revenue act, [HB 757](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/acts/26RS/documents/0161.pdf),
rewrote KRS 139.340 so a remote retailer must register once its sales into Kentucky in the previous or current
calendar year exceed $100,000, now counting services as well as goods, and must register and collect by the first day
of the month at most 60 days after it passes. The Board's chart, which calls itself a summary "as of January 11,
2023", still shows Kentucky's 200-transaction test, so the checker below quotes the act for Kentucky.

Where a count is left, a business with many small orders, such as spare parts, can pass it long before the dollar
amount. A made-up spare-parts seller with 260 orders into Kentucky averaging $300 ($78,000) had nexus there under the
200-order test until July 31, 2026, and doesn't from August 1.

## Which states need both a dollar amount and a number of sales?

Connecticut and New York, where both tests must be met. Connecticut counts $100,000 of gross receipts and 200 retail
transactions, per the Board's chart. New York's
[Tax Department](https://www.tax.ny.gov/pubs_and_bulls/publications/sales/nexus.htm) counts the four preceding sales
tax quarters, in which the seller's gross receipts from goods delivered into the state exceeded $500,000 and it made
more than 100 sales. So a made-up distributor with $520,000 of sales into New York across 90 orders is under, and its
101st order in the window puts it over.

## How do you check your own sales against each state?

Enter each state you ship to with your sales and number of orders into it over the period that state uses. The
checker says whether you are over, within 20% of the threshold, or under, and quotes the state's rule beside the
answer. Physical presence in a state means you register there regardless; see
[what sales tax nexus is](/sales-tax/sales-tax-nexus). If you are over in several of the 24 member states, one
registration covers them: see [Streamlined Sales Tax](/sales-tax/streamlined-sales-tax).

The figures come from your own system: sales by ship-to state, split into resale, exempt and taxable, for any
period. If you can't get that report today, see [how an ERP should handle sales tax](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp).

## What is each state's threshold?

The table below, from the Board's chart except where a state's own newer text replaces it (Kentucky). The chart says
it is a summary and does not override any state's law. Before you register or decide not to, read the state's own
remote seller page, linked from the chart.

Texas exempts components and equipment that physically or chemically change the product; California gives a partial exemption on qualified manufacturing equipment until June 30, 2030. Hand tools, forklifts and office supplies usually stay taxable.

body:
## What do manufacturers usually not pay sales tax on?

Many states exempt some of a manufacturer's purchases, so that the same product isn't taxed twice:
once on the inputs and again when it's sold. What's exempt is each state's own law. Texas is a
useful model, since its rules are spelled out item by item:

| Purchase | Texas | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Steel, castings, fasteners that go into the product | Exempt | Becomes a component of an item made for sale |
| Machines that cut, form, weld or heat-treat the product | Exempt | Causes a physical or chemical change and is essential |
| Quality-control equipment testing products for sale | Exempt | Listed by the Comptroller |
| Safety apparel required in production, not resold | Exempt | Listed by the Comptroller |
| Hand tools (a hammer) | Taxable | Excluded even when used in fabrication |
| Forklifts, conveyors, hoists, cranes | Taxable | Intraplant transportation is excluded |
| Molds and dies equipment, air conditioning for comfort | Taxable | Manufacturing support, not production |
| Equipment rented for less than a year, R&D items | Taxable | Excluded |

Repair work doesn't qualify in Texas: a shop repairing equipment that belongs to others is not a manufacturer for
the exemption. A job shop that both makes parts and repairs customers' equipment buys for the two differently.

## What does California exempt, and how much does it save?

Part of the tax on qualified manufacturing equipment: 3.9375 percentage points of the rate, on up to $200 million of
purchases a year. California has a partial exemption, not a full one: manufacturers (and certain research and development and
electric power businesses) may get a partial exemption on qualified machinery and equipment used primarily in
manufacturing. Three conditions apply: the buyer is a "qualified person" by its line of business, the property is
qualified, and it's used in a qualified way. The law behind it, Revenue and Taxation Code section 6377.1, runs to
June 30, 2030. CDTFA's [guide for purchasers](https://cdtfa.ca.gov/industry/manufacturing-and-research-and-development-equipment-exemption/purchasers.htm)
puts the partial exemption at 3.9375 percent, caps a qualified person's (or combined reporting group's) purchases under
it at $200 million a calendar year with no carry-over, and needs no application: you give the seller a timely partial
exemption certificate (CDTFA-230-M). Ask CDTFA in writing for your case.

A worked example: a $250,000 CNC lathe bought by a qualified manufacturer saves $250,000 × 3.9375% = **$9,843.75** of
tax. The rest of the rate, including local and district taxes, is still due.

## How do you claim it?

By giving your vendor an exemption certificate when you buy, not by paying and asking for a refund, in most cases: you give your vendor an exemption certificate when you buy.
In Texas, a manufacturer gives a properly completed Form 01-339 exemption certificate describing the item, the
reason it's exempt, and signed and dated. Your vendor keeps it on file, the same way you keep your customers'
[resale certificates](/sales-tax/resale-certificates). Where a vendor charged tax on an exempt purchase anyway,
states have refund procedures.

## What is divergent use, and how is its tax worked out in Texas?

Exempt equipment used for something other than making products for sale is in "divergent use". Texas lets you buy
the equipment exempt, then pay tax on the share of use that diverges, measured in hours or output each month. If
divergent use is 5% or less in a month, no tax is due that month, and after four years there's no tax on divergent
use. A plant that runs a machine for its own maintenance parts part of the time needs the machine's hours split
by purpose, which is a shop-floor record, not an accounting one.

The Comptroller's [formula](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/publications/94-124.php): the month's divergent hours
divided by its total hours give the divergent share, and the tax due is 1/48 of the purchase price × that share × the
tax rate at the time of purchase. A worked example: a $120,000 press brake bought exempt where the rate was 8.25%
runs 200 hours in March, 20 of them making racks for the plant itself: 10% divergent. Tax for March =
$120,000 ÷ 48 × 10% × 8.25% = **$20.63**. In April it runs 8 of 200 hours for the plant, 4%: at 5% or less, $0.

## What should your records show?

What you bought tax-free, why each purchase was exempt, and that it was used that way: the three things an auditor
checking a manufacturer's exemption asks. The system that answers them holds:

- the exemption reason on each purchase order line and vendor bill, not just "no tax"
- the item's use: a component on the bill of materials, production equipment, or neither
- machine hours by job, which split production from other use for divergent use
- materials issued from stock to something other than a product for sale, such as maintenance or samples, which
  owe [use tax](/sales-tax/use-tax)

A [job shop ERP](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp) that records material issues and machine hours by job already has most
of this; see [how an ERP should handle sales tax](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp) for the rest.
Our US [boiler demo](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing) logs time on job cards by work center, the
record a divergent-use split starts from; it doesn't yet keep an exemption reason on purchase lines or produce the
monthly divergent-use figure, which we'd build for a manufacturer that claims the exemption.

title: Resale and exemption certificates: what to collect

body:
## What is the difference between a resale and an exemption certificate?

The reason: a resale certificate says the buyer will sell the item on; an exemption certificate says the purchase is
exempt for another reason, such as use in manufacturing.

| Certificate | The buyer says | Typical buyers of a manufacturer or distributor |
|---|---|---|
| Resale | "I will sell this item, or it becomes part of something I sell" | Distributors, dealers, other manufacturers buying components |
| Exemption | "This purchase is exempt for another reason" | Manufacturers buying production equipment or materials, nonprofits, government, farms |

Both do the same thing for you as the seller: with a valid certificate on file, the sale is not taxable and the tax
is no longer your liability. Without one, an auditor treats the sale as taxable and bills you for the tax you
didn't charge, plus interest.

## What is the Streamlined Certificate of Exemption (F0003)?

The one multistate form the Streamlined member states accept, for resale and the other exemptions it lists. The
[form itself](https://www.streamlinedsalestax.org/docs/default-source/forms/exemption-certificateb926a7ab4a0d43e1ad4fe8eb19e79cbb.pdf?sfvrsn=857843d_5)
says it goes to the seller, never to the Board, and that not every state allows every exemption on it: the buyer is
responsible for being eligible in the state it claims. The buyer ticks a box if the certificate is for a single purchase
and names that invoice or purchase order.

## Which form do you accept?

The Streamlined certificate in member states, and each other state's own form or a multistate one elsewhere:

- **Streamlined states.** The Streamlined Sales Tax exemption certificate is accepted by all 24 member states, for
  resale and the other exemptions it lists. Not every member allows every exemption on it, and some want a
  state-specific ID number. See [Streamlined Sales Tax](/sales-tax/streamlined-sales-tax).
- **Other states.** Each has its own form or accepts a multistate one: California's general resale certificate is
  CDTFA-230; in Texas, the back of Form 01-339 is the Texas Sales and Use Tax Exemption Certificate.

A certificate is good for the kind of goods it describes. California's guidance is that the property may be listed
item by item or by a general description; if a customer buys something it doesn't normally sell, ask for a
certificate that names that property.

## What must a certificate say?

Each state sets its fields, but they usually include:

- the buyer's name, address and sales tax permit or registration number
- a description of the items, or the type of items, bought tax-free
- the reason the purchase is exempt (resale, manufacturing, an exempt organization)
- the buyer's signature and the date

Texas lists the description, the reason, and the signature and date for a manufacturing exemption certificate.

## Do you have to check the buyer's number?

In Streamlined states, the seller doesn't have to verify the buyer's ID number (the Board notes Georgia as the
exception). You do have to accept it in good faith: a certificate for goods that obviously don't fit the buyer's
business, such as office furniture "for resale" from a machine shop, isn't one. The buyer carries the penalty for
misusing a certificate, and California says intentional misuse can be prosecuted.

## How do drop shipments work?

When you buy from a supplier who ships straight to your customer, the supplier needs your resale certificate. In
Streamlined states, a drop shipper that receives a completed certificate from you is not liable for the tax on what
it delivers to your customer, and the ID number you give may be one issued by another state. Outside Streamlined,
check the delivery state's own rule for drop shipments.

## What happens if a customer's certificate doesn't cover a state you ship to?

The sale into that state is taxable to you, and an auditor bills the tax you didn't charge plus interest. A worked
example: a made-up distributor sells $180,000 a year to one dealer, $60,000 of it shipped to Texas, where no
certificate is on file. At the Texas maximum combined rate of 8.25%, that's $4,950 of tax for the year, unless a valid
certificate is obtained in time. The fix is mechanical: the order system checks the ship-to state against the
certificates on file before the invoice is issued.

Our demos don't hold certificates yet: the electronics and boiler demos send each line as taxable or not to
QuickBooks. We'd build certificate storage and the ship-to check for a distributor that sells for resale across
states.

## Where do certificates go?

Not to the state. The buyer gives the certificate to the seller and keeps a copy; the seller keeps it on file and
produces it in an audit. In practice that means each certificate should sit on the customer's record with:

- which states it covers, and which exemption
- the date received, and an expiry or renewal date where the state sets one
- the customer's ship-to states, so an order to a state with no certificate on file is taxed

Manufacturers claiming exemption on their own purchases do the same in reverse: see
[the manufacturing exemption](/sales-tax/manufacturing-sales-tax-exemption), and for exempt purchases later used
another way, [use tax](/sales-tax/use-tax). How an order system should hold all this:
[how an ERP should handle sales tax](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp).

The rates themselves are best taken from a rate service, not typed in.
