body:
## What does sales tax ask of your system?

Five things, and only the first is the tax calculation most people think of:

| The system must | Because |
|---|---|
| Tax each invoice line by the ship-to address and the item's taxability | Rates and rules are set by the delivery location, down to city and district |
| Know which customers buy tax-free, in which states, and why | A missing certificate makes the sale taxable to you |
| Total sales and orders by ship-to state, split into resale, exempt and taxable | That's how you see an [economic nexus threshold](/sales-tax/economic-nexus-thresholds) coming |
| Flag purchases that owe use tax | Untaxed bills and stock taken for internal use |
| Give each state's return figures | Taxable sales, exempt sales by reason, tax by jurisdiction |

## Where does the rate come from?

From where the goods are delivered, in most cases. Texas, for example, puts local use tax at the location where the
order is shipped or delivered when it isn't fulfilled from a Texas place of business, and also offers remote
sellers a single local rate (1.75% when checked) in place of each destination's local tax. California adds district
taxes. A ZIP code is not precise enough, because district and city boundaries cut across ZIP codes.

So the system should not hold a rate table someone types in. It should send the ship-to address, item tax code and
amount to a rate service and store the answer on the invoice line: the jurisdictions, the rates and the tax. The
certified service providers in the [Streamlined Sales Tax](/sales-tax/streamlined-sales-tax) program do exactly
this, free in member states for remote sellers who qualify; commercial rate services do it everywhere.

## Can a remote seller use one Texas rate instead of every local rate?

Yes: Texas lets remote sellers collect a single local use tax rate, 1.75% when checked, instead of each
destination's local tax, on top of the 6.25% state rate. Texas local taxes can reach 2%, so the choice matters per
shipment. A worked example with a made-up $10,000 shipment into a Texas city whose local taxes total 2%: at the
destination's own rate, 6.25% + 2% = 8.25%, or $825; at the single local rate, 6.25% + 1.75% = 8.00%, or $800. A
business located in Texas can't use the single rate, and the system has to know which rate the seller has chosen.

## What has to be on the customer record?

The customer's certificates, its ship-to addresses, and a rule that taxes any order with no certificate behind it:

- Each [resale or exemption certificate](/sales-tax/resale-certificates): the states it covers, the exemption, the
  date received and any renewal date, and the file itself.
- The customer's ship-to addresses, since one customer can be exempt in one state and taxable in another.
- A rule at order entry: an order shipping to a state with no certificate on file is taxed, and someone is told.

## How does it see nexus coming?

With one report that most small-business systems can't produce: sales and order count by ship-to state for any
12 months, with resale, exempt and taxable sales apart. Two details matter:

- **Related companies count together** in some states. California's $500,000 test counts combined sales by the
  retailer and all persons related to it, so a group with two companies needs the report across both.
- **Marketplace sales** need their own column: some states leave them out of your threshold, and Texas wants their
  records kept for at least four years.

Run it monthly against the thresholds. A spreadsheet export into the
[nexus checker](/sales-tax/economic-nexus-thresholds) is enough to start.

## What about use tax and manufacturing?

Purchases are the other half. Every vendor bill line should carry its tax treatment: taxed, exempt with a reason,
or untaxed and owing [use tax](/sales-tax/use-tax). A manufacturer claiming the
[manufacturing exemption](/sales-tax/manufacturing-sales-tax-exemption) also needs material issues and machine hours
by job, so exempt purchases can be shown to have been used as claimed.

## What if QuickBooks keeps the books?

Then decide which system calculates the tax. With QuickBooks Online's automated sales tax, QuickBooks works out the
tax itself from the ship-to address, and charges none for a state it isn't set up to collect in, even when your order
system did charge it. Set up the same states in both, and compare the two totals on every invoice. Details, from our
own sandbox tests: [connecting QuickBooks Online](/manufacturing/quickbooks-integration).

That is how our US demos work today: the [boiler demo](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing) and the
electronics distribution demo send each invoice line as taxable or not with the ship-to address, and QuickBooks
works out the tax, against an Intuit sandbox company. Neither demo holds customers' exemption certificates, reports
sales by state or accrues use tax yet; those are the parts we'd build for a client that collects in several states.

## How do you test a vendor's sales tax handling?

With six checks on your own data, in the demo:

1. An invoice to a ship-to address in a city with a district tax: are the jurisdictions shown?
2. The same customer shipping to a state where you hold their certificate, and one where you don't.
3. Sales by ship-to state for the last 12 months, resale, exempt and taxable apart.
4. A vendor bill with no tax from an out-of-state supplier: is it flagged?
5. Stock taken from inventory for your own use: does it create a use tax line?
6. The figures for one state's return, without a spreadsheet.

A system that fails 3 and 6 will have you rebuilding the numbers by hand at every return. For choosing between a
package and a system built to fit, see [custom vs off-the-shelf ERP](/manufacturing/custom-vs-off-the-shelf-erp).

You have it through physical presence, such as an office, warehouse, staff or inventory in the state, or, since South Dakota v. Wayfair in 2018, through economic nexus: sales into the state above its threshold.

body:
## What does nexus mean for sales tax?

Nexus is the connection between your business and a state that lets the state make you collect its tax. Once you
have it, you register with that state, charge its sales tax on taxable sales delivered there, file its returns and
keep the records it asks for. Without it, the buyer owes the state [use tax](/sales-tax/use-tax) instead, and
usually doesn't pay it.

There are two ways to have nexus:

| Kind | What creates it | Since |
|---|---|---|
| Physical nexus | An office, plant, warehouse, inventory, employees or representatives in the state | Always |
| Economic nexus | Sales into the state above its threshold, with no presence at all | South Dakota v. Wayfair, June 21, 2018 |

## What counts as a physical presence?

Each state lists its own. Texas, for example, counts a location you operate, an employee or representative who
sells, delivers or takes orders, services performed in the state, and delivering in your own or leased vehicles.
California's examples include keeping inventory or an office there, having representatives who take orders or
install, and leasing equipment such as a server in the state.

Two cases catch manufacturers and distributors out:

- **Stock in someone else's warehouse.** Inventory you keep in a state is usually a presence there, even in a
  rented or third-party warehouse: California's examples start with maintaining inventory in the state.
- **Installation and service crews.** A team that installs equipment or does warranty work in a state is presence,
  even if the sale was made from home.

A physical presence means registering whatever the amount of sales. The thresholds only apply to remote sellers.

## What did the Supreme Court decide in South Dakota v. Wayfair?

That a state can make a seller collect its tax on sales delivered into it even with no physical presence there. The
Court decided the case on June 21, 2018, overruling its earlier physical-presence rule (Quill, 1992, and National
Bellas Hess, 1967), which it called "unsound and incorrect" in the
[opinion](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/17-494) ([docket](https://www.supremecourt.gov/docket/docketfiles/html/public/17-494.html)).
The South Dakota law it upheld covered sellers that each year deliver more than $100,000 of goods or services into the
state or make 200 or more separate sales into it, and the Court pointed to the state's membership of the Streamlined
Sales and Use Tax Agreement as one reason the law didn't burden small sellers unduly. Every state with a sales tax now has an economic nexus rule: most at $100,000 of sales a year,
some with a transaction count as well. See [every state's threshold, with a checker](/sales-tax/economic-nexus-thresholds).

## When do you have to start collecting?

Each state sets its own start. Texas gives an example: a remote seller whose Texas revenue passes $500,000 over
twelve months must get a permit and start collecting no later than the first day of the fourth month after the
month it passed: a seller whose rolling twelve months pass $500,000 in July 2026 must collect by November 1, 2026.
Kentucky, since August 1, 2026, wants registration and collection by the first day of the month at most 60 days after
the threshold is reached, per its [2026 act](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/acts/26RS/documents/0161.pdf).
Other states expect registration from the day you pass, or from the start of the next month or
quarter. Look up the state's own page before the threshold is near, not after.

If you are already registered and collecting in a state, keep doing so: the Streamlined Sales Tax Governing Board's
guidance is to continue, and dropping a registration has its own procedure in each state.

## Do marketplace sales count?

Where a marketplace collects the tax for you, most states let you leave those sales out of your own filing, and
Texas does not require a permit for a seller that sells only through a marketplace that collects for it. Whether
marketplace sales count toward your own threshold differs by state; the state's rule says. Keep the marketplace's
reports either way: Texas asks sellers to keep records of all marketplace sales for at least four years.

## What should you do once you have nexus in a state?

Register, collect the paperwork from tax-free buyers, and keep watching your sales by state:

1. List the states where you have a physical presence, including stock held by others and crews working there.
2. Run your last 12 months of sales by ship-to state through the [nexus checker](/sales-tax/economic-nexus-thresholds).
3. Register in each state you're over, directly or, in the 24 member states, once through the
   [Streamlined Sales Tax registration system](/sales-tax/streamlined-sales-tax).
4. Collect [resale and exemption certificates](/sales-tax/resale-certificates) from customers who buy tax-free,
   before you invoice them in a new state.
5. Make your order system report sales by state every month, so the next threshold doesn't arrive as a surprise:
   see [how an ERP should handle sales tax](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp).

title: Streamlined Sales Tax: member states and free services

question: What is the Streamlined Sales Tax Agreement, and who can use its free services?
answer: The Streamlined Sales and Use Tax Agreement is a set of uniform sales tax rules that 24 states follow: 23 full members and Tennessee as an associate. A seller can register in all of them with one free application and use one exemption certificate, and a remote seller can have a certified provider calculate, file and pay the tax in those states at the states' cost.

body:
## Which states are in Streamlined Sales Tax?

Twenty-four: 23 full members and Tennessee as an associate member, as the Governing Board lists them on 5 November
2026:

| Status | States |
|---|---|
| Full members (23) | Arkansas, Georgia, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, Nevada, New Jersey, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Utah, Vermont, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, Wyoming |
| Associate member (1) | Tennessee |
| Not members | Every other state, including California, Texas, New York, Florida, Illinois and Pennsylvania |

A full member's laws already follow the agreement; an associate has substantially complied. The states with the
most manufacturing and distribution sales, California, Texas and New York, are not members, so a growing seller
deals with them directly whatever it does in Streamlined states.

## What do member states have in common?

The agreement standardizes how sales tax works, not the rates. Member states share definitions of products, a
single state-level administration, simpler rate structures and other uniform rules. When the Supreme
Court decided South Dakota v. Wayfair, it pointed to South Dakota's membership as one reason its law did not burden
interstate sellers unduly.

For a seller, three things follow:

- **One registration.** The Streamlined Sales Tax Registration System registers you in any or all member states
  with one application, free. You still file a return with each state you register in.
- **One exemption certificate.** The Streamlined exemption certificate is accepted by all 24 member states, and you
  don't need to be registered through Streamlined to use it. See
  [resale and exemption certificates](/sales-tax/resale-certificates).
- **Published taxability and rates.** Each member state publishes a taxability matrix and rate and boundary files
  in a common format, which is what a tax engine loads.

## Can a remote seller get sales tax filing for free?

Yes, in member states, for remote sellers. The Board contracts with certified service providers (CSPs); on
5 November 2026 it lists Avalara, TaxCloud, Sovos, AccurateTax and Avior as offering the free service. A seller
that is a "CSP-compensated seller" in a member state gets, at the state's cost:

- setup and integration of the provider's system with yours
- tax calculated on each sale
- returns prepared and filed, and the tax remitted
- help with that state's notices and audits

To qualify in a state, you register through the Streamlined system, contract with a CSP under the Streamlined
contract, and in the 12 months before registering had no fixed place of business there for more than 30 days, less
than $50,000 of property and of payroll there, under 25% of your total property or payroll there, and weren't
collecting there to qualify as a state supplier. A remote seller that only has to collect because it passed the
economic threshold qualifies. The provider may charge for states where you don't qualify, for non-member states and
for extra services.

## Can a certified provider charge a distributor that sells mostly for resale?

Yes, in part. The Board's [free services page](https://www.streamlinedsalestax.org/for-businesses/free-sales-tax-services)
lets a provider charge to process non-taxable transactions when they exceed 30% of all the transactions it processes
for that seller in a member state in a year. A worked example: a made-up remote seller is over the threshold in Ohio,
Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Georgia and Washington, with no presence in any of them. One free registration covers all
six, and a provider files them at the states' cost. But if 70% of its Ohio transactions are sales for resale, the
provider may charge for processing those in Ohio. Ask each provider for its price on non-taxable volume before you
sign.

## Is Intuit a certified service provider?

Not for the free service. The Board lists Exactor, an Intuit subsidiary, among the providers whose systems are
certified but that don't currently offer free services under the Streamlined contract. QuickBooks Online's
automated sales tax works out the tax inside QuickBooks; it isn't one of the providers offering the free service.

## Is it worth registering through Streamlined?

For a manufacturer or distributor that has passed the threshold in several member states and has no presence
there, usually yes: one registration, and a provider files those states for free. It doesn't help with California,
Texas or New York. Check where you are over with the [nexus checker](/sales-tax/economic-nexus-thresholds), and
see [how an ERP should handle sales tax](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp) for connecting a provider to your order
system.

title: Use tax for businesses: when you owe it yourself
question: When does a business owe use tax on its purchases?
answer: Use tax is the other half of sales tax: when you buy something taxable for your own use and the seller doesn't charge your state's tax, you owe the same tax yourself. It catches untaxed purchases from out-of-state suppliers, and goods bought tax-free for resale or manufacturing that you then use another way. A registered business usually reports it on its regular sales tax return.
description: Use tax for US businesses: what it is, when you owe it on purchases, goods bought exempt and then used, how it's reported, and credit for tax paid elsewhere.

body:
## What is use tax?

Sales tax is collected by the seller; use tax is paid by the buyer when the seller didn't collect. The rate is the
same, and the point is the same: a taxable item used in the state is taxed once, wherever it was bought. Texas
describes use tax as complementary to sales tax, on the storage, use or consumption of taxable items in the state.

For a household, use tax is mostly theory. For a business it's an audit finding waiting to happen, because
auditors read your purchase ledger, not just your sales.

## When does a business owe it?

Whenever it uses something taxable on which the seller didn't charge its state's tax. The usual cases:

| Situation | Example | You owe use tax on |
|---|---|---|
| An out-of-state supplier didn't charge your state's tax | Shop supplies from a supplier not registered in your state | The price of the supplies |
| You bought for resale, then used it yourself | A distributor takes a drill from stock for its own warehouse | The cost of the drill |
| You bought exempt for manufacturing, then used it another way | Steel bought exempt, used to build a rack for your own plant | The cost of the steel |
| Exempt equipment used partly for other purposes | A machine also used for your own maintenance parts | The divergent share (Texas) |
| The supplier charged a lower rate than your location's | Bought at a counter in an area with no local tax | The local tax not charged |

The Streamlined Sales Tax Governing Board puts the rule in one line: when the seller doesn't collect the tax due,
the customer must pay use tax directly to the state unless it can claim an exemption.

## How much use tax do you owe, and what if another state's tax was paid?

The same rate as the sales tax where you use the item, less any sales tax you already paid on it elsewhere (where your
state gives that credit, as Texas does). Worked examples at a made-up Texas plant where state and local tax total
8.25% (the 6.25% state rate plus 2% local):

| Purchase | Tax charged by the seller | Use tax owed |
|---|---:|---:|
| $4,000 of shop supplies from an out-of-state supplier | $0 | $330.00 |
| The same supplies, with the supplier's own state's 6% charged ($240) | $240.00 | $90.00 |
| A $1,800 drill taken from resale stock for the warehouse | $0 (bought for resale) | $148.50 |

## How do you report it?

A business with a sales tax permit reports use tax on its regular sales and use tax return, as taxable purchases;
Texas has a line for it. A business without a permit files a separate use tax return. If you paid another state's
tax on the item first, Texas allows a credit for it; check your own state's rule.

The reverse also works: California lets a buyer that paid sales tax on an item, then resold it before using it,
take a deduction when it reports the sale.

## How does a system catch it?

Use tax is missed when nobody looks at the tax line of a vendor bill. The checks are mechanical:

- **Vendor bills with no tax** on taxable items, from vendors not registered in your state: flag for accrual.
- **Stock issued to internal use**: an issue from resale or exempt stock to maintenance, samples or your own
  buildings creates a use tax line at cost.
- **Exempt purchases** carry the reason they were exempt, so a later use that doesn't match it shows up. See
  [the manufacturing exemption](/sales-tax/manufacturing-sales-tax-exemption) and
  [resale and exemption certificates](/sales-tax/resale-certificates).
- **A monthly accrual report** by state and rate, which goes onto the return.

For how these fit with the rest of sales tax in an order system, see
[how an ERP should handle sales tax](/sales-tax/sales-tax-in-erp).

title: Performance guarantee, security deposit and defect liability

body:
## What is a performance guarantee?

A performance guarantee is security the contractor gives the client, at the start of the contract, that it will
perform the contract; the client can claim it if the contractor doesn't. On CPWD works, Clause 1 of the General
Conditions of Contract 2023 requires an irrevocable performance guarantee at the percentage in Schedule E of the
tendered amount, on top of the other deposits in the contract, within the period Schedule F allows after the letter
of acceptance. Schedule E of GCC 2023 sets it at 5% of the tendered value.

## In what form can a performance guarantee be given?

As an insurance surety bond, an account payee demand draft, a fixed deposit receipt, or a bank guarantee from any
commercial bank, under Clause 1. If a bank can't pay against a fixed deposit receipt given as part of the guarantee,
the loss falls on the contractor, who must make it good on demand.

## How long must a performance guarantee be valid?

Up to the stipulated date of completion plus at least 6 months, and longer if the time for completion is extended:
the contractor must get its validity extended to cover the extended time. If it doesn't, the Engineer-in-Charge may
claim the full amount. The CPWD Works Manual 2022 put it differently (valid at least sixty days beyond completion of
all contractual obligations), and CPWD amended Clause 1 and Schedule E by a circular on 27 February 2026; check the
version of the GCC your contract names.

## When is the performance guarantee returned or forfeited?

It's returned, without interest, once the competent authority records the completion certificate. The client can
claim it only for amounts it's entitled to under the contract: the full amount if the contractor fails to extend its
validity, or an amount the contractor owes and hasn't paid within 30 days of a notice. If the contract is determined
or rescinded, the whole guarantee is forfeited. On contracts that include maintenance after construction, half of it
is kept as security deposit and returned year by year.

## What is the difference between a performance guarantee and a security deposit?

The performance guarantee is given once, up front, and returned at completion; the security deposit is built up from
the bills and kept until the defect liability period has run. On CPWD works, 2.5% of the gross amount of each running
and final bill is deducted until the deposit reaches 2.5% of the tendered amount (Clause 1A). Private contracts call
it retention money and set their own rate; see [RA bills](/construction/ra-bills) for how it comes off each bill.

| | Performance guarantee | Security deposit |
|---|---|---|
| Amount (CPWD) | 5% of tendered value | 2.5% of tendered value |
| How given | Up front: bank guarantee, surety bond, FDR or DD | Deducted from each running and final bill |
| Returned | After the completion certificate | After the defect liability period, or when the final bill is passed, whichever is later |

## Can the security deposit be released against a bank guarantee?

Yes. Under Clause 1A, the security deposit deducted from bills can be released against a bank guarantee from a
scheduled bank once at least ₹5 lakh has built up; each guarantee except the last must be for at least ₹5 lakh, and
its validity must follow Clause 17 and any extension of time. That frees cash during the job, using the contractor's
bank guarantee limits instead.

## What is the defect liability period?

The time after completion during which the contractor must make good, at its own cost, defects that appear in the
work from faulty materials or workmanship: twelve months after the completion certificate, or six months for works
costing ₹10 lakh or less (except road works), under Clause 17. If the contractor doesn't fix them after written
notice, the Engineer-in-Charge can have them fixed by others and recover the cost from any money due to the
contractor or from the security deposit.

## When is the security deposit refunded?

Not before the defect liability period ends, or until the final bill has been prepared and passed, whichever is
later. For road works, half may be refunded after six months and the rest after twelve, if the Engineer-in-Charge
thinks half is enough to cover the contractor's liabilities. CPWD issued an advisory on releasing security deposit on
18 November 2025; ask the division for the current procedure.

## What does this look like on a ₹2 crore work?

A made-up CPWD work with a tendered amount of ₹2,00,00,000, stipulated completion 31 December 2026, actual
completion certificate 15 January 2027 (within an extension granted):

| Item | Amount | Held until |
|---|---|---|
| Performance guarantee, 5% (bank guarantee) | ₹10,00,000 | Completion certificate (15 January 2027); validity at least 6 months beyond the extended completion date |
| Security deposit, 2.5%, from bills | ₹5,00,000 | 15 January 2028, or when the final bill is passed, if later |
| Security deposit released against a bank guarantee | ₹5,00,000 | The guarantee then stays in place instead of the cash |

## How should a contractor track guarantees and deposits?

- Every bank guarantee with its amount, purpose (performance, security deposit, mobilisation advance), bank, expiry
  and the date it must be extended to.
- Security deposit deducted per bill, the running total against the cap, and any release against a guarantee.
- The completion certificate date, the defect liability period, defects notified and fixed, and the refund date.
- Bank guarantee commission and limits used, per job.

The CPWD Works Manual itself asks divisions to monitor bank guarantees given for earnest money, performance,
security deposit, mobilisation advance and milestones; a contractor needs the same list from its side. The
[construction demo](/industries/construction-company) doesn't track bank guarantees, security deposits or the defect
liability period yet; those are parts we'd build, from the same RA bills and completion dates. For the price side of
a long contract, see the [price escalation clause](/construction/price-escalation-clause).

title: Certified payroll under Davis-Bacon: WH-347 explained

body:
## What is certified payroll?

Certified payroll is a weekly payroll report, signed under a statement of compliance, that a contractor files on a
construction job covered by the Davis-Bacon and Related Acts. It shows every laborer and mechanic who worked on the
contract that week, the work they did, their hours and what they were paid, so the agency can check that each got at
least the prevailing wage set for the job. The law behind it, the Copeland Act, says each contractor and subcontractor
"each week must furnish a statement on the wages paid each employee during the prior week".

## Which jobs need certified payroll?

Federal and federally funded or assisted contracts over $2,000 for construction, alteration or repair, including
painting and decorating, of public buildings or public works. "Related Acts" are the laws under which federal
agencies help pay for construction through grants, loans, loan guarantees and insurance, so a state or city job
paid partly with federal money can be covered too. The contract says so: it carries the Davis-Bacon clauses and the
wage determination for the job.

## Who has to submit it?

Every contractor and subcontractor with laborers or mechanics on the covered work, weekly, for each week in which
covered work is done. Payrolls go to the federal agency when it is a party to the contract, or otherwise to the
applicant, sponsor or owner that keeps the records for the agency. The prime contractor is responsible for getting
every sub's certified payroll in, so a late or wrong payroll from a sub is the prime's problem too.

## Do I have to use Form WH-347?

No, but you must report the same information weekly. DOL's WH-347 is optional; a covered contractor can use its own
format or an electronic system the agency or prime allows, as long as it has every required field and the signed
Statement of Compliance (page 2 of WH-347, or a document with identical wording). Each weekly payroll is numbered,
starting at 1 for the project, and the last one is marked final.

## What goes on a certified payroll?

For each worker: name, Social Security number, last known address, telephone number and email, the classification of
the work actually done, the hourly rate paid including fringe benefits, the daily and weekly hours worked in total
and on each covered contract, deductions made, and the actual wages paid. The payroll also names the project, the
contract number, the wage determination numbers that apply, and the week-ending date.

## What does the Statement of Compliance certify?

That the payroll is accurate and complete, that the required records are kept, and that each laborer and mechanic,
including registered apprentices, was paid at least the required prevailing wage, including fringe benefits, for the
work done. Falsifying it can bring civil or criminal prosecution under 18 U.S.C. 1001 and the False Claims Act
(31 U.S.C. 3729).

## How are prevailing wages and fringe benefits paid?

At no less than the rate for each worker's classification on the job's wage determination, which the Department of
Labor sets from local prevailing wages. The fringe part can be paid into bona fide benefit plans, or as cash in lieu
of fringe benefits. A made-up example: a classification at $38.50 an hour plus $14.20 in fringe, paid entirely in
cash, for 40 hours in a week:

| | Amount |
|---|---|
| Base wages, 40 hours × $38.50 | $1,540.00 |
| Fringe paid in cash, 40 hours × $14.20 | $568.00 |
| **Gross for the week** | **$2,108.00** |

A worker doing work in more than one classification may be paid the rate for each for the time actually worked in
it, if the payroll records show that time accurately.

## Is overtime required on Davis-Bacon jobs?

On prime contracts over $100,000, yes: the Contract Work Hours and Safety Standards Act requires laborers and
mechanics, including guards and watchmen, to be paid at least one and a half times their regular rate for every hour
over 40 in a workweek. The Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime rules may also apply.

## How long must certified payroll records be kept?

During the work and for 3 years after all the work on the prime contract is completed. The underlying payroll records
must be kept for the same period, and an electronic system used to submit payrolls must give the contractor, the
agency and DOL access to them for at least 3 years.

## Did the Davis-Bacon rules change recently?

Yes. DOL's final rule updating the Davis-Bacon regulations took effect on 23 October 2023. On 24 June 2024 a federal
court in the Northern District of Texas enjoined three of its provisions nationwide (on material suppliers, on-site
time of delivery truck drivers, and applying the clauses by operation of law when an agency left them out of a
contract); the rest of the rule is in effect. Check DOL's page for the current status before relying on those three.

## What should a contractor's system do for certified payroll?

Keep, per worker and per day, the job, the classification of the work done and the hours, so the weekly payroll can
be built rather than retyped:

- Each job flagged as covered, with its wage determination and the rate per classification.
- Daily hours per worker per classification and per job, from the field.
- Rates paid, fringe paid in cash or into plans, deductions and net pay, per week.
- A weekly payroll per job in WH-347 layout, numbered, with the Statement of Compliance for signature.
- Subcontractors' weekly payrolls received and checked by the prime.

The same jobs, crews and hours feed each job's [pay applications](/construction/pay-applications) and the payments to
subs that [prompt payment acts](/construction/prompt-payment-acts) time, so they belong in one system.

The [construction demo](/industries/construction-company)'s US build has daily attendance per worker and job and a
monthly pay register with crew totals; payroll taxes stay with the payroll provider. It doesn't do certified payroll:
no wage determinations, classifications per hour of work, weekly WH-347 reports or subcontractor payroll tracking.
That would be a part we'd build for a contractor on federal work.

body:
## What is a change order in construction?

A change order is a written agreement between owner and contractor that changes the work, the contract price, the
contract time, or all three. It is signed by both (and usually the architect), and once signed its amount is added to
the contract sum. AIA's standard form is G701; many owners use their own form with the same content: what changes,
the price, the days, and the signatures.

Most disputes on a job are about changes: extra work done on a verbal OK, priced after the fact, argued about at
closeout. The fix is procedural: no change is real until it is written, priced and approved, and every one is tracked
until it is billed.

## What's the difference between a change order and a construction change directive?

A change order is agreed by both sides; a construction change directive orders the work to go ahead before the price
or time is agreed. AIA describes its G714 directive as for use where the owner and contractor "have not agreed on
proposed changes in the contract sum or contract time", and under AIA's general conditions the owner can issue one
without the contractor's signature. You do the work, keep the cost records, and the price is settled later, by a
change order once it's agreed.

| | Change order (G701) | Change directive (G714) |
|---|---|---|
| Price and time | Agreed | Not yet agreed |
| Contractor signs | Yes | No |
| Work starts | After signing | On the directive |
| Billed | Once signed, as its own line | Once agreed and turned into a change order (or as the contract says) |

## Do I have to do extra work without a signed change order?

It depends on the contract and the state, but in Texas you may refuse once unsigned work gets too big. Since
1 September 2023, a Texas contractor or sub may decline owner-directed additional work without a written, fully
executed change order once that work, plus earlier unsigned owner-directed work, exceeds 10% of the original contract
amount, and isn't liable for damages for declining (Property Code 28.0091). On a $400,000 contract the line is
$40,000: with $36,000 of unsigned work already done, a new $6,000 directive takes it to $42,000, and the contractor may
decline it.

On federal jobs, a written or oral order from the contracting officer that changes the work counts as a change order
only if you give written notice saying you regard it as one.

## Will I get paid for work done on a verbal OK?

Often not without a fight. A verbal approval is hard to prove at closeout, and contracts usually say changes must be
in writing. Get the scope and price in writing before you start, even as an email, and keep dated photos, daily
reports and costs for any work done before the paperwork caught up.

## How do I price a change order?

Build it from quantities, labor hours at your rates, material quotes and equipment, then add overhead and profit as
the contract allows, with the backup attached:

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Labor: 40 hours × $65 | $2,600 |
| Material (supplier quote attached) | $3,400 |
| Equipment rental | $500 |
| Subtotal | $6,500 |
| Overhead and profit, 15% | $975 |
| **Change order** | **$7,475**, 3 days added |

The figures are made up. Ask for the time as well as the money: a change that adds work but no days can leave you
paying liquidated damages for a delay the owner caused.

## How long do I have to claim a change?

As the contract says; on federal jobs under FAR 52.243-4, you must assert your right to an adjustment within 30 days
of the change order or your notice. Costs incurred more than 20 days before your written notice aren't adjusted
(except for defective specifications), and nothing can be claimed after final payment. Under that rule, notice given
on 1 March 2026 covers costs from 9 February 2026 onward. Private contracts, such as AIA's general conditions, have
their own deadlines: read the changes article before the job starts.

## What about hidden or different site conditions?

Give written notice promptly, before you disturb them. On federal jobs FAR 52.236-2 requires notice "before the
conditions are disturbed" of subsurface or latent conditions that differ materially from the contract, or unusual
unknown ones; if they do differ, the contract is adjusted in writing. No request is allowed after final payment.

## Can I bill a pending change order?

No: bill only approved changes, each as its own line on the schedule of values, so the
[pay application](/construction/pay-applications) shows the original contract sum, net change by change orders and
the revised sum. Pending changes are tracked, not billed, and they belong on the
[WIP schedule](/construction/wip-schedule), because their costs are already in the job.

| | Amount |
|---|---|
| Original contract sum | $400,000 |
| CO 1, approved | $12,000 |
| CO 2, pending | $8,500 (tracked, not billed) |
| CO 3, rejected | $4,000 (kept for the record) |
| **Revised contract sum** | **$412,000** |

## Can signing a lien waiver give up a pending change order?

It can. A waiver that releases all claims through a date may release the extra work you haven't been paid for yet;
read what each [lien waiver](/construction/lien-waivers) covers, and list pending changes as an exception where the
form allows.

## What should a contractor's system keep for change orders?

- A change log per job: number, description, who asked, date of notice, status, price and days.
- The backup for each price, linked to the job's cost codes, so actual cost can be compared later.
- Approved changes added to the contract value and the schedule of values, once.
- Pending exposure: the total of unapproved changes per job, reviewed weekly.

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company)'s US build, a change order is raised as its own estimate
against the accepted contract estimate; once accepted, its lines join the schedule of values labeled CO 1, CO 2 and
are billed apart on the pay application. On the sample tower job, change order 1 adds $6,504 to a $245,856 schedule
of values. It doesn't yet keep a change log with notice dates and days, or change directives billed before a price is
agreed; those are parts we'd build.

body:
## Which law governs contract labour in construction now?

The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (the OSH Code). It repeals the Contract Labour
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, and the OSH (Central) Rules, 2026, published on 8 May 2026, replace the Contract
Labour Central Rules, 1971. PF, ESIC and the building workers' cess now sit in the Code on Social Security, 2020. The
Central Rules apply where the Central Government is the appropriate government; states make their own rules for the
rest, so check the state's rules for your site.

## Does a construction contractor need a contract labour licence?

Yes, once it employs 50 or more contract workers. The contract labour part of the OSH Code applies to every
establishment that employed 50 or more contract workers through contract on any day of the preceding twelve months,
and to every manpower supply contractor that employed 50 or more. A contractor it applies to can't supply or engage
contract labour, or execute work through it, without a licence. Under the Central Rules no licence is needed up to 49
contract workers, and a licence is valid for five years, applied for online.

It doesn't apply where the work is only intermittent or casual, but work done for more than 120 days in the preceding
twelve months, or seasonal work for more than 60 days a year, doesn't count as intermittent.

## Who pays contract workers, and what if the contractor doesn't?

The contractor pays the wages of each worker it employs, through a bank transfer or other electronic mode, and tells
the principal employer electronically what it paid. If the contractor doesn't pay in time, or pays short, the
principal employer must pay the wages in full or the unpaid balance, and can recover it from the contractor. Under the
Central Rules, when wages aren't paid within seven days of the end of the wage period, the principal employer pays
within fifteen days and recovers the amount from the contractor.

| | Contractor | Principal employer |
|---|---|---|
| Licence (50 or more contract workers) | Holds it | Engages only licensed contractors |
| Wages | Pays, by bank transfer, and reports to the principal employer | Pays if the contractor doesn't, and recovers |
| Work order | Reports it within 15 days of receiving it | |
| Returns | Half-yearly, in Form XVIII | |

## Can contract labour be used for core work?

Not in an establishment's core activities, with exceptions. The Code prohibits contract labour in the core activity of
any establishment, but allows it where that work is ordinarily done through contractors, where it doesn't need
full-time workers for most of the day, or for a sudden increase in work that has to be finished in a set time. Civil
and other construction work, including maintenance, isn't treated as a core activity of an establishment that isn't
set up for it, so a factory or office hiring a contractor to build or repair is not affected.

## When do PF and ESIC apply to a contractor?

PF applies to every establishment with twenty or more employees, and ESIC to every establishment with ten or more
persons (other than a seasonal factory), under the First Schedule of the Code on Social Security. The Code counts a
contractor as an employer, and a worker hired through a contractor for an establishment's work is treated as employed
in it. So a contractor's site gangs and office staff can bring it over these thresholds, and its compliance matters to
the principal employer too.

## What records should a contractor keep for contract labour?

- Each worker's identity and KYC, with the site they work on.
- Attendance per day per site, which sets the days paid.
- Wages, deductions and the bank transfer that paid them, per wage period.
- PF and ESIC contributions, where the thresholds are crossed.
- The licence number and validity, work orders reported, and the half-yearly returns.

A made-up gang of 12 workers at ₹700 a day for 26 days earns ₹2,18,400 for the month; paid by bank transfer within
seven days of the end of the wage period, with the amount reported to the principal employer, the contractor has met
its wage duty for that period.

## How does this connect to labour cess and TDS?

Separately. [Labour cess](/construction/labour-cess) is 1% of the cost of construction paid to the building workers'
welfare board; income-tax [TDS on payments to contractors](/construction/tds-on-contractor-payments) is deducted
from what a principal employer pays the contractor. Neither replaces the contractor's duty to pay its workers.

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), each worker's KYC is captured on a phone (Aadhaar's
last four digits only, PAN, bank, UAN), attendance is marked per site, and the monthly wage register works out days,
PF and ESIC for workers on the company's rolls, TDS for subcontractors, advances and gang totals; gate passes need
complete KYC. It doesn't track contract labour licences, work-order reporting or the half-yearly return; those are
parts we'd build. See [daily-wage payroll](/services/daily-wage-payroll).

On CPWD works the official site records are the site order book, the cement register and an online inspection register; hindrances go in the site order book. A DPR from the phone feeds all of them.

body:
## What is a daily progress report (DPR)?

A daily progress report is the record of one site for one day: the work done against each BOQ item, the labour and
machines on site, the material used, the weather, any hindrance, and photos. It is the contractor's own record, kept
whether or not the client asks for it, because it's what later proves progress for a bill, cost for the margin, and
the cause of a delay for an extension of time.

## What should a daily progress report record?

Everything that happened on the site that day that someone may later have to prove:

- **Work done**, per BOQ item and location, in the item's unit.
- **Labour**, by trade, from that day's attendance, with absentees and the reason.
- **Machines** on site and the hours each ran.
- **Material** used from site stock, per item.
- **Weather**, issues and hindrances, with who caused them and since when.
- **Instructions** received from the client's engineer.
- **Photos**, dated, of the work done and of any problem.

## Which site records does CPWD require?

On CPWD works the Works Manual names the site documents: the site order book, a physical inspection register where
applicable, the cement register and the dismantle register, kept under its standard operating procedure SOP 5/14.
For projects, the inspection register is online, through CPWD's project management system, for senior officers to
record their observations from the start of work to completion.

## What is the site order book, and why does it matter?

It's the book on site where the client's engineer writes instructions to the contractor. Under CPWD's general
conditions, the contractor's technical representative notes down instructions conveyed by the Engineer-in-Charge in
the site order book and signs it, and the Engineer-in-Charge's decision as recorded there is final and binding on the
contractor. Anything the engineer orders on site should therefore be in the site order book and, on the contractor's
side, in that day's DPR.

## How are hindrances recorded on CPWD works?

In the site order book. The physical hindrance register was dropped for works whose tenders were uploaded on or after
19 February 2019; now, when a hindrance causing delay comes to the junior or assistant engineer's notice, he writes it
in the site order book and reports it to the Engineer-in-Charge at once. A contractor should record the same hindrance
in its DPR the same day, with the date it started and photos, because extensions of time are argued from these dates.

## Who should approve a daily progress report?

The project manager, before it counts. A report filed by the site engineer and approved by the PM is a checked
record: only approved work should move the site's progress, feed the next measurement and bill, or count toward the
weekly report to the client. A report sent back with a note is corrected and filed again.

## Why file the DPR from a phone?

Because the work is on site and the evidence is on site. A report written in the evening from memory misses
quantities and photos; one filed on a phone from the site, with attendance marked there, carries the time, the place
and the pictures. Officers also inspect works often to check quality and specifications, and a dated photo record
answers their questions quickly.

## How do daily reports become the weekly report and the bill?

By adding them up rather than rewriting them. The week's approved reports give work done per BOQ item, labour
man-days by trade, material used, machine hours, issues and photos for the client's weekly progress report; the
same approved work feeds the [measurement book](/construction/measurement-book) and the material check against BOQ
norms in [material consumption](/construction/material-consumption-vs-boq).

## What does the construction demo do?

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), the site engineer files one report per site per day
from a phone: quantity done against each BOQ line, labour by trade filled from that day's attendance, material used
from the site's own stock, machine hours, weather, issues and up to six photos, shrunk on the phone before upload.
Attendance is marked per worker on site, and a mark made away from the site's map pin is flagged. The project manager
approves the report or returns it with a note, and only approved work counts toward progress. The weekly report for
the client is built from the week's approved reports as a PDF, with sections chosen per client, and an approved
report is posted to the site's Telegram group where one is set up. Datum AI answers "which sites haven't sent
today's report?". It doesn't keep the site order book or the cement register in CPWD's format, or record hindrances
as their own entries for an extension of time claim; those are parts we'd build.

title: GST on works contracts: rate, ITC and GST TDS

answer: Under GST, a works contract is a contract for building, construction, repair or similar work on immovable property where goods pass to the client in the course of the work. Government clients deduct GST TDS (1% CGST + 1% SGST) on contracts over ₹2.5 lakh, and input tax credit is blocked for building your own premises.

body:
## What is a works contract under GST?

A works contract is a contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting
out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any **immovable
property**, where property in goods passes in the course of the work (section 2(119) of the CGST Act, 2017). The GST
Council's note stresses the limit: only work on immovable property qualifies. Painting a car or fabricating a
machine with your own material is a composite supply, but not a works contract.

## Is a works contract a supply of goods or of services?

Of services. Schedule II, paragraph 6(a) of the CGST Act treats a works contract as a supply of services, so the
whole contract value, materials included, is taxed as one service, not split into goods and labour as it was under
VAT and service tax.

## What is the GST rate on a works contract?

Generally 18%: 9% CGST plus 9% SGST (or 18% IGST), with lower rates only for the works a rate notification names.
The rates are in serial number 3 of Notification 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), as amended. The GST Council's 2017 note
listed the general entry at 9% + 9% and lower entries at 6% + 6% for works such as roads and bridges for public use,
low-cost housing and some government works. Those lower entries have been changed several times since; from 22
September 2025, Notification 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) moved items (vii), (viii) and (x) of serial 3 to 9% CGST.
Take the rate for your contract from the notification as it stands on the date of supply, or from your tax adviser,
not from an old article.

## Can the client claim input tax credit on my bill?

Not when the client uses your works contract to build its own immovable property, such as an office or a factory
shed: section 17(5)(c) blocks that credit, except for plant and machinery. A main contractor that buys a
subcontractor's works contract to supply its own works contract can take the credit.

| Who receives the works contract service | Input tax credit |
|---|---|
| A business building its own office, factory shed or other immovable property | Blocked (section 17(5)(c)) |
| The same, for plant and machinery | Allowed: plant and machinery is excluded from the block |
| A main contractor buying a subcontractor's works contract to supply its own works contract | Allowed |

## Can a contractor claim ITC on cement, steel and other inputs?

Yes, when they go into a works contract you supply to a client: you charge GST on that supply and set the credit
against it. Section 17(5)(d) blocks credit only for goods and services used to construct immovable property on your
own account, such as your own office or godown (other than plant or machinery).

## What is GST TDS, and when does the client deduct it?

Tax deducted at source under section 51 of the CGST Act: government departments, local authorities, government
agencies and other notified persons deduct 1% CGST plus 1% SGST from payments for
a contract whose taxable value exceeds ₹2.5 lakh. It's worked out on the value excluding GST, and the deductor pays it
to the government within ten days after the end of the month. It isn't deducted when the supplier's location and the
place of supply are in a state other than the one where the recipient is registered. It is separate from
[income-tax TDS](/construction/tds-on-contractor-payments); both can come off the same bill.

On a ₹18,50,000 RA bill to a state department, GST TDS is ₹18,500 CGST plus ₹18,500 SGST: ₹37,000.

## Which state's GST applies to a works contract?

The state where the property is. The GST Council's note says the place of supply "would be where the immovable
property is located" when supplier and recipient are both in India. So a Gujarat contractor working on a site in
Maharashtra charges IGST to a client registered in Gujarat; CGST plus SGST apply where the contractor and the site are in
the same state.

## When is GST due on an RA bill?

At the time of supply: for services, the earlier of the invoice date (if the invoice is issued in time) and the date
payment is received (section 13). Each [running account bill](/construction/ra-bills) is a supply, so the contractor
issues a tax invoice for the bill's value with GST on top.

| Line | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Gross value of RA bill #3 | 18,50,000 |
| CGST 9% | 1,66,500 |
| SGST 9% | 1,66,500 |
| **Invoice value** | **21,83,000** |

The figures are made up.

## Is GST payable on a mobilisation advance or on security deposit?

Ask your adviser before you decide. For services, receiving a payment can fix the time of supply, but whether an
interest-bearing mobilisation advance is a payment for the supply is argued both ways. Security deposit is deducted
from a bill whose full value has already been invoiced; how a deposit that is later forfeited is taxed is a separate
question, and practitioners disagree on it.

## What should a contractor's system do for GST?

- Classify each contract as a works contract or not, with the place of supply (where the property is).
- Issue a GST invoice for each RA bill from the [measured](/construction/measurement-book) value.
- Keep input tax credit apart where it is blocked (your own buildings) and where it is allowed.
- Record the GST TDS each government client deducts against the bill it belongs to.
- Reconcile GST invoices with RA bills and payments, so nothing is billed or credited twice.

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), RA bills and trading invoices carry HSN or SAC codes
and the CGST and SGST or IGST split, and the month's GST checklist shows output tax and the GSTR-1 summary by
customer and HSN, with what's missing and the due dates. It doesn't yet record GST TDS deducted by clients or tag
input tax credit as blocked or allowed; those are parts we'd build.

title: Job cost and margin per site for construction contractors
metaTitle: Job cost and margin per site for contractors
question: How does a contractor work out the cost and margin of each site, and spot a site losing money?
answer: Add up every cost that belongs to the site (material used, site labour, plant and machines, site cash and subcontractors) and set it against the value of work done to date: the difference is the margin so far. Divide cost to date by progress to project the final cost, and compare it with the estimate. ICAI's AS 7 defines which costs belong to a contract, and says a loss expected on a contract is recognised at once, not when the job ends.
description: Job cost and margin per site: which costs belong to a construction contract under AS 7, margin to date, projected cost, losing sites, and a worked example.

sources.title: Accounting Standard (AS) 7, Construction Contracts (revised 2002)
sources.publisher: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India

checks.quote: costs that relate directly to the specific contract;
costs that are attributable to contract activity in general and can be allocated to the contract; and
site labour costs, including site supervision;
costs of materials used in construction;
costs of moving plant, equipment and materials to and from the contract site;
the estimated costs of rectification and guarantee work, including expected warranty costs;
general administration costs for which reimbursement is not specified in the contract;
depreciation of idle plant and equipment that is not used on a particular contract.
the proportion that contract costs incurred for work performed upto the reporting date bear to the estimated total contract costs; or
Progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the work performed.
When it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognised as an expense immediately.

body:
## What is job cost per site?

It's the total of every cost that belongs to one site or contract, kept separately from every other site. A
contractor running several sites at once can be profitable overall while one site loses money; job cost per site
shows which one, while there's still time to act. It also tells you whether the estimate you bid was right, which is
what the next bid depends on.

## Which costs belong to a construction contract?

ICAI's Accounting Standard 7 (Construction Contracts) says contract costs comprise costs that relate directly to the
contract, costs attributable to contract activity in general that can be allocated to it, and other costs the
contract makes chargeable to the customer. Direct costs include:

- Site labour, including site supervision.
- Materials used in construction.
- Depreciation of plant and equipment used on the contract, and hire of plant and equipment.
- Moving plant, equipment and materials to and from the site.
- Design and technical assistance directly related to the contract.
- Estimated rectification and guarantee work, including expected warranty costs, and claims from third parties.

## Which costs should not be charged to a site?

General administration costs the contract doesn't reimburse, selling costs, research and development the contract
doesn't pay for, and depreciation of idle plant and equipment not used on that contract, under AS 7. Head office rent
and salaries stay in the company's overheads; an idle mixer in the godown isn't a cost of the site it isn't on.

## How do you work out the margin so far on a site?

Subtract cost to date from the value of work done to date. The value of work is the approved quantity of each BOQ
item times its rate, not what has been billed or received: AS 7 notes that progress payments and advances may not
reflect the work performed.

A made-up site with a contract value of ₹40,00,000 and an estimated cost of ₹28,00,000:

| | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Value of approved work to date (60% of the contract) | 24,00,000 |
| Material used on site | 9,60,000 |
| Site labour, from attendance and wages | 6,40,000 |
| Site cash (kharchi) spent | 1,20,000 |
| Machine days on site | 80,000 |
| **Cost to date** | **18,00,000** |
| **Margin to date** | **6,00,000 (25%)** |

## How do you project a site's final cost?

Divide cost to date by progress, so the rest of the job is assumed to cost at the same rate. The site above is 60%
done for ₹18,00,000, so it projects to ₹30,00,000 against an estimate of ₹28,00,000: a projected margin of
₹10,00,000 instead of the ₹12,00,000 planned, and ₹2,00,000 over budget. The projection is rough early in a job, so
wait until some of the work is done (the demo waits for 5%) and check it against a fresh estimate to complete.

## How do you know when a site is losing money?

When its projected cost is above its contract value, or its margin to date has turned negative. AS 7 is strict about
it: when it's probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss is recognised
as an expense immediately, whatever stage the work is at. A site that is merely over its estimate is over budget; one
projected to cost more than it earns is losing money, and needs attention now.

## How does percentage of completion relate to job cost?

AS 7 allows the stage of completion to be measured by the cost incurred for work done against the estimated total
cost, by surveys of work performed, or by the physical proportion of the work completed. A contractor that measures
progress by approved BOQ quantities is using the physical method; the cost-to-cost method needs a regular estimate to
complete. Your accountant decides which applies in your accounts.

## What records does job cost per site need?

One record per cost, tagged with its site at the moment it happens:

- Material issued to each site, valued at its purchase rate, from the stores records.
- Attendance per worker per site per day, and each worker's wage.
- Site cash spends, with receipts, per site.
- Machine days per site, with a day rate for owned machines.
- Subcontractor bills against the site.
- The approved quantity of each BOQ item, from daily reports or measurements, and the contract rates.

See [material consumption against BOQ](/construction/material-consumption-vs-boq) for the check that explains the
material line, and [RA bills](/construction/ra-bills) for what's billed against the same work.

## What does the construction demo do?

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), the director dashboard shows each site's contract, work
done (approved work at BOQ rates), billed, received, cost to date and margin. Cost to date is material used on site
at its rate, labour from attendance and wages, site cash spent, and machine days at each machine's day rate. Margin
to date is work done less cost; once 5% of the work is done, projected cost is cost to date divided by progress, and
projected margin is the contract less that, set against the planned margin from the estimate. Sites are marked on
track, over budget or losing money, and Datum AI answers "is the Bhatt site making money?" with the same figures. It
doesn't add subcontractor bills or head office allocations to a site's cost, or take a fresh estimate to complete;
those are parts we'd build.

title: Labour cess on construction: the 1% BOCW cess explained
question: What is labour cess on construction in India, who pays it and how is it collected?
answer: Labour cess (the building and other construction workers' cess) is 1% of the cost of construction, excluding land, paid by the employer carrying out building or other construction work to the state's Building Workers' Welfare Board. It now sits in section 100 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, which repeals the 1996 Cess Act, and the 1% rate was notified under it on 8 May 2026. Government and PSU clients deduct it from contractors' bills.

body:
## What is labour cess on construction?

Labour cess is a levy of 1% of the cost of construction, paid by whoever carries out building or other construction
work, to fund the social security and welfare of building workers through each state's Building Workers' Welfare
Board. It's often called BOCW cess, after the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996, which
first levied it.

## What law levies labour cess now?

Section 100 of the Code on Social Security, 2020, which repeals the 1996 Cess Act. On 8 May 2026 the Ministry of Labour notified the rate under section 100(1) as one per
cent of the cost of construction, replacing the 1996 notification (S.O. 2899) that had set the same 1%. The Code allows
a rate between 1% and 2%; the notified rate is the minimum.

## Who pays labour cess?

The employer carrying out the building or other construction work, which under the Code includes a contractor. In
practice the owner who gets the building approved pays it in advance, and on government and PSU works the client
deducts it from the contractor's bills. Who bears the cost between owner and contractor is a matter for the contract,
so read the tender's terms before you price.

## Which works are covered, and which aren't?

Building or other construction work is defined widely: buildings, streets, roads, railways, airfields, irrigation,
drainage, power lines, water works, pipelines, towers, dams, bridges, tunnels and more, including construction,
alteration, repair, maintenance and demolition. It doesn't include:

- Work related to a factory or a mine.
- Work that employed fewer than ten workers in the preceding twelve months.
- An individual's (or group's) own house costing no more than ₹50 lakh, or a higher amount notified, within the
  worker numbers the government notifies.

## How is the cost of construction worked out?

All the cost of construction incurred by the employer, except the cost of land and any compensation paid to workers
or their families under the Code's employee compensation chapter. The Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026 have the
employer self-assess it using the state PWD's or CPWD's schedule of rates, another applicable schedule, or the figures
filed with RERA for a building, for the year the work started, certified by a chartered engineer.

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Total project cost | ₹2,60,00,000 |
| Less cost of land | ₹60,00,000 |
| Cost of construction | ₹2,00,00,000 |
| **Cess at 1%** | **₹2,00,000** |

The figures are made up.

## When is labour cess paid?

In advance, at approval or before work starts, on a self-assessment certified by a chartered engineer. Where a local
authority approves the building, the approval application must carry proof that the cess has been paid online to
the Welfare Board; a project expected to run more than a year can pay for the first year's construction cost and the
rest as it falls due. Within sixty days of completing the work, the employer pays the balance on its final
self-assessment and files a return.

## How is labour cess deducted from a contractor's bills?

On works for a government or a public sector undertaking, the client deducts the cess at the notified rate from the
bills it pays and deposits it with the state's Welfare Board within thirty days. On a ₹18,50,000
[RA bill](/construction/ra-bills), 1% is ₹18,500, deducted alongside TDS and security deposit. Keep each deduction
against its bill, so the final self-assessment counts what was already paid.

## What if labour cess is paid late or short?

The employer owes interest at 1% a month, or part of a month, from the due date until it's paid. If the amount in an
assessment order isn't paid by its date, the cess is treated as in arrears and the authority can impose a penalty of
up to the amount of the cess, after giving the employer a hearing.

## Is labour cess the same as GST or TDS?

No. It's a separate levy under labour law, paid to the Building Workers' Welfare Board, not a tax under the GST or
income-tax laws. A government client may take all three off the same bill: income-tax TDS, GST TDS and labour cess.

## What should a contractor's system track for labour cess?

- Each job's cost of construction, excluding land, and who bears the cess under the contract.
- Cess paid in advance, deducted from each RA bill, and still due on completion.
- Deposit and return dates, so nothing attracts interest.
- The state Welfare Board each job's cess goes to.

The [construction demo](/industries/construction-company) doesn't track labour cess: RA bills carry GST, and payroll
handles PF, ESIC and TDS for subcontractors, but cess paid or deducted per bill isn't recorded. That would be a part
we'd build. For the workers themselves, see [contract labour compliance](/construction/contract-labour-compliance).

title: Lien waivers: conditional, unconditional, progress, final
question: What is the difference between a conditional and an unconditional lien waiver?
answer: A conditional lien waiver gives up lien rights only once the payment actually reaches the signer; an unconditional waiver is effective when signed, paid or not. Each comes in a progress and a final version. Several states, including Arizona, California, Florida, Texas and Wyoming, set the wording by statute, and a waiver that doesn't follow the statutory form can be unenforceable.

body:
## Why do lien waivers exist?

A lien waiver is a signed release of mechanic's lien rights for work that has been paid for. On a US private job,
anyone who supplied labor or material and wasn't paid can usually file a mechanic's lien against the property, even
if the owner paid the general contractor in full. So owners and lenders ask for a waiver from the contractor, and
from each subcontractor and supplier, for every payment: proof that the money reached them and that they give up the
lien for what they've been paid.

## What are the four types of lien waiver?

There are four: conditional or unconditional, each for a progress payment or the final payment.

| | Progress payment | Final payment |
|---|---|---|
| **Conditional** | Releases lien rights through a date, once this payment clears | Releases all lien rights for the job, once the final payment clears |
| **Unconditional** | Releases lien rights through a date; effective when signed | Releases all lien rights for the job; effective when signed |

[Arizona's statute](https://www.azleg.gov/ars/33/01008.htm) uses exactly these four forms and makes a waiver unenforceable unless it follows them
substantially. Its conditional forms take effect only when the check has been endorsed and paid by the bank; its
unconditional forms carry a notice that they are enforceable even if you haven't been paid, so if you haven't been,
use a conditional form. California and Texas use the same four forms, with a similar notice on the unconditional ones.

## Which states have statutory lien waiver forms?

Arizona, California, Florida, Texas and Wyoming are among the states whose statutes set the wording of lien
waivers; in each, a waiver on the wrong form can fail to release the lien. Several other states also prescribe forms by statute,
and most states set none, leaving the wording to the contract. Before using any form, check the statute in the state
where the project is.

| State | Statute | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| Arizona | [ARS 33-1008](https://www.azleg.gov/ars/33/01008.htm) | Four forms; a waiver is unenforceable unless it substantially follows them |
| California | [Civil Code 8132–8138](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8132), with [8124](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8124) and [8126](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8126) | Four forms; a waiver given before payment, or for a single or joint payee check, is void unless it is in substantially the statutory form. Any other statement waiving lien rights is void unless it follows the statute or the claimant has been paid in full |
| Florida | [713.20](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0713/Sections/0713.20.html) | Progress and final forms; lien rights can't be waived in advance, and nobody may require a waiver different from the statutory forms |
| Texas | [Property Code 53.281–53.287](https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/PR/htm/PR.53.htm) | Four forms; a waiver is unenforceable unless it substantially complies with 53.284. The current forms have no notary block |
| Wyoming | [29-10-101](https://wyoleg.gov/statutes/compress/title29.pdf) | One waiver form, completed in substantially the statutory wording; it reserves retainage and amounts still unpaid, and ends with a notary's acknowledgment. The same section sets the preliminary notice to the owner, which attaches a waiver form |

"Statutory form" in practice means: copy the statute's form word for word, fill in the blanks, and don't add terms.
Extra releases in a custom form, such as a waiver of claims for pending changes, are the usual reason a form is
challenged.

## What happens if you sign the wrong lien waiver?

Signing an unconditional waiver before the money arrives is the expensive mistake: in states with statutory forms it
is enforceable against you even if you are never paid. California's unconditional forms say so in a notice that must
be in type at least as large as anything else on the form, and Texas prohibits anyone from requiring an
unconditional waiver for a payment the signer hasn't received in good funds.

The other mistakes:

- **A conditional waiver for the wrong amount or through-date.** It releases what it says once paid, so check both
  against the payment.
- **A final waiver for a progress payment.** It gives up everything, including [retainage](/construction/retainage)
  and unbilled work.
- **Missing exceptions.** California's progress forms release rights for change orders fully signed before the
  waiver unless they are listed as exceptions; retention and unpaid extras stay outside. List anything still owed.
- **A non-statutory form in a statutory state.** It may not release the lien at all, which the owner's lender will
  find before you do.

## How do lien waivers work with joint checks?

When the owner or general contractor pays a subcontractor and its supplier with one check payable to both, the
waiver given for it should be conditional. California's and Texas's statutes both require the conditional form when
a single or joint payee check is given in exchange for the waiver, and California treats the payee's endorsement on
a check paid by the bank as evidence of payment. Florida lets a lienor condition a waiver on the check clearing.

In practice: name the maker, amount and payees of the check on the conditional waiver, and give the unconditional
waiver only after the check has cleared and the supplier has been paid its share.

## What is the difference between a progress and a final lien waiver?

A progress waiver releases lien rights for work through a stated date, for one payment; a final waiver releases all
lien rights for the job. Florida's statutory progress form says it doesn't cover retention or work after the date
specified, and California's progress forms leave out retention and unpaid extras. The final forms leave room only
for disputed claims, so anything not listed is given up.

| | Progress waiver | Final waiver |
|---|---|---|
| Covers | Work through the through-date, for this payment | The whole job |
| Retainage | Usually excluded | Included: the final payment normally is the retainage |
| When given | With each [pay application](/construction/pay-applications) and payment | At closeout, with the final payment |
| Exceptions to list | Earlier unpaid progress payments, retention, unpaid extras | Disputed claims for extras |

## Is a preliminary notice the same as a lien waiver?

No. A preliminary notice protects lien rights at the start of the work; a lien waiver gives them up once paid. In
many states a subcontractor or supplier must send a notice to the owner to keep the right to file a lien at all, and
missing the deadline can lose it:

| State | Notice | Deadline |
|---|---|---|
| California | Preliminary notice ([Civil Code 8204](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=8204)) | Within 20 days of first furnishing work; a late notice covers only work from 20 days before it was served |
| Florida | Notice to owner ([713.06](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0713/Sections/0713.06.html)) | Before starting, or within 45 days of starting; missing it is a complete defense to the lien |
| Texas | Notice of claim for unpaid labor or materials ([53.056](https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/PR/htm/PR.53.htm)) | By the 15th day of the third month after the month the work was done (second month on residential projects) |

So the same subcontractor sends a notice when it starts, then a conditional waiver with each payment request and an
unconditional one once paid.

## How do you track lien waivers per pay application?

Track one row per payer, payee and payment: who owes a waiver, which of the four types, the amount and through-date,
and whether the signed copy is in. A made-up example for pay application 3 on a job paying $63,000:

| From | Type | Through | Amount | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| General contractor | Conditional progress | Mar 31 | $63,000 | Sent with pay app 3 |
| General contractor | Unconditional progress | Feb 28 | $45,000 | Signed after the pay app 2 payment cleared |
| Steel subcontractor | Unconditional progress | Feb 28 | $16,200 | Received |
| Electrical subcontractor | Unconditional progress | Feb 28 | $5,400 | **Missing: hold its next payment** |

The lender's draw usually asks for the conditional waiver for this application and the unconditional waivers for
the last one, from the contractor and every subcontractor paid from it.

## What should lien waiver software do?

When comparing systems, check that it can:

- Generate the waiver on the statutory form for the project's state, with the amount and through-date filled from
  the pay application, not typed.
- Track all four types per payment, and switch conditional to unconditional only when the payment is recorded.
- Show which subcontractor waivers are missing, and block their next payment until they are in.
- Record joint checks with their payees, and preliminary notices received with their dates.
- Keep the signed file against the payment it covers.

Our [US construction demo](https://construction-erp-us.ahromlabs.com/demo) tracks lien waivers per pay application.

question: How does a contractor check material used on site against the BOQ, and what wastage does CPWD allow?
answer: Work out the theoretical quantity each BOQ item should have used, from its consumption norm and the work done, and compare it with the material actually issued to the site. On CPWD works Clause 38 of the GCC sets the rule: cement and bitumen from the Schedule of Rates constants, steel as designed plus 3% for cutting, pipes and cables plus 5%, sheets plus 10%, with a further variation allowed in Schedule F. Beyond that, the difference is questioned.
description: Material consumption against BOQ norms: CPWD Clause 38 theoretical quantities, wastage for steel, pipes and sheets, worked examples, reconciliation.
