body:
## What is material consumption against BOQ norms?

It's the check that the material a site has used matches what its work should have needed. Each BOQ item has a
consumption norm (so much cement per cubic metre of concrete, so many bags of mortar per square metre of repair):
multiply the norm by the quantity of work done and you get the theoretical quantity; compare it with what was
actually issued to the site. Material used above the norm is wastage, theft or rework; material below it can mean
work done thinner than specified, or issues not recorded.

## What does CPWD's Clause 38 say about theoretical consumption?

On CPWD works, Clause 38 of the General Conditions of Contract 2023 works out the theoretical quantity of material
after completion, and at any intermediate stage if the materials issued don't reconcile:

| Material | Theoretical quantity |
|---|---|
| Cement and bitumen | Quantity per item from the Schedule of Rates named in Schedule F; for other items, a formula the Engineer-in-Charge sets |
| Steel reinforcement and structural steel | Quantity as designed or authorised, including laps and chairs, plus 3% for cutting, compared diameter-wise and section-wise |
| GI and CI pipes, conduits, wires, cables, pig lead | Quantity actually required and measured, plus 5% for cutting |
| GI and MS sheets | Quantity actually required, plus 10% |
| Any other material | Actual requirements |

A further variation over these theoretical quantities is allowed as specified in Schedule F of the contract. For
non-scheduled items the Superintending Engineer decides the theoretical quantity.

## How do you work out theoretical consumption of steel?

From the design quantity for each diameter, plus 3%. A made-up example for 12 mm bars:

| | Tonnes |
|---|---|
| Design quantity, including laps and chairs | 12.000 |
| Plus 3% for cutting | 0.360 |
| **Theoretical quantity** | **12.360** |
| Issued to the work | 12.800 |
| Excess over theoretical | 0.440 (3.6%) |

Whether 0.440 t is acceptable depends on the variation Schedule F allows; beyond it, the department questions the
difference. Each diameter and section is compared separately, so a surplus of 16 mm can't hide a shortfall of 12 mm.

## How do you check cement or mortar against the BOQ?

Multiply the work done on each item by its constant from the schedule of rates (or the norm in your own BOQ), add the
items up per material, and compare with the bags issued. A made-up example from a repair job with a norm of 0.45 bag
of repair mortar per square metre: 700 m² of approved work should have used 315 bags; 360 bags were issued, 45 bags
(14%) over, which is worth investigating before the next order.

## Why does material reconciliation matter to a contractor?

Because it's where a site's margin leaks first, and where a client's audit looks. A site that uses 10% more material
than its norm on a material-heavy job can lose most of its margin without anyone noticing until the end; on CPWD
works, consumption of steel and cement is monitored under the Works Manual's standard procedures, with a cement
register kept at site. Checking each week, against approved work, finds the problem while the job can still recover.

## Which records does a reconciliation need?

The norms, the work done and every movement of material to and from the site:

- The BOQ with a consumption norm for each item and the material it uses.
- Work done per item, from approved daily reports or the [measurement book](/construction/measurement-book).
- Every issue of material to the site, and every return, with dates.
- Stock at site at the date of the check, so material lying on site isn't counted as used.
- The variation allowed in the contract, so the check uses the same limit as the client.

## How does this connect to job cost?

Material is often the largest part of a site's cost. The value of material issued, at its purchase rate, is the
material line of the site's [job cost](/construction/job-cost-per-site); the reconciliation explains whether that
cost is what the work should have cost.

## What does the construction demo do?

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), each BOQ line can carry a norm: so much of one
material per unit of work. Expected use of a material is the approved work on each line times its norm; actual use
is what the site's daily reports issued from site stock. The site's Material tab shows expected, actual and the
difference with its value, and flags anything more than 10% over or under. Datum AI answers "is the Bhatt site
wasting material?" from the same figures. It doesn't apply CPWD's Clause 38 allowances (3%, 5%, 10%) by material or
compare steel diameter-wise; those are parts we'd build.

title: Measurement book (MB): recording work for payment
question: What is a measurement book in construction, and how is it kept?
answer: The measurement book (MB) is the record of every quantity of work done, measured on site item by item, from which each running bill and the final bill is paid. In CPWD and most government works, measurements follow the contract's rules of measurement, are test-checked by senior engineers, and are now entered electronically as an e-MB; private contractors keep the same record for their clients and subcontractors.

body:
## What is a measurement book (MB)?

The measurement book is the record of every quantity of work measured on site, item by item, from which each
[running account bill](/construction/ra-bills) and the final bill is paid. CPWD's general conditions say running
bills are submitted "on the basis of such recorded measurements", so a quantity that isn't in the MB isn't billed.
Private contractors keep the same record for their own clients and, in the other direction, for the subcontractors
they pay.

## What details go into an MB entry?

For each BOQ item, every time it's measured: the date, the location (floor, grid, chainage), the dimensions taken
(number, length, breadth, depth), the quantity worked out, who measured it and who accepted it for the contractor.

| Item | Location | No. | L (m) | B (m) | D (m) | Qty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RCC M25 in columns | Ground floor, C1–C8 | 8 | 0.45 | 0.30 | 3.20 | 3.456 m³ |
| Brickwork 230 mm | First floor, grid A–D | 1 | 18.40 | 0.23 | 3.00 | 12.696 m³ |

The figures are made up. How each item is measured (deductions for openings, which faces count) comes from the
contract's mode of measurement, usually an IS 1200 part or the department's schedule; see
[measurement rules for interior BOQs](/boq/measurement-rules) for the same idea applied to interiors.

## Who records and test-checks measurements?

On CPWD works, site engineers record the measurements and the officers named in CPWD's standard operating procedure
SOP 5/24 test-check them. The officer who records or test-checks an item is responsible for its quality, quantity and
dimensional accuracy, which is why measurements are signed, not just entered. The contractor (or its representative)
accepts each measurement, so a disagreement is settled before the bill, not after it.

## What is an e-MB?

CPWD's electronic measurement book: measurements and payments are entered through its e-MB module on PFMS, the
government's financial management system. Where a physical MB is still used, CPWD's SOP 5/20 sets the rules for
writing it, recording measurements, moving and transferring it, reviewing it and what to do if it's lost.

## How does the MB become an RA bill?

The abstract adds up each item to date, multiplies by the agreement rate, and takes off what was paid in earlier
bills; the difference is this bill. An item "PU membrane", BOQ quantity 500 m² at ₹850:

| | Quantity | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Previous bills | 300 m² | ₹2,55,000 |
| This bill | 180 m² | ₹1,53,000 |
| Up to date | 480 m² | ₹4,08,000 |

Every bill is cumulative, so a mistake in one measurement is corrected in the next bill's up-to-date figure rather
than lost. The [RA bill page](/construction/ra-bills) shows the deductions that follow.

## What are extra and deviated items?

Extra items are needed to complete the work but aren't in the agreement; a deviation is an increase or decrease in an
agreement item's quantity. Quantities within the deviation limit in the contract's Schedule F are paid at the
agreement rate; beyond it, and for extra items, the rate is worked out as Clause 12 of the general conditions
prescribes. The CPWD manual gives the Engineer-in-Charge 30 days to decide a claim within his own powers, longer when
it goes to a higher authority.

If the same PU membrane item reaches 640 m² against 500 m² in the BOQ, it's 28% over. Whether the excess is paid at
the BOQ rate or a new one depends on the Schedule F limit for that work.

## What happens to items the department won't pay?

They are still measured and recorded, under a separate heading as inadmissible items claimed but not included in the
payment, so the quantity is on record if the claim is accepted later.

## Can work be paid before it is measured?

On conditions. CPWD's rules allow an advance on a running bill for work measured but not yet checked, or done but
not yet measured, adjusted once the measurements are recorded; see [RA bills](/construction/ra-bills).

## What should a contractor's system keep for measurements?

- Measurements entered on site, per BOQ item and location, with the dimensions, not only the quantity.
- Who measured, who checked, and the contractor's acceptance, with dates.
- A running total per item against the BOQ quantity, flagging deviation beyond the contract's limit.
- Extra items held apart until their rate is approved.
- Each [RA bill](/construction/ra-bills) built from the measurements since the last bill, so nothing is paid twice.
- The same records feeding [TDS](/construction/tds-on-contractor-payments) and
  [GST](/construction/gst-on-works-contracts) on each bill.

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), measurements are recorded per BOQ line with the date,
quantity, a note and who measured, entered by hand or filled from approved daily reports; once work is reported
against a line only its quantity can change, and quantities beyond the BOQ are flagged. It doesn't yet record
dimensions (number × length × breadth × depth), test checks or the contractor's acceptance; those are parts we'd build.

title: Mechanics lien deadlines and preliminary notices by state
metaTitle: Mechanics lien and preliminary notice deadlines
question: When must a contractor send a preliminary notice and file a mechanics lien?
answer: It depends on the state and your place in the chain. In California a sub sends a preliminary notice within 20 days of starting and records a lien within 90 days of completion (30 days after a notice of completion); in Florida the notice to owner is due within 45 days and the lien within 90 days of last work; Texas counts to the 15th day of a later month; New York allows 8 months. On federal jobs you claim against the payment bond instead.
description: Mechanics lien and preliminary notice deadlines in California, Texas, Florida and New York, the Miller Act on federal jobs, worked dates and how to track them.

body:
## What is a mechanics lien?

A mechanics lien is a claim against the property itself for unpaid work or materials on it: if the bill isn't paid,
the claimant can ask a court to have the property sold to pay it. Every state has its own lien statute, and each has
deadlines. Miss one and the lien is lost, even if the money is owed. Many states also require some claimants to send
a notice early in the job (a preliminary notice, notice to owner or notice of claim) to keep the right to a lien.

## What is a preliminary notice, and who has to send one?

A preliminary notice tells the owner, and usually the general contractor and lender, that you're working on the
project and may claim a lien if you aren't paid. Subcontractors and suppliers usually have to send it; a general
contractor with a contract directly with the owner often doesn't. It isn't a lien and it isn't a
[lien waiver](/construction/lien-waivers); it only keeps the right open.

## What are the deadlines in California, Texas, Florida and New York?

| State | Preliminary notice | Lien deadline | Suit to enforce |
|---|---|---|---|
| California | Within 20 days of first furnishing work (Civil Code 8204) | Direct contractor: after completing its contract, before the earlier of 90 days after completion of the project and 60 days after a notice of completion (8412). Others: before the earlier of 90 days after completion and 30 days after a notice of completion (8414) | Within 90 days of recording the lien (8460) |
| Texas | Subs and suppliers: notice of claim by the 15th day of the third month after the month the work or materials were provided (2nd month on residential projects) (Property Code 53.056) | Lien affidavit by the 15th day of the fourth month after the month work was completed (third month on residential projects) (53.052) | Within one year of the last day to file the affidavit (53.158) |
| Florida | Notice to owner before starting or within 45 days of starting, for those not in contract with the owner (Statutes 713.06) | Within 90 days after final furnishing of labor, services or materials (713.08) | As the statute sets |
| New York | Not required by Lien Law 10 | Within 8 months after completion or final furnishing; 4 months for a single-family home; 90 days after retainage was due for a retainage lien (Lien Law 10) | As the statute sets |

These are the main deadlines only. Each statute has its own form, service rules and exceptions, so read the state's
text, or ask a construction lawyer, before relying on a date.

## How do you count a California lien deadline?

From completion, or from the owner's notice of completion if one is recorded, whichever gives the earlier date. A
subcontractor on a project completed on 1 June 2026, where the owner records a notice of completion on 10 June, must
record its lien by 10 July 2026: 30 days after the notice, which is earlier than 30 August, 90 days after completion.
The general contractor has until 9 August, 60 days after the notice. Each then has 90 days after recording to sue.

## What happens if a California preliminary notice is late?

You don't lose everything, but you lose the work before it. A late notice still protects work done within the 20 days
before it was served and after. A sub that started on 2 March 2026 should have served notice by 22 March; serving on
1 April protects only work from 12 March onward.

## How do you count a Texas lien deadline?

By months, not days: to the 15th day of a month after the month the work was done. A subcontractor on a commercial
job that provided labor in March 2026 and wasn't paid must send its notice of claim by 15 June 2026 (the third month
after March) and, if work ended that month, file its lien affidavit by 15 July 2026 (the fourth month). A suit to
foreclose must follow by 15 July 2027.

## How long do you have in Florida and New York?

Florida: 90 days after you last furnished labor, services or materials, with the notice to owner served within 45
days of starting. Work that started on 2 March and ended on 1 June 2026 needs notice by 16 April and the claim of
lien recorded by 30 August 2026. New York: 8 months after completion or your last work, so work last done on 1 June
2026 can be liened until 1 February 2027 (1 October 2026 for a single-family home).

## Can you put a lien on a federal project?

The remedy on a federal job is the prime contractor's payment bond, under the Miller Act, rather than a lien on the
property. A sub or supplier with a contract directly with the prime can sue on the bond once it hasn't
been paid in full 90 days after its last work. A second-tier sub or supplier, in contract with a sub but not the prime,
must first give the prime written notice within 90 days of its last work. Any suit must be brought within one year of
the last labor or material.

## Can a lien be filed for unpaid retainage?

Yes, where the statute allows it, often on its own clock. In New York a lien for [retainage](/construction/retainage)
can be filed within 90 days after the date the retainage was due to be released; in Texas a sub claiming a lien for
retainage has its own affidavit deadline, counted from the month the original contract was completed, terminated or
abandoned (Property Code 53.052(d)).

## How should a contractor track lien deadlines?

From the dates the system already has: the day each job and each sub started, the last day each worked or delivered,
completion, any notice of completion, and the state of the project. From them, every deadline can be worked out per
job and per party:

- Preliminary notices due and sent, per sub and supplier, with proof of service.
- Lien deadlines per job, counted under that state's rule, with a reminder well before each.
- Lien waivers received against each payment, so nobody is paid without one.
- Retainage still held, with its release date and any lien deadline for it.

The [construction demo](/industries/construction-company)'s US build tracks lien waivers per pay application, ours
and our subs' and suppliers', conditional or unconditional. It doesn't yet send preliminary notices or work out lien
deadlines by state; those are parts we'd build.

title: Pay applications (AIA G702 and G703), explained
question: How does a construction pay application work?
answer: A pay application is a contractor's monthly bill on a construction job: each line of the schedule of values with the work completed before and this period, materials stored, the retainage held back, and the amount now due. AIA's G702 is the one-page summary and certificate; G703 is the line-by-line continuation sheet. The architect or owner certifies the amount before the owner pays.

body:
## What goes into a pay application?

A pay application is the contractor's monthly bill against progress: for every line of the schedule of values it
shows the work completed before this period, the work completed this period, materials stored, the total to date,
the [retainage](/construction/retainage) held, and the amount now due. US construction contracts are usually paid
this way rather than on milestones.

The American Institute of Architects (AIA) publishes the most used forms, G702 and G703. They are paid, copyrighted
documents (AIA offers free partial samples of [G702](https://aiacontracts.com/samples/aia-g702-1992-pay-application-sample.pdf) and [G703](https://aiacontracts.com/samples/aia-g703-1992-continuation-sheet-sample.pdf)); many owners and general contractors use their own form with the same
columns and arithmetic.

## What is the difference between G702 and G703?

G702 is the summary: one page of totals that the contractor signs to apply for payment and the architect signs to
certify it. G703 is the continuation sheet: one row per line of the schedule of values. [AIA's instructions](https://help.aiacontracts.com/hc/en-us/articles/1500009308302-Instructions-G703-1992-Continuation-Sheet) have the
contractor fill in G703 first and carry its totals to G702, then sign G702 and send both to the architect.

| | G702, Application and Certificate for Payment | G703, Continuation Sheet |
|---|---|---|
| What it holds | Contract sum, change orders, totals, retainage, previous certificates, payment due | Each schedule of values line with its scheduled value, work and stored materials |
| Who signs | Contractor (application, notarized) and architect (certificate) | Nobody separately; it is attached to G702 |
| Change orders | Summarized in a change order box and line 2 | Usually listed as their own lines |

## What is a schedule of values, and who prepares it?

The schedule of values is the contract sum broken into lines (general conditions, concrete, steel, electrical and
so on) that every pay application bills against. The contractor prepares it and submits it to the architect at the
start of the job, as the general conditions require; AIA [doesn't publish](https://help.aiacontracts.com/hc/en-us/articles/1500009387461-summary-g702-1992-application-and-certificate-for-payment) a standard schedule of values form. AIA's
instructions say the breakdown, whether by sections of work or by subcontractor, should stay consistent through the
project.

Its total must equal the original contract sum. Owners and architects watch for **front-loading**: early items
valued high so the contractor is paid ahead of the work. Agree the lines and values before the first application;
changing them later is harder than getting them right.

## How do you fill in G703, column by column?

| Column | Holds | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| A | Item number | |
| B | Description of work | |
| C | Scheduled value | Starts at the original contract sum; change orders are usually added as their own lines |
| D | Work completed, from previous application | Previous D plus previous E |
| E | Work completed, this period | Includes stored material from earlier periods now installed |
| F | Materials presently stored | Not in D or E; value moves to E as the material is installed |
| G | Total completed and stored to date | D + E + F, with % complete (G ÷ C) |
| H | Balance to finish | C − G |
| I | Retainage, if the rate varies by line | Only needed where variable retainage applies |

A worked G703 on a made-up $400,000 contract with one approved $20,000 change order, at the end of month three:

| Item | C Scheduled | D Previous | E This period | F Stored | G To date | % | H Balance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 General conditions | $40,000 | $12,000 | $4,000 | | $16,000 | 40% | $24,000 |
| 2 Concrete | $120,000 | $60,000 | $30,000 | | $90,000 | 75% | $30,000 |
| 3 Structural steel | $140,000 | $18,000 | $20,000 | $10,000 | $48,000 | 34% | $92,000 |
| 4 Electrical | $100,000 | | $6,000 | | $6,000 | 6% | $94,000 |
| CO 1 Added canopy | $20,000 | | | | | 0% | $20,000 |
| **Total** | **$420,000** | **$90,000** | **$60,000** | **$10,000** | **$160,000** | **38%** | **$260,000** |

## How is retainage calculated on a pay application?

Retainage is a percentage of the work completed (columns D + E) plus a percentage of the materials stored (column
F); the two rates can differ if the contract says so. G702 then takes it off the total to date and deducts what was
certified before. With 10% on both, the totals above go onto G702 like this:

| G702 line | Calculation | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Original contract sum | | $400,000 |
| 2 Net change by change orders | | $20,000 |
| 3 Contract sum to date | Line 1 ± 2 | $420,000 |
| 4 Total completed and stored to date | G703 column G | $160,000 |
| 5a Retainage on completed work | 10% × (D + E) = 10% × $150,000 | $15,000 |
| 5b Retainage on stored material | 10% × F = 10% × $10,000 | $1,000 |
| 5 Total retainage | 5a + 5b | $16,000 |
| 6 Total earned less retainage | Line 4 − line 5 | $144,000 |
| 7 Less previous certificates for payment | Line 6 of the last certificate: $90,000 − $9,000 | $81,000 |
| 8 **Current payment due** | Line 6 − line 7 | **$63,000** |
| 9 Balance to finish, including retainage | Line 3 − line 6 | $276,000 |

Check: this period's $60,000 of work plus $10,000 stored is $70,000; less 10% is $63,000. If the contract retains
nothing on stored material, line 5b is zero and line 8 becomes $64,000. When retainage is reduced (for example at
50% complete), line 5 falls and the release shows up as extra payment on line 8, so the reduction must be written in
the contract or approved in writing first.

## Can you bill for stored materials?

Usually yes, if the contract allows it and you can prove the material exists and is yours to sell to the owner.
Stored material goes in column F at its value; it is not deducted when the owner pays for it, only moved to column E
as it is installed. Owners and lenders typically ask for the supplier's invoice, photos, proof of insurance, and for
material stored off site, a bill of sale or other proof of title.

On federal jobs, [FAR 52.232-5](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/52.232-5) lets the contracting officer count material delivered to the site. Material held
elsewhere counts only if the contract specifically allows it and the contractor gives satisfactory evidence that it
has acquired title and that the material will be used on the contract.

## Does a G702 need to be notarized?

The G702 form has a notary block under the contractor's signature, and [AIA's instructions](https://help.aiacontracts.com/hc/en-us/articles/1500009308242-Instructions-G702-1992-Application-and-Certificate-for-Payment) say the contractor should
sign it and have it notarized. Whether a notarized signature is legally required depends on the contract and the
owner; many owners and lenders insist on it, some accept electronic signatures without it. Check the contract's
payment section before the first application rather than finding out when it is returned.

## What is a pencil draft, and when is a pay application due?

A pencil draft (or pencil copy) is an unsigned draft of the pay application sent to the owner's representative or
architect a few days before the real one, so they can agree the percentages before anything is notarized. It is
common practice, not something the AIA forms require. The contract sets the period the application covers, the day
it is due each month and how long the owner has to pay; a late or rejected application usually waits for the next
cycle, which can cost a month of cash.

On federal jobs the due date is set by [FAR 52.232-27](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/52.232-27): a progress payment is due 14 days after the designated billing
office receives a proper payment request, and a request that isn't proper must be returned within 7 days with the
reasons.

## Who approves a pay application, and can they approve less?

The architect (or the owner's representative where there is no architect) checks the application against the work
on site and certifies the amount due, which may be less than applied for. AIA's instructions say the architect then
initials every figure changed on G702 and G703 and attaches an explanation; the owner pays the amount certified.
Lenders often want [lien waivers](/construction/lien-waivers) from the contractor and from the subcontractors paid
from the previous application before releasing money.

On federal jobs, FAR 52.232-5 sets the rules: progress payments monthly on estimates of work accomplished, approved
by the contracting officer, with an itemization of the amounts by element of work, a listing of each subcontractor's
work, subcontract value and previous payments, and a certification with every request or payment isn't made. The
certification says, among other things, that subcontractors and suppliers have been paid from previous payments.

## Why do pay applications get rejected?

Most rejections come from a handful of causes:

- **The arithmetic doesn't tie.** G703 totals don't match G702, or line 7 isn't line 6 of the last certificate.
- **Percent complete ahead of the site.** The architect sees less work in place than billed.
- **Stored material without proof.** No invoice, title or insurance, or it's off site without contract approval.
- **Unapproved change orders billed.** Only executed [change orders](/construction/change-orders) belong in column C.
- **Missing lien waivers** for the previous payment, from the contractor or subcontractors.
- **Missing signature, notarization or certification**, or the wrong period.
- **A changed schedule of values** that no longer matches the approved one.

Each of these is cheaper to prevent with a pencil draft than to fix after the application is returned.

## What should pay application software do?

When comparing systems, check that it can:

- Hold the schedule of values per job, locked once approved, with change orders added as their own lines.
- Take quantities or percentages from site progress, not typed in at month-end.
- Carry each certified application forward, so column D and line 7 always match what was certified, including any
  amount the architect cut.
- Compute retainage per line, with separate rates for work and stored material, and its reduction and release.
- Move stored material to installed when it is used, without double counting.
- Track the lien waivers owed per application, and block payment of a subcontractor until theirs is in.
- Produce the application in the owner's format, and keep each submitted and certified version.
- Feed the same figures to the [WIP schedule](/construction/wip-schedule), so billing and cost are compared per job.

Our [US construction demo](https://construction-erp-us.ahromlabs.com/demo) runs G702/G703-style pay applications on
a schedule of values with 10% retainage, change orders and lien waivers per pay application; it has no WIP
schedule.

## Can pay applications go to QuickBooks?

Yes, if the system posts each one as an invoice on the right job. In our construction demo, connected to a
QuickBooks Online sandbox company, each project becomes a job under its client in QuickBooks, and each pay
application goes there as an invoice on that job when it is issued; payments follow when marked paid. Job reports
in QuickBooks then match the project. How the connection works, and who calculates the sales tax, is in
[connecting QuickBooks Online](/manufacturing/quickbooks-integration).

title: Price escalation in CPWD contracts: clause 10CC worked out
metaTitle: Price escalation clause 10CC, worked out
question: How does the price escalation clause (10CC) work in a CPWD contract, and how is escalation calculated?
answer: Clause 10CC of CPWD's General Conditions of Contract 2023 adjusts the contract price each quarter for rises and falls in the prices of cement, steel, labour, fuel and other materials. It applies to 85% of the work done in the quarter, split by the component percentages in Schedule F, and moves each component by the change in its index since the last date for tenders. Where 10CC doesn't apply, clause 10C pays only for changes caused by new laws.

body:
## What is a price escalation clause?

A price escalation clause adjusts a fixed-price contract for changes in the cost of materials and labour while the
work is done, so a contractor isn't ruined by a steel price jump on a long job and the client gets the benefit when
prices fall. In CPWD contracts it is Clause 10CC of the General Conditions of Contract 2023: the contract amount is
"varied" by a formula worked out every quarter, both up and down. Private contracts often copy it or write their own.

## Does every CPWD contract have clause 10CC?

No: the NIT approving authority marks it applicable or not applicable in Schedule F for each work, and sets the
component percentages there. Where 10CC applies, Clause 10C doesn't; where 10CC isn't applicable, 10C applies instead.
Check Schedule F of your contract first.

## What does clause 10CC cover, and for which period?

Work done during the stipulated period of the contract, plus any extension justified under Clause 5 without action
under Clause 2 (the clause for the contractor's own delay). So escalation stops for work done during a delay the
contractor caused. The base date for every index is the last stipulated date for receipt of tenders, including any
extension.

## How is the cost of work for escalation worked out?

From the quarter's bills, in four parts, then 85% of the total:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| C | Gross value of work done in the quarter (A, to this quarter, less B, to last quarter) |
| F | Secured advance paid in the quarter less secured advance recovered |
| I | Other advance payments made in the quarter less those recovered |
| J | Amounts paid at market rates for deviations and extra items under Clause 12 |
| M | C + F + I − J |
| **W** | **0.85 × M**, the cost of work on which escalation is worked out |

Items paid at market rates under Clause 12 are taken out because their rates are already current.

## What is the 10CC formula?

Escalation for the quarter is W times each component's percentage times the change in its index since the base
date, added up:

VW = W × (1/100) × [CP × (CI − CO)/CO + LP × (LI − LO)/LO + CMP × (CMI − CMO)/CMO + EMP × (EMI − EMO)/EMO + FP × (FI − FO)/FO + SP × (SI − SO)/SO + BP × (BI − BO)/BO]

CP, LP, CMP, EMP, FP, SP and BP are the percentages of cement, labour, other civil materials, E&M materials, fuel,
steel and bitumen in Schedule F; the "O" values are the indices on the base date and the "I" values those for the
quarter. During a maintenance period, only labour, civil and E&M materials and bitumen count.

## Which indices does clause 10CC use?

For materials, the wholesale price indices published by the Office of the Economic Adviser (for example the index for
Pozzolana cement, mild steel long products, high speed diesel and bitumen). For labour, the minimum daily wage of an
unskilled adult mazdoor fixed under law: whatever happens to other wage categories, only the unskilled rate counts.

## How is 10CC escalation calculated, in numbers?

A made-up quarter: gross value of work done ₹48,00,000, secured advance paid ₹4,00,000 and recovered ₹2,00,000, no
other advances or deviation items at market rates.

| | ₹ |
|---|---|
| C, work done in the quarter | 48,00,000 |
| F, secured advance (4,00,000 − 2,00,000) | 2,00,000 |
| M = C + F | 50,00,000 |
| W = 0.85 × M | 42,50,000 |

Schedule F: cement 10%, labour 25%, steel 15%. Index changes since the base date: cement 140 → 147 (+5%), unskilled
wage ₹700 → ₹735 (+5%), steel 150 → 144 (−4%).

VW = 42,50,000 × (10 × 5% + 25 × 5% − 15 × 4%) ÷ 100 = 42,50,000 × 1.15 ÷ 100 = **₹48,875** payable for the quarter.

Steel's fall reduces the escalation: the clause works both ways.

## When is escalation paid?

Quarterly, on the bills paid in the three calendar months of each quarter, with the date the contractor submitted each
bill deciding which quarter it falls in. The first payment is made three months after the month in which the
commencement letter is issued; the last period may be shorter than three months, ending on completion.

## Can escalation reduce what the contractor is paid?

Yes. If prices or wages fall, the cost of work is adjusted downward by the same formula and the amount is deducted.

## What is the difference between clause 10C and clause 10CC?

Clause 10C pays (or recovers) only price changes caused directly by a new law, statutory rule or order after the
tender date, such as a change in minimum wages, and not changes in GST rates. Clause 10CC follows market indices.
A contract has one or the other, as Schedule F says.

## What should a contractor's system do for escalation?

- Hold the base date, the Schedule F percentages and the base indices for each contract.
- Group bills by quarter on their submission date, and separate secured advance, other advances and Clause 12 items.
- Record the quarter's indices and work out VW, ready to claim.
- Stop the calculation for work done in a delay not justified under Clause 5.

The [construction demo](/industries/construction-company) builds [RA bills](/construction/ra-bills) from
measurements against the BOQ, but doesn't calculate price escalation; a 10CC claim worked out from the same bills and
the published indices would be a part we'd build. Its "escalation" means chasing overdue payments, not this clause.
For how measured work becomes those bills, see the [measurement book](/construction/measurement-book).

title: Prompt payment acts: how fast contractors must be paid
question: How quickly must an owner pay a contractor, and a contractor pay its subs, under prompt payment laws?

On federal jobs a progress payment is due 14 days after a proper request and subs are paid within 7 days of the prime. In Texas a private owner pays within 35 days and the contractor pays subs within 7; California sets 30 days and 7; New York 30 days after approval and 7. Late money carries interest, often 1% to 2% a month.

body:
## What is a prompt payment act?

A prompt payment act is a law that sets how quickly an owner must pay its contractor, and each contractor its subs
and suppliers, and what is owed when a payment is late. The federal government has one for its own contracts, and
many states have their own, some for public jobs only and some for private jobs too. The contract usually sets the
billing cycle; the act puts a ceiling on how long payment can take and adds interest or a penalty after it.

## How fast must the federal government pay a contractor?

Within 14 days after the designated billing office receives a proper payment request for a progress payment, under
FAR 52.232-27 and the Prompt Payment Act (31 U.S.C. 3903); interest runs on an approved payment left unpaid after
that. The prime must pay its subs for satisfactory work within 7 days of being paid (31 U.S.C. 3905), and the
subcontract must say so.

## What are the deadlines in Texas, California, New York and Florida?

| State | Owner pays the contractor | Contractor pays its subs | If late |
|---|---|---|---|
| Texas, private | 35 days after a written payment request (Property Code 28.002) | 7 days after receiving the owner's payment | 1.5% a month (28.004) |
| Texas, public | Overdue on the 31st day after the later of delivery, completion or invoice (Government Code 2251.021) | 10 days after receiving payment (2251.022) | As chapter 2251 sets |
| California, private | 30 days after notice demanding payment, unless agreed otherwise in writing (Civil Code 8800) | 7 days after each progress payment, unless agreed otherwise in writing (Business and Professions Code 7108.5) | 2% a month, owner and contractor alike |
| New York, private, $150,000 and up | Approve or reject within 12 business days; pay within 30 days of approval (General Business Law 756-a) | 7 days after receiving good funds, once documents and waivers are in | As article 35-E sets |
| Florida, private | When the contract says, once the request, payment from above and waivers are in (Statutes 715.12) | Same rule, once the contractor has been paid for that work | Statutory rate plus 12% a year, from the 14th day after due |
| Florida, public | Undisputed portion by the contract date or 20 business days after the request, whichever is earlier (255.073) | 10 days after the contractor is paid; 7 days for a sub paying its subs | As the statute sets |

These are the main payment deadlines only; each act has its own exceptions, definitions and project thresholds.

## Can an owner hold back part of a payment?

Yes, for a good-faith dispute, but only so much. In California an owner may withhold no more than 150% of the
disputed amount from a progress payment, and a contractor the same from its sub. In Texas the withholding in a
good-faith dispute is capped at the difference in dispute (110% of it on detached homes up to a quadruplex). In New
York an owner who rejects part of an invoice must say in writing which items aren't approved and why.

## How is interest on a late payment worked out?

At the statute's rate, from the day after the payment was due. A $43,200 progress payment on a Texas private job,
due 35 days after the request and paid a month late, carries 1.5% for that month: $648. In California the same
amount wrongfully withheld for a month costs the owner 2%, $864. Florida's private-job rate is the statutory judgment
rate plus 12% a year, starting 14 days after the payment was due.

## Can a contractor stop work if it isn't paid?

In some states, after notice. In Texas a contractor or sub may suspend work on the 10th day after giving the owner
(and the lender, where required) written notice that an undisputed payment hasn't been received; that right doesn't
apply to single-family homes up to a quadruplex or to public jobs. In New York a contract clause saying a party can't
suspend work when the other doesn't pay promptly is void (General Business Law 757).

## Do prompt payment rules cover retainage?

Usually, with their own deadlines. In California the owner pays retention within 45 days after completion and the
contractor passes each sub's share on within 10 days of receiving it (Civil Code 8812, 8814); in New York retainage is
released within 30 days of final approval. See [retainage](/construction/retainage) for each state's caps.

## Can the contract override the prompt payment law?

Partly, and less than most contractors think. California's 30-day and 7-day rules give way to a different written
agreement; Texas makes an attempted waiver of chapter 28 void, apart from a longer period allowed on single-family
homes; in New York the contract governs except where the article says otherwise, and payment terms that differ from
its payment sections are void. Read the contract's payment clause against the state's act before signing.

## What should a contractor track to enforce prompt payment?

The dates the law counts from, per pay application: when the request was delivered, when it was approved, when the
owner paid, and when each sub was paid from it. With those, the system can flag a late payment, work out the
interest, and show that you paid your own subs on time, which matters when you are the one being chased.

- The date each [pay application](/construction/pay-applications) was submitted and approved.
- Payments received against each application, and payments made to each sub from it.
- The state of the project, so the right deadline and rate apply.
- Disputed items, with the written reason, kept apart from undisputed amounts.

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), receivables are aged from the due date (not due,
1–30, 31–60, 61–90, over 90 days), each overdue bill becomes a weekly follow-up for its project manager, and anything
past 30 days goes to the director. It doesn't work out statutory interest or track the deadline for paying each sub;
those are parts we'd build. Missed deadlines also matter for liens: see
[mechanics lien deadlines](/construction/mechanics-lien-deadlines).

title: RA bills: deductions, advances and the final bill
question: What is an RA bill in construction, what is deducted from it, and how are advances and the final bill handled?
answer: A running account (RA) bill is a contractor's interim bill for work measured so far, paid as an advance against the final bill while the work goes on. Each is drawn from the measurement book, to date less earlier bills, with GST on top and deductions taken off: security deposit (2.5% of each bill on CPWD works), TDS, GST TDS on government work, and recovery of any mobilisation or secured advance. The final bill closes the contract.

body:
## What is an RA bill?

A running account (RA) bill is an interim bill for the work measured so far, paid while the work continues; the
final bill closes the contract. On an item-rate contract the contractor is paid by measured quantity at the agreed
rate for each BOQ item, so the work is billed in stages: the 1st RA bill, the 2nd, and so on. CPWD's general
conditions treat every such payment as an advance against the final payment, so an RA bill doesn't mean the work has
been accepted. Most private contracts in India follow the same pattern, with the rates and deductions their own
contract sets.

## How is an RA bill calculated?

From the [measurement book](/construction/measurement-book), cumulatively: the value of all work measured to date at
the agreement rates, plus approved extra and deviated items, less the gross of all earlier bills. The deductions are
then taken from this bill's value.

| Line | Example (made up) |
|---|---|
| Value of work done to date, item by item at agreement rates | ₹48,00,000 |
| Add: extra and deviated items approved | ₹1,50,000 |
| Gross value to date | ₹49,50,000 |
| Less: gross of previous RA bills | ₹31,00,000 |
| **Gross value of this bill** | **₹18,50,000** |

## Which works are paid by RA bills on CPWD contracts?

Works estimated to cost more than ₹20 lakh. Under Clause 7 of CPWD's General Conditions of Contract 2023, a work
estimated at ₹20 lakh or less is paid only after the whole work is completed and the completion certificate given.
Bigger works are billed monthly on recorded measurements, on the date the Engineer-in-Charge fixes, and a bill is due
only once the work done since the last one reaches the minimum set in the contract's Schedule F.

## What is deducted from an RA bill?

Up to five things, each set by the contract or the law:

- **Security deposit (retention money):** a percentage of each bill held until the defects period ends.
- **Income-tax TDS** at 1% or 2%: see [TDS on payments to contractors](/construction/tds-on-contractor-payments).
- **GST TDS**, when the client is a government department or agency: 1% CGST plus 1% SGST; see
  [GST on works contracts](/construction/gst-on-works-contracts).
- **Recovery of advances:** mobilisation advance with its interest, and secured advance once the material is used.
- **Recoveries for materials the client issued**, water, electricity, and any penalties the contract allows.

## How much security deposit is deducted from an RA bill?

On CPWD works, 2.5% of the gross amount of each running and final bill, until 2.5% of the tendered amount has been
held (GCC Clause 1A). On a ₹2 crore work that is ₹5 lakh in all; a ₹18,50,000 bill gives up ₹46,250. Private
contracts usually call it retention money and set their own rate. CPWD lets the deposit be released against a bank
guarantee from a scheduled bank once at least ₹5 lakh has built up.

## When is the security deposit refunded?

After the defect liability period, or once the final bill is passed, whichever is later. Under GCC Clause 17 that
period is 12 months after the completion certificate, or 6 months for works costing ₹10 lakh or less (except road
works); the contractor must make good defects that appear in it, and the department can pay for them from the
deposit. Clause 1 and the release of security deposit have been amended by CPWD circulars since 2023; check the
contract's own GCC version.

## What is a mobilisation advance, and how is it recovered?

An advance to set up the work (site office, labour camp, testing lab, godown, plant and machinery, shuttering), up to
10% of the tendered amount, when the contract provides for it. Under GCC Clause 10B it's asked for in writing within
six months of the order to start, paid in instalments of no more than 5% each (the next only after the last is shown
to be used), and carries simple interest at 8% a year. Recovery starts once 10% of the work's gross value has been
executed and paid, in proportion to each bill, so that all of it is back by the time 80% has been executed and paid.

On a ₹2 crore work with a ₹20 lakh advance, recovery runs over the ₹1.4 crore of work between 10% and 80%: 14.29% of
each bill's gross value. Interest is charged on the amount still outstanding up to each recovery.

## What is a secured advance?

An advance on materials brought to site for work not yet done: up to 75% of the assessed value of materials that are
non-perishable, non-fragile and non-combustible, properly stored and not yet built in (GCC Clause 10B). When the
material is used in the work, the advance is recovered from the next payment. It isn't paid on high-risk materials
such as ordinary glass, sand, petrol or diesel; perishable or fragile materials qualify only with insurance and the
Engineer-in-Charge's approval. Cement and steel on site assessed at ₹4,00,000 give an advance of ₹3,00,000, recovered
in full from the bill in which they are built in.

## What does a full RA bill look like with every deduction?

RA bill #3 on a made-up ₹2 crore CPWD-style work, contractor a company, client a government department:

| Line | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Gross value of this bill | 18,50,000 |
| Add GST at 18% (the contractor's tax invoice) | 3,33,000 |
| **Invoice value** | **21,83,000** |
| Less security deposit, 2.5% of the gross | 46,250 |
| Less mobilisation advance recovered (14.29% of the gross) | 2,64,286 |
| Less interest on the advance outstanding (₹18,42,857 × 8% × 31 days) | 12,521 |
| Less income-tax TDS at 2% on the value excluding GST | 37,000 |
| Less GST TDS, 1% CGST + 1% SGST | 37,000 |
| **Net payable** | **17,85,943** |

The figures are made up; the days of interest are illustrative. Recovery of the advance started on bill #2, so
₹1,57,143 of it had already come back.

## How soon must an RA bill be paid?

On CPWD works, at least 75% of the net bill as an ad-hoc payment within 10 working days of submission, and the rest
after final checking within 28 working days (GCC Clause 7). If a bill that's in order isn't paid within 45 days of
submission, the department pays simple interest at 5% a year from the end of the time limit. On the bill above, the
ad-hoc payment is at least ₹13,39,457.

For a private client: if you're a registered micro or small enterprise, the MSMED Act caps the agreed credit period
at 45 days from acceptance; see the [MSME payment rule](/systems/msme-payment-rule).

## When must the final bill be submitted and paid?

Within three months of physical completion, or one month of the final completion certificate, whichever is earlier
(GCC Clause 9). Once it's submitted, no further claims can be made: they are treated as waived. The undisputed items,
and disputed ones at the approved quantity and rate, are paid within three months of the bill being received, with
5% a year interest if the department is late on a bill submitted in time. Work completed on 15 January 2027 with the
final certificate on 10 March 2027 needs its final bill by 10 April 2027.

## Can I get paid before the work is measured?

Sometimes. The CPWD manual allows advance payments on a running bill for work measured but not yet checked, or done
but not yet measured, on conditions, adjusted when the measurements are recorded. GCC Clause 7 also lets the
Engineer-in-Charge pay 75% of the assessed value of a building floor's work up to lintel or slab level without
detailed measurement, adjusted in the next bill.

## What should a contractor's system track on RA bills?

- The BOQ with agreement rates, and each RA bill taken from the measurements, never typed totals.
- Every bill cumulative, so this bill is always to date less previous.
- Each deduction by type across bills: security deposit held, advances still to recover with their interest, TDS and
  GST TDS deducted.
- Extra and deviated items kept apart until approved, so they're billed once.
- Due dates for the ad-hoc payment, the balance and the final bill, and the refund date of the security deposit.

The [construction demo](/industries/construction-company) builds each RA bill from measurements against the BOQ
(previous, this bill and up to date per line, the GST split and the amount in words, as a PDF), moves it from draft
to submitted, certified and paid, and flags quantities beyond the BOQ. It doesn't yet take security deposit, TDS,
GST TDS or advance recoveries off the bill, or produce a separate final bill; those are parts we'd build.

body:
## What is retainage in construction?

Retainage (also called retention) is part of each progress payment that the owner holds back until the job is
finished, as security that the contractor completes the work and fixes defects. Each
[pay application](/construction/pay-applications) bills the work completed and stored to date, takes off the
retainage percentage, and the balance is paid. The amount held builds up over the job and is paid at the end. The
general contractor usually holds the same percentage from each subcontractor, so retainage runs down the whole chain.

## How much retainage is normal?

Often 5% or 10% of each payment, as the contract sets it, and less where the state caps it. Some contracts lower the
rate later in the job; federal rules allow the amount withheld to be adjusted as the contract nears completion. Agree
the rate before the job starts and read the contract's retainage clause before you sign it.

A made-up $400,000 job at 10%, at the end of month three:

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Work completed to date | $160,000 |
| Materials stored on site | $8,000 |
| Total completed and stored | $168,000 |
| Less retainage at 10% | $16,800 |
| Total earned less retainage | $151,200 |
| Less previous certificates | $108,000 |
| **Current payment due** | **$43,200** |

Over the whole job, $40,000 waits for the end, often months after the work it covers. The same job under a California
private contract signed in 2026 could hold at most 5%: $8,400 at this point and $20,000 over the job.

## Which states cap retainage, and at what rate?

California, New York, Texas and Florida each have rules, in different shapes:

| State | Private jobs | Public jobs | Release |
|---|---|---|---|
| California | 5% of each payment and 5% of the contract price in total, for contracts signed from 1 January 2026 (Civil Code 8811); not on residential projects of four stories or fewer that aren't mixed-use | 5% (Public Contract Code 7201) | Owner pays within 45 days after completion (Civil Code 8812) |
| New York | 5% of the contract sum on projects of $150,000 or more (General Business Law 756, 756-c, 757) | Not covered by these sections | Within 30 days after final approval; 1% a month interest if late |
| Texas | The owner must reserve 10% until 30 days after completion, for lien claimants (Property Code 53.101); the contract's own retainage is separate | 10% under $5 million, 5% at $5 million or more (Government Code 2252.032) | As the contract says; payment requests are due within 35 days (Property Code 28.002) |
| Florida | As the contract says | 5% of each payment on contracts over $200,000 (Statutes 255.078) | Same time limits as any payment request |

For any other state, read that state's own statute for where the project is. In New York, a private contract clause
asking for more than 5% is void under General Business Law 757.

## What are the rules on federal jobs?

Federal contracting officers pay in full when progress is satisfactory and may hold back up to 10% only when it isn't
(FAR 52.232-5). FAR 32.103 adds that retainage "should not be used as a substitute for good contract management". At
substantial completion the officer keeps only what protects the Government and releases the rest; retained amounts are
due as the contract says or, if it's silent, 30 days after the officer approves their release (FAR 52.232-27).

## When must retainage be released?

When the contract says, and no later than the state's deadline. In California the owner must pay the retention within
45 days after the work is completed; in New York within 30 days after final approval of the work; on federal jobs
within 30 days of the contracting officer approving release when the contract is silent. Release usually needs
paperwork first: final [lien waivers](/construction/lien-waivers), closeout documents and a finished punch list.

## Can the owner keep retainage for punch-list items or a dispute?

Only a limited amount. In California, if there is a good-faith dispute, the owner may withhold no more than 150% of the
disputed amount from final payment. On the $400,000 job with $20,000 retained and $3,000 of punch-list work disputed,
the owner may hold $4,500 and must pay the other $15,500 within 45 days of completion.

## Can a GC hold more retainage from a sub than the owner holds from the GC?

Not in California or New York: a subcontract's retainage percentage can't exceed the one in the owner's contract with
the GC. On federal jobs the prime contractor must pay subs for satisfactory work within 7 days of being paid (31 U.S.C.
3905), and the subcontract may permit retainage on the sub as agreed.

## What happens if the owner pays late?

The owner owes interest or a penalty at the rate the state sets. In Texas an unpaid amount bears interest at 1.5% a
month, so a $43,200 payment made a month late costs the owner $648. In California an owner who wrongfully withholds a
progress payment owes 2% a month; in New York, retainage released late carries 1% a month.

## Does retainage apply to stored materials?

Yes on a standard pay application: retainage is taken on the total completed and stored, so stored materials carry it
too. Texas caps the rate on public jobs per line of the schedule of values, "including materials and equipment
delivered on site to be installed".

## How should a contractor track retainage?

Per job and per subcontractor, from the pay applications, never as one figure in the books:

- **Retainage receivable** is money you've billed and earned but can't collect yet. It sits inside "billed to date" on
  the [WIP schedule](/construction/wip-schedule); cash collected doesn't include it.
- **Retainage payable** is what you hold from each sub, released on the same terms once the owner pays you.
- **Release dates**: completion, final approval and the state's deadline, so a late release is chased with interest.
- **Release paperwork**: lien waivers, closeout documents and the punch list, tracked per job.

The [construction demo](/industries/construction-company)'s US build holds retainage on every pay application, on
work completed and stored materials, at a rate set per application. It doesn't yet bill a retainage release or track
retainage held from subcontractors; those are parts we'd build for a contractor.

body:
## What replaced section 194C?

Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025: TDS on payments to contractors is now serial number 6 of the table in
that section, "Payments to contractors, fees for professional and technical services, etc." The 2025 Act replaced
the Income-tax Act, 1961 from 1 April 2026, so payments made from that date are reported under section 393, not
194C. Older documents, such as the CPWD Works Manual 2022, still refer to section 194C.

## What is the TDS rate on payments to contractors?

1% when the contractor is an individual or a Hindu undivided family (HUF), and 2% for any other contractor (a
company, firm or LLP), under Table serial 6(i). The contractor's status, from its PAN, sets the rate.

| Paid to | Rate | On a ₹5,00,000 bill |
|---|---|---|
| A proprietor (individual) or HUF | 1% | ₹5,000 |
| A company, firm or LLP | 2% | ₹10,000 |

## When does TDS apply to a contractor payment?

When a single payment exceeds ₹30,000, or the payments to that contractor in the year add up to more than ₹1,00,000.
Payments to a subcontractor of ₹25,000, ₹28,000, ₹32,000 and ₹20,000 run to ₹25,000, ₹53,000, ₹85,000 and ₹1,05,000:
the third payment is over ₹30,000 on its own, and the fourth takes the year past ₹1,00,000. How the earlier payments
are treated once the total crosses the limit is a question for your adviser.

## Who has to deduct TDS from a contractor?

A "designated person", as section 402 of the Act defines it for serial 6(i): the Central or a State Government, local
authorities, corporations set up by law, companies, co-operative societies, housing and development authorities,
registered societies, trusts, universities, foreign governments and enterprises, firms, and individuals, HUFs and
others whose sales, gross receipts or turnover in the previous year was over ₹1 crore (business) or ₹50 lakh
(profession).

Other individuals and HUFs deduct under serial 6(ii) instead: 2% on payments for work, but only once their payments
in the year pass ₹50 lakh.

| Payer | Contractor | Rate | Deduct when |
|---|---|---|---|
| A designated person | Individual or HUF | 1% | One payment over ₹30,000, or the year's total over ₹1,00,000 |
| A designated person | Anyone else | 2% | Same limits |
| An individual or HUF not otherwise required to deduct | Any contractor | 2% | Payments for work over ₹50 lakh in the year |

## What counts as "work" for contractor TDS?

Any work under a contract, including supplying labour to carry it out. The Act's definition also brings in
advertising, broadcasting and telecasting, carriage of goods or passengers by any mode other than rail, catering, and
making or supplying a product to a customer's specification with material bought from that customer. Making a product
to specification with material bought from someone else isn't work for this purpose; that is a purchase of goods.

## Does a main contractor deduct TDS from its subcontractors?

Yes, the same way, if it is a designated person: 1% or 2% on each subcontractor's bills once the limits are crossed.
The main contractor suffers TDS on its own bills from the client and deducts it from what it pays its subs; each claims
credit for what was deducted from it.

## Is TDS deducted on the GST part of the bill?

It depends on the guidance under the Act, so confirm with your adviser whether to deduct on the bill's value with or
without the GST shown separately on the invoice, and set your system to match.

## How does TDS sit on an RA bill?

It's deducted from each [running account bill](/construction/ra-bills) at the rate in the table, on the bill's value.
On a ₹18,50,000 RA bill to a company contractor, income-tax TDS at 2% is ₹37,000. A government client may also deduct
GST TDS of ₹37,000 (1% CGST + 1% SGST) from the same bill; that is a separate deduction under the GST law, covered in
[GST on works contracts](/construction/gst-on-works-contracts).

## What happens after TDS is deducted?

The payer deposits it, reports it in its TDS statement and gives the contractor a certificate; the contractor claims
credit for it against its own tax. Check the deposit and filing dates for the year in the rules under the 2025 Act.

## Did the rates change in 2026?

The rates and limits above are read from the table in section 393 as enacted. Rates can be changed by a Finance Act,
so check the table as amended for the year you pay in.

## What should a contractor's system do for TDS?

- Hold each contractor's PAN and status (individual or HUF, or other), which sets the rate.
- Track payments to each contractor through the year, so the ₹1,00,000 total is caught on the bill that crosses it.
- Deduct on the base your adviser confirms, and show TDS as its own line on the
  [measurement-based bill](/construction/measurement-book).
- Record TDS clients deduct from your own bills, so the credit can be matched before you file.
- Produce the deposit and return data per contractor, and the certificate each one needs.

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company), the monthly wage register deducts 1% TDS from
subcontractors' wages once they pass the limits, and the TDS register lists deductions by quarter with deposit and
return dates; the return itself stays in Tally. The demo still labels these deductions "194C", and it doesn't yet
record TDS that clients deduct from the contractor's own RA bills; those are changes we'd make.

title: The WIP schedule: over and under billing, explained
question: What is a WIP schedule in construction, and how is over or under billing worked out?
answer: A WIP (work-in-progress) schedule lists every open job with its contract value, estimated total cost, cost to date, percent complete and billings to date. Percent complete is cost to date over estimated total cost; earned revenue is that share of the contract value. Billed more than earned is overbilling, less is underbilling. Banks and surety companies read it to judge a contractor's jobs, and it's the earliest warning of a job losing money.

body:
## What is a WIP schedule?

A WIP (work-in-progress) schedule is a monthly list of every open job showing what each has earned against what it
has billed. One row per job:

| Column | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| Contract value | Original contract plus approved [change orders](/construction/change-orders) |
| Estimated total cost | The current estimate to complete the job, reviewed by the project manager |
| Estimated gross profit | Contract value less estimated total cost |
| Cost to date | Job cost posted so far: labor, material, subcontractors, equipment |
| Percent complete | Cost to date ÷ estimated total cost |
| Earned revenue | Contract value × percent complete |
| Billed to date | Total of the [pay applications](/construction/pay-applications), including [retainage](/construction/retainage) |
| Over or under billing | Billed to date less earned revenue |

## How do you calculate percent complete?

Divide cost to date by the estimated total cost: the cost-to-cost method. It is the same comparison the federal tax
law uses for the percentage of completion method, which compares costs incurred before the end of the year "with the
estimated total contract costs" (26 U.S.C. 460). A job with $170,000 spent of an estimated $340,000 is 50% complete.

## How do you work out over and under billing?

Earned revenue is contract value times percent complete; billed to date less earned revenue is the over or under
billing. Two made-up jobs at the end of a month:

| | Job A | Job B |
|---|---|---|
| Contract value | $400,000 | $250,000 |
| Estimated total cost | $340,000 | $215,000 |
| Cost to date | $170,000 | $129,000 |
| Percent complete | 50% | 60% |
| Earned revenue | $200,000 | $150,000 |
| Billed to date | $230,000 | $120,000 |
| **Over (under) billing** | **$30,000 over** | **$30,000 under** |

## What is overbilling, and is it bad?

Overbilling is billing ahead of the work earned: Job A has billed $30,000 more than it has earned, so its cash is
ahead and that money is owed back in work. Some overbilling is normal, since a schedule of values often bills set-up
and early items ahead. A large overbilling without the cash to match it can mean the cash was spent elsewhere, which is
what a surety looks for.

## What is underbilling?

Underbilling is work earned but not yet billed: Job B has done $30,000 more work than it has billed. It is often slow
billing or [change orders](/construction/change-orders) not yet approved, and sometimes cost that will never be billed
because the job is losing money.

## Where do over and under billings go on the balance sheet?

Overbillings are usually shown as a liability (billings in excess of costs and estimated earnings) and underbillings
as an asset (costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings). The totals on the WIP schedule, $30,000 each in the
example, should tie to the balance sheet; your accountant decides the presentation under the accounting standard you
report under.

## Why does the estimate to complete matter most?

Because percent complete depends on it. If Job A's estimate is stale and the real figure is $380,000, the job is about
45% complete, has earned $178,947 and is overbilled by $51,053, with less profit left than the schedule said. A WIP
schedule is only as good as the monthly re-estimate on each job, which is why sureties ask who makes it and how.

## What is profit fade?

Profit fade is a job's estimated gross profit falling from month to month as the estimate to complete grows. Job A
showed $60,000 of gross profit last month ($400,000 less $340,000). This month the project manager raises the estimated
total cost to $360,000: gross profit is now $40,000, a $20,000 fade, and the same $170,000 of cost makes the job 47%
complete, so earned revenue drops to $188,889 and the overbilling grows to $41,111.

## Why do sureties and banks ask for a WIP schedule?

It shows, job by job, whether the company is making the margin it bid and whether its billing is ahead of or behind
the work. The SBA's surety bond program asks for it on its own form: "Small businesses seeking a surety bond use this
form to list any work they're currently performing" (SBA Form 994F, Schedule of Work in Process). Lenders and sureties
look for:

- Jobs whose estimated gross profit fell since last month.
- Large underbillings, which may be costs that will never be billed.
- Large overbillings without the cash to match.
- Whether the schedule ties to the financial statements.

## Do small contractors have to use percentage of completion for taxes?

Not for every job. The federal rule exempts a construction contract the contractor expects to finish within 2 years,
if its average annual gross receipts for the 3 prior years pass the section 448(c) test: $32 million for tax years
beginning in 2026 (Revenue Procedure 2025-32). Residential construction contracts have their own exception. A
contractor with $18 million of average receipts and a 14-month job may use another method for that job; one with $40
million may not. Your tax adviser decides the method.

## Does retainage count as billed?

Yes. Billed to date includes the retainage held on each pay application; cash collected doesn't. A job can be
underbilled on the WIP schedule and still short of cash, because part of what it billed is retainage waiting for the
end of the job.

## How is the cost of each job built up?

From every cost posted to the job as it happens: labor from the field's time records at each person's cost rate,
material issued to the job at its purchase price, subcontractor bills, equipment (owned equipment at a day or hour
rate, rented equipment at its invoice) and job-site expenses. Head office costs stay out unless the contract
reimburses them. The WIP schedule's cost to date is this total, so a cost posted to the wrong job moves two rows at
once: one job looks more complete and the other less.

In the [construction demo](/industries/construction-company)'s US build, each job's cost to date on the director
dashboard is material used, labor from attendance and pay, site cash spent and equipment days, set against the value
of approved work; once 5% of the work is done it projects the final cost at the same cost rate and marks the job on
track, over budget or losing money. Subcontractor bills aren't added to a job's cost yet.

## How often should a WIP schedule be updated?

Monthly, at the same close as the books, with a fresh estimate to complete from each project manager. Post every cost
to a job and cost code as it happens (time from the field, material receipts, subcontractor bills) and produce the WIP
schedule from the same records as the pay applications, so the month-end WIP is a report, not a spreadsheet
assembled from four places.

The [construction demo](/industries/construction-company) shows the inputs per site (contract value, value of
approved work, billed, cost to date and margin against the estimate) but has no WIP schedule: no estimate to complete
and no over and under billing column. A WIP schedule built from those records is something we'd build for a
contractor. See also [WIP tracking for job shops](/manufacturing/wip-tracking) for the manufacturing side.
